News.title: Why is Black Friday called Black Friday? Everything you need to know about the shopping bonanza
News.content:
Next

BLACK Friday is almost upon us once again, with Brits ready to flock to stores for Christmas bargains.

The history of the term has long been disputed though, here, we explain what it’s all about.

Why is Black Friday called Black Friday?

The story behind the name Black Friday is disputed.



Some say that the day is so named as it is the day retailers “move into the black”, meaning they can cover their costs through the years whilst also slashing prices for the sales.



Historically, in UK Black Friday referred to the Friday before Christmas, when extra pressure was put on the police and emergency services, due to festive celebrations.

But since 2014, Black Friday has come to refer to the massive shopping sales event.

Black Friday always falls on the Friday following the Thanksgiving holiday in the USA, and is considered of the Christmas shopping season.



Now, in the UK, retailers including Amazon, John Lewis, and Sainsbury’s offer discounts on Black Friday.

What is Black Friday?

In a bid to attract shoppers in the run-up to Christmas, retailers offer majorly discounted prices on products, throughout the Black Friday weekend.

However, Black Friday has grown into a two-week shopping event, as retailers compete to attract customers.

Many deals will be available online, so shoppers can avoid the long lines and crowded high-streets.



Most Brits shop for Black Friday bargains online, but some prefer to visit physical shops.

This has previously caused chaos on shop floors.

News.title: Labour’s 1.5million homes pledge branded ‘fantasy’ as housebuilding hits ten-year low
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’s housing pledge was branded a “fantasy” last night as the number of new homes fell to a ten-year low.

Just 203,690 homes were added to England’s housing stock in 2025/26 – down two per cent on the previous year, official figures show.



It deals a fresh blow to Labour’s promise to deliver 1.5 million new homes by the end of this Parliament.

Some 300,000 homes a year would need to be delivered on average to hit the target.



Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has already admitted there is only a slim chance of meeting the pledge amid rising construction costs and the fallout from the Iran war.

Sam Richards, of campaign group Britain Remade, said the target was “looking like a fantasy”, adding: “Ministers cannot hide behind global events as an excuse for their failure to deliver.”



A Housing Department spokesman insisted the Government was “not giving up” on its target.

Prices of new-build homes will be slashed by up to £50,000 through a proposed Tory war on red tape.

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith is vowing a blitz on bureaucracy and Net Zero regulations to halt low growth.

Proposals also include backing a third Heathrow runway and scrapping a £1.5billion grocery packaging tax to ease the cost of the weekly shop.



Mr Griffith said: “No one else is coming to save our economy. Only we can inject reality, tell the hard truths and make this a country we are proud to hand on to the next generation.”

The £50,000 price cut for new builds will partly come from scrapping rules such as the Future Homes Standard on reducing carbon emissions.

They make developers include low-carbon technology, such as heat pumps or district heat networks.

News.title: ‘Loud boom’ heard as flight declares emergency over Scotland and emergency crews race to Edinburgh Airport
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FLIGHT DRAMA ‘Loud boom’ heard as flight declares emergency over Scotland and emergency crews race to Edinburgh Airport







Next

A SCOTTISH flight declared an emergency after a deafening bang was heard above a major city.

An EasyJet plane bound for Gatwick left Edinburgh at around 9pm on Thursday night, but shortly after take-off, local residents heard an ‘explosion’ sound overhead.

It is understood the sound, captured on doorbell camera footage which has been shared across social media, indicated an engine failure.

The Airbus A321neo issued a 7700squawk notice, which is code for a general emergency, not long after leaving the ground.





The Aircraft Communications Addressing and Reporting System (ACARS) issued warnings of an engine stall and high exhaust gas temperatures.

The plane’s left engine was reportedly shut down when the aircraft remained at around 5,000 feet.

Emergency crews, including cops and fire crews rushed to the area, and sealed off several roads.

The aircraft circled the area several times before landing safely at Edinburgh Airport.

EasyJet was contacted for comment.

News.title: Huge troop of monkeys ‘take over’ parts of world famous tourist attraction as visitors attacked
News.content:
Next

A RIOTOUS troop of monkeys has overrun swathes of a world-famous landmark amid a string of tourist attacks.

Astonishing footage revealed the scale of the intrusion, with dozens of primates leaping across the grounds mere metres from visitors at India’s Taj Mahal.



But as the monkeys run rampant, attacks have become more frequent.

In September, two visitors – including an 83-year-old Brazilian tourist – were bitted at the iconic landmark and rushed to hospital.



Weeks later Brit tourist Suzanne Ann Barrett was bitten on the hand near the Royal Gate.

She was also transported to hospital.

In August Ayansh, 6, was bitten on the hand near the Mehman Khana on the eastern side of the Taj Mahal complex.

A tourist from South Korea was left with a bleeding hand after being bitten near the eastern gate in July and was rushed to hospital via ambulance.



In a separate clip from a few months ago a troop of monkeys could be seen washing themselves at a water fountain within the Taj Mahal premises.

These incidents are just the latest in a string of attacks renewing tourist safety concerns at the monument, which has increasingly become a hangout for the sometimes-aggressive animals.

Authorities claim to be remedying the problem yet it persists.

Agra Municipal Corporation is responsible for catching the monkeys, while the ASI oversees visitor safety and facilities inside the complex.

Local media cites a lack of coordination among the departments managing the site as further complicating efforts to tackle the issue.



While first-aid facilities are available on site, the repeated incidents have raised questions about when a permanent solution to the monkey problem will be implemented.

According to the landmark’s official website, the Taj Mahal attracts between seven to eight million visitors per year.

It comes as a seven-year-old boy was mauled to death by his pet monkey in Thailand last year.

Ekkarat Srichan had been playing outside his home in Thailand when the crazed monkey – called Choke – pounced on him.

Neighbours said they heard blood-chilling screams as Choke ripped into the schoolchild.



Family members raced to the horror scene to find the youngster covered in bites and the fangs of the family’s pet monkey dripping with blood.

Ekkarat was still alive when his devastated relatives found him and rushed him to Sichon Hospital.

But the seven-year-old later died of his wounds on June 6.

News.title: Doc claims gran declared dead then discovered ALIVE in hospital mortuary before dying again had ‘low chance of survival’
News.content:
Next

A GRAN who was wrongly declared dead and woke up alive in a hospital mortuary before later dying had an “extremely low” chance of survival, a doctor has said.

Olive Martin was making toast in her home, where she lived with her husband Kevin, when she suddenly suffered a seizure and collapsed.



Paramedics attended and declared her dead at the scene before taking the 54-year-old to Darlington Hospital Mortuary rather than A&E.

Olive tragically died from brain damage shortly after staff found she was still alive following the horrifying ordeal back in October 2023.



Now a pre-inquest review hearing heard expert witness Dr Samy Sadek claim her chances of surviving were slim by the time staff discovered she wasn’t dead.

Area coroner Crispin Oliver, discussing a report from Dr Samy Sadek, told the hearing: “[Dr Sadek] says that Olive’s chances of survival by the time she was discovered were extremely low.”

Mr Oliver also confirmed failings in Olive’s pre-hospital care had been admitted.

He described the “extremely distressing event” in which the grandmother regained consciousness, Chronicle Live reports.

The latest assessment comes after questions were raised at an earlier hearing over whether her death could have been prevented.

At a pre-inquest hearing in December 2025, the family’s barrister Tom Barclay-Semple questioned whether there had been a window of opportunity to save her life.



He said: “If Olive had been treated in the way she should have and taken to hospital, would the outcome have been different?

“There is a credible argument to say there was a window of opportunity where Olive received no treatment at all.

“It was clear that there was a real and immediate risk to her life. (Her life) was in the hands of paramedics.”

Olive had been making toast at her home in Darlington, where she lived with her husband Kevin, when she suffered a seizure and collapsed.

She had put bread in the toaster as she prepared to go to work that day.



But emergency crews responding to the incident took her to Darlington Hospital rather than its A&E department.

Staff were stunned to discover she was still alive, with evidence later revealing she had responded to stimuli, including verbally and by gripping.

She had suffered brain damage and tragically died a short time later.

The family’s representative previously told the hearing that around two hours had passed during which Olive received “no treatment at all”.

The latest hearing took place at Crook Coroners Court before area coroner Crispin Oliver.



Five members of Olive’s family attended, alongside representatives from Durham Constabulary and the North East Ambulance Service.

A preliminary hearing is expected to take place in the Spring, when Dr Sadek is due to give his full evidence and the inquest may conclude.

The date and time will be confirmed at a further hearing next Thursday, December 3.

Durham Constabulary concluded its investigation in 2024 without bringing any criminal charges.

The Care Quality Commission also launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding her death.



Olive’s heartbroken family previously paid tribute to the grandmother, describing her as having an “infectious personality”.

They said: “Our mam will always be remembered for her kind heart, her infectious personality and her positivity day in and day out.

“She was our warrior, and she will be deeply missed by every person she has ever met.

“We would request privacy at this difficult time.”

News.title: Sex offender Huw Edwards whines about ‘difficulties’ in ‘woe-is-me’ doc as Channel 4 slammed for giving paedo a platform
News.content:
Next

CONVICTED paedophile Huw Edwards was at the centre of a massive backlash last night after Channel 4 gave him a platform for a “poor me” documentary charting his downfall.

Campaigners, ministers and media figures reacted with fury that the broadcaster was allowing him to explain away his horrific crimes by claiming he had “lost the plot”.



It comes two years since former BBC newsman Edwards admitted possessing 41 images of children, some as young as seven.

BBC star Nicky Campbell last night led a huge backlash against a Channel 4 documentary giving a platform to convicted paedophile Huw Edwards.



Edwards, 65, groomed a vulnerable teenager — paying him for sexual photos and videos — before eventually being handed a six-month suspended jail sentence after admitting possessing 41 vile images of kids, some as young as seven.

Now, two years after his court case, he will feature in an hour-long TV documentary.



Separately, there is a five-part podcast and interview for The Observer, in which he is described as having been in an “unbelievable, terrible fix”.

BBC Radio 5 Live host Campbell wrote on X: I’m rather more concerned for the children in the photographs. What of their lives?”



Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, who jointly led the paper’s 2023 investigation into rapist Russell Brand, wrote: “An ‘unbelievable terrible fix’ is quite the euphemism for someone viewing abuse images of victims as young as 7.”

Sangita Myska, a former BBC Radio Four presenter, added: “The rehabilitation (of) Huw Edwards’ reputation via a ‘personal journey’ documentary is contemptible. He’s a sex offender. What the hell is Channel 4 thinking?”

NEWSMAN’S SICK CRIMES By Emily-Jane Heap DISGRACED BBC anchor Huw Edwards pleaded guilty to three charges of making indecent images of children in July 2024. He was found to be in possession of 41 illegal photos and videos. This included seven category A images, the most serious kind, which showed penetrative sex with a child. Two of the videos featured a sex act involving a boy estimated to be aged between seven and nine. Another showed sexual acts featuring two children thought to be aged between seven and 13. Edwards was also found in possession of 12 category B images, which showed non-penetrative abuse of children, and 22 category C images that featured minors in sexual poses. The former newsreader was given a six-month prison sentence, suspended for two years, at Westminster magistrates’ court. He was also ordered to complete a 40-day treatment programme as well as 25 rehabilitation sessions. And he was placed on the sex offenders’ register for seven years.

Home Office minister Anna Turley said she was “deeply uncomfortable” with the move. She said: “For too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass.”

In a clip released by Channel 4 — which receives public funding — Edwards claimed he had committed child sex offences because he had “lost the plot”.



He is asked by an off-camera producer: “What are you doing?”

Sounding frustrated, he replies: “You want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?”

Later in the trailer, the interviewer asks: “What do you think you were doing?”



Edwards responds: “I’d lost the plot.” The interviewer replies: “Well, come on,” to which Edwards says: “No, not come on!”

Former police detective Mark Williams-Thomas said Edwards’ attitude in the documentary, to be screened on Tuesday, gives “serious cause for concern”.

In a video on X, he went on: “He shows no responsibility for his actions, the destructiveness of his abuse and the blame-shifting.

JOURNOS’ ‘LINKS’ TO HUW FURY QUESTIONS have been raised about the “long-standing connection” between Huw Edwards and the journalists giving him a media platform. Edwards has given interviews for a five-part podcast produced by Tortoise Media and The Observer. It has been made by reporter Ceri Thomas — who was formerly the longest-serving editor of the Beeb’s Today programme and later editor of Panorama. The paper’s Editor-in-Chief James Harding was also Director of News and Current Affairs between 2013 and 2018 at the BBC while Edwards was the top anchor there. Ex-Beeb news presenter Sangita Myska accused Thomas of “absolutely zero transparency”. She wrote on social media: “Ceri Thomas is not just a ‘reporter’ he was a very senior exec at the time Edwards was a presenter. They would have met socially and professionally and have a longstanding connection.” The Beeb’s ex-religious affairs correspondent Christopher Landau also hit out at past links not being made clearer. He said: “I find it surprising that Ceri Thomas, billed here simply as ‘the reporter’, does not mention his many years as a senior BBC editor, and thus his longstanding prior connection with Edwards.” He added: “He wasn’t just any random journalist getting in touch.” Edwards denied on his Substack blog that his participation is a “comeback attempt” and insisted that his and Mr Thomas’ “paths rarely crossed” at the BBC.

“His mental health is not a reason for his offending. In my mind Edwards still remains a significant risk to children.”

It is understood the documentary has even angered Channel 4 staff. One individual close to the project told The Times: “It’s not universally popular. Some people just don’t think that our eyes should be sullied with him ever again.”



A BBC executive also told the paper: “I can’t believe that any broadcaster would want to air it.”

Sacha Mirzoeff, senior commissioning editor at Channel 4, defended the show as a “quest for answers from a man who is trying to come to terms with his abuse of power”. The programme’s director Patrick Forbes said it was “an important film to make”.

Outrage on socials



Edwards shared online a picture of himself walking on a picturesque beach near his home in Wales, taken during filming in October.

In a blog about the show, he describes his “difficulties” and claims reporting on his crimes had been “misleading or simply untrue”.

He says it was a “relief” to “give my own account of the events which led to my fall”, adding: “I know that some will rush to call this self-indulgent. I can only say that answering pointed and intrusive questions felt like the opposite of self-indulgence.”

The Observer’s five-part podcast series will be fronted by Ceri Thomas, an ex-editor of Radio 4’s Today and of BBC One’s Panorama who has worked with Edwards.



It said it was based on “extensive interviews with Edwards, friends, former colleagues and lawyers, and readings of court documents”.

The Sun’s exposure of Edwards’ vile behaviour came when he was at the height of his fame.

In 2023 we reported that a high-profile BBC star had paid thousands of pounds for sordid ­pictures. Edwards was eventually named publicly by his wife.

His court case the following year heard Edwards paid between £1,000 and £1,500 for sick images sent to him by a paedophile.



Edwards described them as “amazing”.

Asked if he wanted sexual images of a person whose “age could be discerned as being between 14 and 16”, Edwards replied: “Yes xxx.”

At sentencing, Edwards was ordered to complete a 40-day Sex Offender Treatment Programme.

He was also placed on the sex offenders register for seven years — meaning he has to keep the police informed of his whereabouts.

Last night criminal defence lawyer Marcus Johnstone told The Sun that protesting his innocence would be “a difficult argument to raise”.



Mr Johnstone said: “Any offences that involve images of children, I think it’s fairly safe to assume that we’d categorise that person as a paedophile. So I think he’s on a hiding to nothing to argue that he wouldn’t fit the category of being a paedophile.”

The lawyer also warned that the documentary could “add insult to injury” for victims of such offending.

He explained: “All the kids who are abused for men like him — for him to then say, ‘Well, you know, really I’ve not done anything wrong’, if that’s what he’s saying in the documentary, I think many people would find that upsetting.”

Reform UK chairman Lee Anderson called the interview an “insult to the victims”.

He said: “Over the years the BBC has been home to a plethora of perverts. This filthy pervert needs to crawl back under his rock.”

News.title: Peter Mandelson promised ‘light touch’ vetting before doomed US ambassador appointment
News.content:
Next

LORD Peter Mandelson was promised only “light touch” vetting ahead of his doomed appointment as US ambassador, newly released files reveal.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged political reform in Westminster in response to the latest developments over the disgraced peer’s ill-fated stint in Washington.



Lord Mandelson was sacked by then PM Sir Keir Starmer in September 2025 after seven months in the role when more details of his friendship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein emerged.

The latest documents were held back by the Met Police, which has a separate probe into allegations that Lord Mandelson passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.



They reveal the then Foreign Office boss Sir Olly Robbins warning Lord Mandelson that his shares in advisory firm Global Counsel risked a perceived ­conflict of interest.

While Mandelson was trying to sell his shares, Sir Olly promised him “light touch” vetting over his ambassador appointment.



Foreign Affairs Committee chair Dame Emily Thornberry said it shows “how wholly inappropriate” the appointment was.

She added: “Officials in the FCDO seemed to be well aware of the risks that Mandelson’s business interests posed.”

Mr Burnham vowed to address change in his ten-year plan for Britain.

He said: “I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country.”



Lord Mandelson caused more fury yesterday by publishing an essay advising the PM on EU negotiations.

Tory MP Charlie Dewhirst said: “No apology, no humility, just more advice. It is staggering arrogance.”

Security Minister Dan Jarvis insisted the Government was not taking any advice from Lord Mandelson.

News.title: Rock legend’s son plunges to death at celebrity-filled Hollywood apartment block as real-estate agents waited next door
News.content:
LEFT DISTRAUGHT Rock legend’s son plunges to death at celebrity-filled Hollywood apartment block as real-estate agents waited next door







Next

A ROCK legend’s son fell to his death from a Hollywood apartment block, just weeks after losing his famous father and amid revelations about his family’s mounting debts.

Chris Kacher, 58, was viewing a luxury condo at the exclusive Sierra Towers in West Hollywood, California, on November 24 when he died.



His death has since been ruled a suicide, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office.

His father was legendary guitarist Del Casher, who helped pioneer the iconic wah-wah pedal and performed alongside stars including Elvis Presley and Sonny and Cher.



Chris had built a career of his own in finance, working as a portfolio manager and stock market analyst after earning a doctorate in nuclear physics from the University of California, Berkeley.

The investor had toured the luxury condo the previous day and expressed interest in buying it before arranging a second viewing, according to local news outlet WEHOonline.



The two real estate agents reportedly became concerned when Chris failed to rejoin them during the viewing and began searching for him.

His body was later discovered in the backyard of an apartment building, authorities confirmed to the Los Angeles Times.

The outlet also reported that he left behind a note although its contents remain unknown.

The exclusive residential tower has attracted some of Hollywood’s biggest stars over the years, including Cher, Elton John, Sandra Bullock and Adam Sandler.



Family friend Al Burg told the California Post that Chris was still “distraught” after his father died of cancer aged 88 on October 1.

Burg said Chris was “definitely upset about all the financial problems and having to sell and trying to help his mom move forward.”

The longtime family friend had recently been helping Chris sell his parents’ belongings and find suitable accommodation for his 89-year-old mom, Eiko Kacher, who was struggling to live independently.

Just weeks before Chris’s death, Burg launched a $14,000 GoFundMe campaign to help the elderly widow settle some of her debts and move into assisted living.



It has pulled in around $7,500 from over 100 donations so far.

According to the appeal, Casher’s recording studio business had been devastated by the coronavirus pandemic, forcing the musician to sell valuable guitars and equipment to stay afloat.

Burg explained that the couple had taken out a reverse mortgage on their multimillion-dollar Beverly Hills property, estimating that the outstanding debt now accounted for more than 70 percent of the home’s value.

He said Eiko was also saddled with huge credit card debts and feared she would be left with nothing after selling the property, paying off the mortgage and settling her taxes and other bills.



In an update to the appeal following Chris’s death, Burg revealed, “Eiko is now mourning the loss of the only two family members left in her life and is facing mounting bills that she is not prepared to handle.”

Documents obtained by The U.S. Sun show Chris’s parents had begun borrowing against their Beverly Hills property nearly two decades ago.

In May 2007, Casher and his wife took out a $500,000 credit line against the property through Washington Mutual Bank.

On December 1, 2018, the couple took out a reverse mortgage through Finance of America Reverse LLC, with a maximum loan amount of $7.725 million listed in the agreement.

The mortgage allowed them to borrow money against their home without making monthly repayments, with unpaid interest building up over the years.



The documents do not disclose how much the couple actually borrowed or how much remains outstanding today.

The family’s Beverly Hills home was put on the market for $6.95 million on October 29, less than a month after the rock legend’s death.

Just 11 days later, the asking price was slashed by $510,000, and the property was available for $6.44 million, according to a listing seen by The U.S. Sun.

The nearly 4,500-square-foot residence boasts four bedrooms, five bathrooms, a swimming pool, private sauna, wet bar and sweeping canyon views.

The gated property, situated in one of Los Angeles’ most sought-after neighborhoods, is being offered for sale for the first time in 49 years.

News.title: Tube strikes live: London Underground commuters face difficult journeys with all lines impacted
News.content:
Tube strikes are impacting people on the London Underground following action by members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) - but TfL says more drivers are working than expected

People on the London Underground face delays due to industrial action.

The strike is the first of a series of 24-hour strikes by London Underground drivers as members of the Rail, Maritime and Transport union (RMT) walk out. Passengers have been warned by Transport for London (TfL) to check before they travel.

Most services are expected to run but there could be disruption on all lines. No service was expected on the Circle or Piccadilly lines throughout the day or on the Waterloo & City line after midday. However, TfL says more drivers have turned up to work than expected - meaning the Piccadilly line is still running, but with delays.

The Elizabeth line, Overground and DLR are running as usual, but will likely be busier. The action has been slammed as "hugely damaging" by Ruth Duston, chief executive of London Heritage Quarter.

News.title: Bus driver’s £700,000 lottery win to reunite family in Australia after 12 years
News.content:
Bus driver’s £700,000 lottery win to reunite family in Australia after 12 years

Bus driver Graeme Burness, who is from Launceston, Cornwall, is £700,000 richer after buying a National Lottery scratchcard when he "forgot what he needed to do"

View 3 Images Graeme, 44, and Katharine Burness, 37, are celebrating a £700,000 lottery scratchcard win (Image: PA)

A bus driver is set for an emotional reunion with his brother after winning £700,000 on the National Lottery.

‌



‌



Graeme Burness, 44, picked up a Red Hot 7s scratchcard after he went into town to carry out errands and forgot to bring his to-do list with him.

‌



He was still trying to remember what exactly he had set out to do when he looked down at the card - and noticed he had scooped the top prize.

‌



The bus driver joked: "If I'd remembered straight away, I'd probably have done what I needed to do and gone straight home. Looking back now, forgetting that list turned out to be the best thing I've ever done".

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Bus driver Graeme purchased a scratchcard after forgetting his to-do list (Image: PA)

‌



Quarter of lottery players would become 'globetrotters' if they hit the jackpot READ MORE :

Graeme happens to work at the same bus garage in Launceston, Cornwall, as fellow National Lottery Scratchcard winner Steve Goodwin, who won £1million around Easter in 2023.

Now, he and healthcare assistant wife Katharine, 37, are preparing for a emotional once-in-a-lifetime Christmas family reunion in Australia in 2028.

‌



Graeme said: "My brother has lived in Australia for 14 years. I haven't seen him in person for 12 years – that was during his last visit back to the UK – and our three children weren't really old enough at that time to have cherished memories of their uncle. We speak on video calls, but it's not the same.

"The moment we realised we'd won, one of the first things we said was, 'We're all going to Australia for Christmas.' It was just something we knew we had to do. And when I say everyone, I mean all 11 of us in the family in the UK!"

‌



He added: "There will be cousins meeting for the first time, nieces and nephews meeting their aunts and uncles for the first time and our children will finally get to spend time with family they've only ever known through a screen. That's what this win is all about."

View 3 Images The married couple are hoping to buy their own home - and are set for an emotional family reunion in Australia (Image: Richard Dawson/Assignments/Press Association)

‌



When Graeme passed on the good news on the family WhatsApp group, he was initially met with disbelief from his nearest and dearest.

"None of them initially believed it – and some of the language said as much – but I've always believed that anything is possible and this win proves it."

‌



Neither Graeme, Katharine nor any of their three children had ever travelled by plane at the time of their win, so they recently booked a holiday closer to home to help them 'practice' for the big trip.

Graeme said: "We realised that perhaps flying to Australia shouldn't be our first ever flight, so we went to Greece. It was amazing and was also just what we needed."

‌



The life-changing win will also allow renters Graeme and Katharine to buy their first home after spending their adult lives working long hours to provide for their family.

Graeme said: "We can finally buy a home of our own and know that it's something we'll be able to leave behind for our children one day. That has given both of us overwhelming peace of mind."

‌



"We're not the sort of people who would stop working overnight", added Katharine. "But for the first time ever, we can look ahead and see options. That's a wonderful feeling."

But the trip to see his family Down Under comes at the very top for Graeme, who said: "Winning £700,000 is incredible, but the thing we're looking forward to most isn't material possessions. It's standing in Australia with our family around us, watching our children meet relatives they've never met before in-person and being together for Christmas. That's life-changing."

Article continues below

Andy Carter, Senior Winners’ Advisor at Allwyn, operator of The National Lottery said: "Massive congratulations to Graeme and Katharine. We know from experience what winning means for our winners, and it is extra special to see a win like this helping to reunite a family separated by thousands of miles. Fair dinkum, as they say Down Under!"

News.title: Opinium security breach: Personal data and passwords stolen from large firm - what it means for you
News.content:
Opinium security breach: Personal data and passwords stolen from large firm - what it means for you

Polling firm Opinium issued a warning to survey participants after 'a data security incident' resulted in unauthorised access' to names, email addresses, usernames and passwords

View Image Hackers targeted a third-party provider linked to the polling site (file photo) (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

Personal data including names, email addresses, usernames and passwords have potentially been exposed in a hack involving one of Britain's top pollsters.

‌



‌



Opinium emailed users today after recieving reports of "unauthorised access" from a third-party provider involved in running its Panel paid survey website.

‌



The site is currently offline while the firm carries out urgent fixes.

‌



Impacted users have been urged to change their passwords "immediately" on any other online accounts where they reuse the same details.

Nearly £660million was lost to scammers and fraudsters in the first half of this year alone READ MORE :

Have you been affected by this story? Contact webnews@mirror.co.uk

What has Opinium said?

An email sent to Opinium Panel users said: "We are sorry to let you know that there has been a data security incident involving the Opinium panel. We take the security of your personal information very seriously and want to explain what has happened, what we are doing about it and the steps you can take to protect yourself.

‌



"On the evening of Saturday 21 November 2026, someone gained unauthorised access to the systems of one of our technology providers, which helps us operate the Opinium panel website.

"The incident was detected that same evening, the website was immediately taken offline and unauthorised access was blocked. Our investigation so far has found no further unauthorised access since then.

‌



"We are working closely with our technology providers to investigate the incident and ensure the website is secure before bringing it back online."

‌



What personal information has been accessed?

According to Opinium, information accessed during the breach included:

Names

Email addresses

Usernames

Passwords, in an encrypted format

‌



Passwords were stored in a "protected format", the pollster said, though they admitted there "remains a risk" that hackers could attempt to uncover them.

Survey answers and financial information have not been taken, users were told.

‌



UK cybersecurity in the spotlight

British companies have been repeatedly targeted in cyber attacks over recent months as threats grow more sophisticated and defences struggle to keep pace.

‌



On Monday, retailer Next issued a security alert after hackers accessed data on its website via a third-party supplier.

The FTSE-listed company said that no customers’ personal data during the incident, described the information accessed as "limited in nature".

‌



Shares in ASOS dipped by 10% in a single day last month after a hack resulted in millions of customers recieving an app notification which read: "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it."

A hacker group named Xuanye Group claimed responsibility for the cyberattack.

‌



ASOS later confirmed that basic personal details such as names and email addresses may have been accessed in the exploit, while payment card details and account passwords were not believed to be compromised.

One recent cyberattack on supermarket fridges across Europe by suspected Iranian hackers meanwhile caused tens of millions in spoiled stock, and sparked at least 12 fires, after temperatures were dialled up as high as 50C.

Article continues below

A similar threat to British supermarkets was thwarted thanks to a covert joint operation, which saw the UK government, the National Cyber Security Centre, major retailers, and manufacturers roll out emergency firmware patches before hackers could exploit them.

News.title: Pilot dad's chilling warning moments before plane crash killed six family members
News.content:
Pilot dad's chilling warning moments before plane crash killed six family members

Brent Stokes left an airport in New Orleans on Tuesday afternoon with his family, including his 16-year-old son Hunter Stokes, but tragedy loomed moments later

View 3 Images Michael Knox, left, Arlyn Knox, Charles Holden Knox and Truett Knox have now been identified as among those killed in a plane crash near Horn Island (Image: Facebook / Arlyn Knox)

A pilot was warned there was adverse weather in the area shortly before his aircraft crashed into water off the coast — killing him and his five family members.

‌



‌



Brent Stokes, 50, had not experienced any difficulty when he attempted to take his family home but, less than one hour into the short journey, an air traffic controller contacted him. They told Brent there was heavy rainfall in the area but then lost contact, and the single-engine Cessna suddenly began descending at an alarming rate of 10,000 feet per minute.

‌



And Brent, his 16-year-old son Hunter Stokes, sister Arlyn Knox, 43, brother-in-law Michael Knox, 43, and their sons Charles Holden Knox, 12, and Truett Knox, 10, died upon impact when the plane plunged into the sea off the coast of Mississippi, US on Tuesday.

‌



Now the communication between Brent and the air traffic controller at Gulfport–Biloxi International Airport has emerged on the website LiveATC.net. Brent had taken his family on a fishing trip in Louisiana, it has also now been confirmed.

Two bodies found after Loch Leven glider crash as plane plunged into lake READ MORE :

Grand Canyon plane crash leaves 3 dead as missing plane found after huge search READ MORE :

View 3 Images Michael Knox, Arlyn Knox, Charles Holden Knox, and Truett Knox were among six victims killed in a plane crash near Horn Island (Image: Facebook / Arlyn Knox)

‌



The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) today played tribute to Brent, who it confirmed was the president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, Florida. The statement added Brent was an “avid fisherman and life time boater".

Arlyn and Michael Knox ran Knox Technologies, a Fort Myers-based IT company they founded in 2012. The Stokes and Knox families said in a statement: "They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family.

‌



"In the middle of our grief, we are holding on to that, and to how much love they gave us and how much love surrounds us now. We will carry them with us always."

View 3 Images Michael Knox, left, and Arlyn Knox were killed in the crash alongside their children (Image: Facebook / Arlyn Knox)

Article continues below

Conservative youth organisation Turning Point USA said it was “heartbroken” over the death of Hunter Stokes, who it described as the president of its Fort Myers High School Club America chapter. It added: "Hunter was a young patriot who loved his country and led by example."

Responders searched for hours and initially only found three life jackets, a life raft and the plane’s cabin floating in the ocean, U.S. Coast Guard spokesperson Juan Ros said.

News.title: 20 things that ruin group holidays - and how to fix them
News.content:
20 things that ruin group holidays - and how to fix them

Rows over who pays for what, washing-up duties and what activities to do are among the biggest causes of friction on group holidays - but a few ground rules can help keep the peace.

View 4 Images Holidaying with others can be difficult (Image: PinPep)

Disputes over splitting costs, washing-up rotas and activity choices are among the most common flashpoints on group getaways. A survey of 1,000 adults who've been on a break with family or friends revealed 34% have fallen out with them during their stay.

‌



‌



Choosing what activities to do was the biggest source of disagreement (37%), while 29% said they clashed over who pays for what and 21% over whose turn it was to wash up. Another 13% said sharing facilities such as hot tubs can require a bit of compromise, especially when it comes to making sure everyone gets their turn.

‌



Etiquette expert and former royal butler Grant Harrold has partnered with Cottages.com to create an official 'Holiday Prenup', a holiday code of conduct designed to help groups agree on what matters before they go away.

‌



View 4 Images Former royal butler Grant Harrold partners with cottages.com to launch the official ‘Holiday Prenup’ (Image: PinPep)

They said: "Even the best group holidays can come with the occasional difference of opinion, often simply because everyone has their own idea of how the trip should work.

"Good etiquette isn't about having lots of rules but making sure everyone feels considered. Agreeing a few things before you go can avoid awkward conversations later and leave everyone free to enjoy the holiday."

‌



The study found the occasional row hasn't put those polled off group getaways - whether for a main summer break (68%), a milestone celebration (33%) or simply getting everyone under one roof (26%).

For most, the rewards easily outweigh the headaches, led by making lasting memories (61%) and catching up with family and friends (56%). However, 69% agreed you never truly know someone until you've been on holiday with them.

‌



Bathroom etiquette was a particular bugbear, with leaving it in a state among the biggest holiday home crimes.

Never washing up followed closely behind, according to 34%, while 33% took issue with making noise when everyone else was asleep.

‌



View 4 Images The code of conduct is designed to help friends and family agree on ground rules (Image: PinPep)

Money was another potential flashpoint, as 26% found it frustrating when someone ordered the most expensive thing while splitting the bill.

‌



And 23% had been irked by someone regularly 'forgetting' to pay, with the same proportion frustrated by those who conveniently disappeared when it was time to clean up.

Meanwhile, 11% admitted putting their belongings on a bed to claim it, with 10% having rushed in to bag the room they wanted.

‌



When it came to hot tub etiquette, those with an opinion believed 28 minutes was an acceptable amount of time for one person or couple to use it when others were waiting.

More than a quarter (28%) agreed whoever landed the master or best bedroom should pay more than everyone else, according to OnePoll figures.

‌



And among those who put a figure on how much extra a better room was worth, the average premium came to 10%.

View 4 Images Having basic ground rules can help keep the peace (Image: PinPep)

‌



Interestingly, 13% admitted secretly messaging someone else on a group holiday to complain about a fellow traveller who was frustrating them.

But setting expectations before arriving could help keep the peace, as 66% felt that ground rules reduce arguments or tension. And 42% would be likely to use a light-hearted holiday prenup ahead of a group getaway.

‌



A spokesperson for Cottages.com, which hand-picks every property to help match guests with a place that fits their group's specific needs, added: "No two families or friendship groups want exactly the same holiday, and bringing different personalities and preferences together can take a little give and take.

"Our Group Holiday 'prenup' is a fun way to get those conversations started early, so everyone arrives on the same page.

Article continues below

"Whether it's extra bathrooms, outdoor space or separate living areas, cottages.com can help groups find a place that works for everyone."

News.title: UK's 30 favourite smells ranked – from freshly baked bread to petrol
News.content:
UK's 30 favourite smells ranked – from freshly baked bread to petrol

Discover which smells satisfy Brits the most - and some of the more divisive choices.

View 3 Images Brits love everything from the smell of coffee to the rain on warm pavements (Image: St Pierre)

The aroma of freshly baked bread, clean bed sheets, and morning coffee have topped the list of the nation's most-loved smells. A study of 2,000 adults revealed that fresh pastries, a real Christmas tree, and the scent of a newborn baby's head also featured prominently. Sun cream on holiday, rain on warm pavements, and petrol were amongst the other entries rounding out the top 30.

‌



‌



More than eight in 10 (81%) said certain smells instantly improve their mood, while 45% admitted they have stopped what they were doing simply to savour a particularly pleasing scent.

‌



A spokesperson for bakery brand, St Pierre, which commissioned the research, said: “Few things can lift your mood quite like a delicious smell. Scents have an incredible ability to transport us back to a particular place, person or moment in an instant."

‌



View 3 Images Certain smells can help trigger happy memories (Image: St Pierre)

"What's lovely about these results is how many of our favourite smells are really simple, everyday things," they added.

"From the comforting aroma of morning coffee and croissants to the unmistakable smell of fish and chips, these little sensory moments can spark surprisingly strong feelings of happiness and nostalgia.

‌



"It shows you don't always need a grand gesture to brighten your day - sometimes something as simple as a familiar scent is enough."

The research also revealed that 24% of people enjoy smells others might find unusual, including nail polish remover (26%), bleach (14%), and hardware shops (11%).

‌



A third (32%) feel safe or comforted by certain scents, while 43% consider smell one of the most powerful triggers of cherished memories.

View 3 Images Many of the top 30 smells were food related (Image: St Pierre)

‌



More than four in 10 (42%) have been transported back to their childhood after catching a particular scent, while others have been reminded of time spent with grandparents (21%) or cherished family holidays (26%).

The research revealed that food and drink (40%) are the most-loved smells, with favourite food aromas leaving 79% feeling even hungrier than before the scent reached them.

‌



What's more, 33% have even followed the smell of food to work out where it was coming from.

Freshly baked bread (40%), bacon (32%) and warmed croissants and pains au chocolat (21%) are among the hardest smells to resist.

‌



Of those polled via OnePoll, 42% also admitted to buying food they hadn't planned to purchase because they could smell it. This was most likely to happen in a bakery (62%), followed by supermarkets (43%), markets (37%) and pubs (20%).

The St Pierre spokesperson added: "There are some smells that are almost impossible to resist, so we're not remotely surprised to find freshly baked goods topping the table.

‌



"A delicious aroma can stop us in our tracks, make us feel hungry and even tempt us into buying something we had no intention of picking up.

"Smell is closely tied to memory, which perhaps explains why so many of the scents people love are associated with familiar foods and moments.

‌



"Breakfast comes through particularly strongly, from fresh bread, coffee, bacon and pastries all featuring among our favourites.

"There's something special about waking up to the smell of breakfast, and clearly we're not alone in thinking so."
