News.title: Strongman brothers haul 13-tonne truck through London street in latest stunt
News.content:
Strongman brothers haul 13-tonne truck through London street in latest stunt

Britain's strongest brothers Tom and Luke Stoltman dragged a 13-tonne Currys delivery lorry through a street near Wembley Stadium

View 4 Images Tom and Luke Stoltman pulled a 13-tonne delivery truck (Image: PinPep)

The strongman siblings hauled a massive 13-tonne lorry through a street near London's iconic Wembley stadium, relying on nothing but raw power.

‌



‌



Brothers Tom and Luke Stoltman were accompanied by strongwoman Melissa Peacock, as the trio tackled the colossal challenge, dragging the Currys delivery truck through Wembley. Weighing in at 13 tonnes, the lorry was roughly equivalent to two fully-grown African elephants or a single-decker bus.

‌



The massive vehicle was secured to the strongmen and strongwoman using harnesses before they threw their weight into shifting the enormous load down the road.

‌



It marked the start of Currys' Black Friday activity, to highlight how it is there to do the 'heavy lifting' for people looking for a deal.

View 4 Images Strongwoman Melissa Peacock helped pull the Currys delivery truck (Image: PinPep)

Tom and Luke Stoltman said: "We've pulled some pretty ridiculous things over the years, but taking on a 13-tonne Currys truck is definitely one way to get ready for Black Friday.

‌



"When Currys told us Black Friday was getting Bigger, we decided to put that to the test. It's safe to say this was a serious workout, but thankfully shoppers won't have to work quite as hard to bag a bargain."

The stunt comes after research of 2,000 adults found 65% are holding off making a purchase until Black Friday, with shoppers setting aside an average of £528 to spend.

‌



Christmas presents top the shopping list for 41%, while 34% have their sights set on clothes and 20% are prioritising kitchen appliances.

But getting a genuine bargain isn't always as straightforward as it seems.

‌



View 4 Images The truck weighed the same as two African elephants (Image: PinPep)

View 4 Images The stunt marked the beginning of Curry's Black Friday sale (Image: PinPep)

‌



Nearly a third (31%) reckon finding a real good deal is like doing detective work, while 30% compare bargain hunting to a treasure hunt.

And 30% admit they've been tempted into buying something simply because the deal looked too good to miss, only to regret it afterwards.

‌



It also emerged 18% of those polled, via OnePoll, believe the best measure of value for money is simply knowing they actually need what they are buying.

The study also revealed some of the tactics most likely to set alarm bells ringing among shoppers, with 40% suspicious when there is no visible price history.

‌



More than a third (36%) are also wary of warnings claiming there are "only a few left".

Ed Connolly, chief commercial officer at Currys, said: "Black Friday can sometimes feel like a test of endurance, with thousands of deals competing for shoppers' attention.

Article continues below

"So, we called in Britain's strongest to take on a heavyweight challenge and show that Currys is doing the heavy lifting this year."

News.title: Huntingdon train attacker found guilty of all 14 counts of attempted murder
News.content:
A knifeman has been found guilty of attempting to murder 14 people, including 10 on board a train to London.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Anthony Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Some hid in toilets and bike racks before the driver was forced to make an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, where Williams was arrested by armed police.

As well as the train attacks, Williams, of Langford Road, Peterborough, was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Jurors deliberated for 15 hours and 53 minutes before delivering seven guilty verdicts, and then returned an hour later to give the final seven.

The judge, Mr Justice Calver KC, said the victims handled themselves with "great dignity throughout" the trial.

Aside from the attack on the LNER train, Williams also attempted to murder a boy and two men in Peterborough on 31 October 2025, and then a teenager on a DLR train in east London hours later.

The defendant, who appeared at court via a video link from a secure hospital, showed little emotion as each verdict was delivered.

Reacting to the verdicts, Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The fact that nobody was killed in his rampage is down to the courage, quick thinking and good fortune of the people he attacked."

News.title: Knifeman told doctor his psychosis drugs weren't working days before Huntingdon attack
News.content:
Hurtling along at more than 120mph, passengers on an East Coast Mainline train bound for London King's Cross found themselves caught up in one of the worst acts of violence on Britain's rail network in recent times.

Anthony Williams stabbed 10 people in five minutes on board the train last November, near Huntingdon, in Cambridgeshire, leaving some seriously injured. On Thursday, a jury found him guilty of 14 counts of attempted murder.

It has now emerged that, in the month before that attack, the knifeman had twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

But he never saw a doctor and did not receive additional mental health treatment.

Now his trial at Cambridge Crown Court is over, BBC News can also report his long history of violent criminality, revealed through old court transcripts we have obtained.

It stretched back two decades. In his teens Williams robbed people at knife point, including on a train. Even after he had started his 25-hour rampage, culminating in the Huntingdon attack, there were potential opportunities to arrest him.

News.title: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced his frustration with the United States and questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin in an interview with the BBC.

In a picture posted to Truth Social on Saturday, where Trump and Putin embrace, the US president described his Russian counterpart as "my friend".

"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford at his office in central Kyiv.

"He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killerâ¦He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

News.title: UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall
News.content:
The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.

The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.

Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".

"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."

This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.

That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.

In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".

Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.

"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."

News.title: Drug rape husband says wife 'would have been terrified', court hears
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

A husband who admits drugging and raping his wife with strangers has told a court that if she had woken during the abuse, she would have been "terrified".

The defendant, who has admitted multiple sexual offences dating back to 2004, said he drugged his wife so she would be unaware of the abuse by him and other men.

He changed his pleas earlier this year and admitted offences including rape, sexual assault and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence, as well as inviting 13 other men to take part in the abuse.

Nine of those men have pleaded not guilty to sexual offences against the woman and are standing trial at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's right to anonymity, entered the witness box to give evidence for the prosecution.

The court has heard that the man, who is in his 60s, filmed and photographed his offending as his wife lay "out of it" on their bed before sharing the material online.

Prosecutors say that, by 2023 at the latest, he had begun inviting other men to the couple's home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, where it is alleged they sexually abused her while she was unconscious.

Asked by prosecutor Louise Oakley KC why he was now telling the truth, he said: "So the court knows what happened. So my wife knows and my children know.

"I am here to tell the truth and give my account of what actually happened."

He told jurors he had drugged his wife so she would be unaware of the abuse by him and other men.

"She would never agree to do any of this," he said. "She would have been terrified and scream."

Following his guilty pleas in September, the husband gave police a written statement detailing his offending.

He told the jury the process had been "very difficult" because of the "guilt and shame" he felt and the "pain" he had caused his wife.

He accepted responsibility for his actions and for facilitating contact between other men and his wife.

Asked whether she had ever consented to what happened to her, he replied: "Never."

He said his wife did not know any of the men he invited to the house and had never spoken to them.

News.title: Burnham joined by former PMs at Ann Widdecombe service
News.content:
Andy Burnham was joined by former prime ministers as he attended a memorial service for the late politician Ann Widdecombe.

Hundreds gathered for the Service of Remembrance at Westminster Cathedral on Thursday afternoon, including David Cameron, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage and deputy leader Richard Tice, along with former Conservative Chancellor Philip Hammond and Speaker of the House of Commons Sir Lindsay Hoyle, were also in attendance.

Bishop James Curry, the Auxiliary Bishop of Westminster, led the service after the Archbishop of Westminster, Richard Moth, was taken to hospital earlier.

News.title: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
News.content:
Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles â whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.

UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald told the BBC that the sharp rise in flu cases was happening earlier compared to last winter and previous flu seasons.

"Flu is very, very unpredictable and we don't know what the flu season will look like until it has unfolded," she said, adding that although last year's flu season arrived early, it peaked at "moderate levels".

She said it is not known if this flu season will go on for longer, or peak higher, but urged people to get vaccinated, saying said thousands of people die from the flu every year.

However, flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practice good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible have taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives".

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

News.title: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction
News.content:
Disgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.

Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.

A government minister, Anna Turley, told LBC, external she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, and that "for too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass".

Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.

During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp â including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"

Asked again, he replies: "I'd lost the plot."

The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."

Despite that apparent combative stance, Edwards wrote on his blog on Thursday: "I want viewers to know that I did not avoid a single question, and that I answered each as honestly as I could, including those about deeply personal matters: my relationships, my temperament, my sexuality."

Explaining his reasons for giving the interviews, he said: "My difficulties became front-page news, and the account that took hold was, in places, misleading or simply untrue.

"Those promoting false narratives are also, unsurprisingly, the ones questioning my right to set the record straight.

"I was left with a choice: to let that faulty account stand forever, or to offer my own."

In a statement, Forbes said it was "an important film to make".

"It's rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues â whether it's celebrity culture or the power of the media â as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment," he said.

Channel 4's documentary, titled Huw Edwards - Guilty, will be broadcast on Tuesday.

In the clip for his separate interview with the Observer and its Tortoise Investigates podcast, Edwards is seen saying: "Lots of the advice I've had is just be quiet, don't say anything."

Interviewer Ceri Thomas, a former editor of the BBC's Today programme and Panorama, said he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

The interviews have been criticised by two people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday that Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Meanwhile Rosamund Urwin, chief news correspondent for the Sunday Times, who jointly led the paper's 2023 investigation into Russell Brand, reacted to Thomas's statement by saying: "An 'unbelievable terrible fix' is quite the euphemism for someone viewing child abuse images of victims as young as 7."

The podcast will be released on Tuesday. Tortoise Media, which owns the Observer, has a deal to make some podcasts available on BBC Sounds, but the BBC said the Huw Edwards series would not be among them.

Channel 4 and the Observer said Edwards had received no payment for the interviews or had any editorial input.

News.title: Burnham says UK net migration now under 'sufficient' control
News.content:
The ONS said net migration had "fallen to levels not typically seen since the 1990s".

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

A fall had been expected because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp argued the Conservatives should receive credit for the decrease in net migration.

He added: "We now need to go even further with an annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels.

"British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour's high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesman Paul Kohler said Britain faces "serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage welcomed the drop in numbers, but said he was concerned about "a lot of high skilled big tax paying people" leaving the UK and being replaced by people "who are paying far less in tax".

Meanwhile, his party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said the fall "came about solely because I went to see Rishi Sunak" in 2023 whilst an immigration minister in the Conservative former prime minister's government.

Jenrick, who defected to Reform earlier this year, told the BBC: "I threatened to resign unless he made a series of changes. He did".

"And as a result of those changes to the immigration system, we've got where we are today".

But he added that the changes "didn't go as far as I wanted to," adding this had been behind his resignation from the Tory government a few days later.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and asylum seekers is not a measure of success."

Additional reporting by Thomas Mason

News.title: Mandelson kept shares as ambassador despite conflict of interest fears, documents show
News.content:
Lord Mandelson still held shares in his lobbying company eight months after becoming US ambassador, despite government concens about conflicts of interest, newly released documents show.

The peer was sacked as ambassador last year by Sir Keir Starmer following revelations about the extent of his relationship with the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

This 85-page release is the third since MPs voted to publish documents aiming to reveal behind-the scenes-discussions about how he was appointed to the role.

The documents were previously withheld due to the Metropolitan Police investigation into allegations Lord Mandelson had passed market-sensitive government information to Epstein.

Sir Olly Robbins was sacked as head of the Foreign Office by Sir Keir Starmer during the scandal when it emerged Lord Mandelson had been granted clearance for the role despite concerns being raised by vetting officials.

The newly released documents highlight that Lord Mandelson was able to keep his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he co-founded, while serving as ambassador to Washington.

They reveal civil servants' concerns about the risk of perceived conflict of interest.

But selling the shares was clearly not a condition of him taking up the role.

Part of that is because of the desire in Sir Keir's government at the time to have Lord Mandelson in Washington as quickly as possible.

That is exemplified in an email from Sir Olly, saying a process to police Mandelson's conflicts of interest could be "up and running in a light touch way".

Another factor is selling shares in a private company like Global Counsel, which advised high-profile clients including Chinese-owned TikTok, US tech firm Palantir and pharmaceutical firm GSK. requires finding a new buyer or selling them back to the company.

But the documents also reveal Lord Mandelson had not sold his shares back to Global Counsel because their offer was not the "fair value". Another attempt to sell to a different buyer fell through.

The result was Mandelson kept his shares, and while in office tried to set up a meeting between Global Counsel and a key Donald Trump advisor, as well as taking the firm's advice on a speech on Britain's role in the world.

Lord Mandelson remained a shareholder until February 2026, the same month the company went into administration.

News.title: Tommy Robinson charged with failing to give phone Pin code to police
News.content:
Far-right activist Tommy Robinson has been charged with failing to provide his phone's pin code to police at Heathrow Airport.

The alleged incident happened when Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was detained after returning to the UK from Russia via Turkey on 13 June this year.

The 43-year-old is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 14 December, the Metropolitan Police said.

Posting on X after being charged, Robinson, describing himself as a journalist, said he "refused the Pin because it held private messages from grooming gang survivors".

He described the charge as "pure state persecution".

Robinson, from Bedfordshire, was detained under the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019 in June and has been charged under the same act.

Prior to his arrival in the UK Robinson posted a video on X showing him meeting Elon Musk's father in Moscow.

Robinson is currently awaiting sentencing after being convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists.

A jury at Southwark Crown Court found him guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence.

The case concerned Robinson's response to Daily Mail and Mail Online articles from August 2024, showing him on holiday in Cyprus while riots took place in England following the Southport murders.

Robinson was granted bail ahead of his sentencing, scheduled for 16 December.

Robinson had denied the charges, saying he had "panicked" and had been "scared" when the Daily Mail published a story accusing him of "stoking race riots from his sunbed".

News.title: Chief medical officer Gregor Smith resigns on mental health grounds
News.content:
Smith said: "It has been a privilege to be the CMO of Scotland for the last six-and-a-half years, but it has become very clear to me that the nature and purpose of the role is not generally understood.

"Like many colleagues across the health system, those years of the pandemic and afterwards have taken their toll.

"Events over the last few days have shown me that I don't currently enjoy the good mental health necessary to continue with the exceptional challenges that this role can expose you to."

He added: "No-one in public life is unaccountable. I am confident, however, that the review initiated by the cabinet secretary will show that I provided my advice in relation to Grampian hepatobiliary service consistent with the role of the chief medical officer."

Dominiczak was appointed as the Scottish government's chief health scientist in July 2022 and is regius professor of medicine at the University of Glasgow.

The Scottish government described her as a "world-leading cardiovascular scientist and clinical academic".

Constance said: "Dame Anna has played a key role in driving medical innovation in her time as chief scientist and she brings a wealth of clinical experience to the role of interim chief medical officer.

"I know she will be keen to work collaboratively with health and care staff across the country as we continue to ensure people are able to access the right care in the right place."

News.title: Nearly 100 Labour MPs including ministerial aides oppose Rosebank oil field
News.content:
Ministerial aides are among nearly 100 Labour MPs who have signed a letter to the prime minister to express their opposition to the Rosebank oil field.

The government could also face resignations from junior ranks if the project goes ahead, the BBC has been told.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is due to make a decision on whether to give the go-ahead for drilling in the oil field off the north-west coast of Shetland within weeks.

The government has remained tight-lipped - both publicly and privately - about what it is likely to do.

Those close to the energy secretary insist that she has not yet made her decision.

But 92 Labour MPs have signed a letter, sent to the prime minister today, urging him not to allow the project to go ahead. Ministerial aides - the most junior rank of government - are among the signatures.

The MP who organised the letter, Catherine Fookes, said: "If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies - but it will not make an iota of difference to my constituents' energy bills.

"The oil belongs to private companies, and will only be shipped overseas to the highest bidder.

"What it will do, however, is accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating winter floods like those we saw in Monmouthshire last year, and fuelling wildfires across our green landscapes in summer."

It's the most visible demonstration yet of the deep divides in the Labour Party over the issue.

The decision about whether to approve Rosebank involves a legal process which technically lies solely with the energy secretary.

Fahnbulleh has, in the past, been regarded as someone personally opposed to the oil field.

Others in the cabinet, including Chancellor John Healey, have let it be known that they would like to see the project given the go-ahead; while the prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to take a "pragmatic" approach to North Sea oil and gas.

But Fahnbulleh insisted last month that she alone would make the final decision and claimed the courts would ultimately side with her if colleagues attempted to overrule her.

Influential pro-Rosebank voices suggested that senior ministers had toned down vocal support as the decision draws closer.

They suggested this wasn't a sign that Rosebank would be vetoed, but because any obvious attempts to pressure the energy secretary might mean her final decision would be subject to a legal challenge.

News.title: UK reservists contacted as 'threat environment' rises, Streeting says
News.content:
The Ministry of Defence has written to ex-military personnel to check their contact details and skills against the backdrop of a rising "threat environment", Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has said.

It comes after The Times and the Telegraph reported that reservists who previously served in the Armed Forces have received letters telling them to prepare to be called up for war.

Streeting told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this meant should they ever be needed "either for a national disaster here at home or for a more serious threat or conflict elsewhere" then they would "know where our strategic reserve is" and what their skills were.

"I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," he said.

"You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," Streeting told Today.

"We saw last Friday a very serious incident â the incursion into Polish airspace by Russian missiles, we've seen state-sponsored terrorism waged by Russia across Europe, we've obviously had incidents concerning Iran around RAF bases here in the UK.

"And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks."

He added: "Because the more ready we are the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war, that is my goal, that is the goal of this government."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast that "if, God forbid, this country did find itself at war" and there was then an inquiry, the Ministry of Defence would be criticised if the government had not kept its records up-to-date."

The Telegraph reported that the letters offered opportunities to volunteer, external for training and exercises.

This is not a case of pressing the panic button for imminent war, but more one of good housekeeping.

When Britain went to war in Iraq in 2003 the MoD had a poor grasp of who might be available to serve, what current skills they had and what their up-to-date contact details were. So they obviously don't want to be in that situation if there is a national crisis in the future that triggers a mobilisation.

Twenty three years on, the Ukraine war has changed everything. It's brought a hot war to the very borders of Nato, it's exposed the dangers of having too few troops available, but most of all it has changed the nature of warfare.

People who have spent their adult lives never touching a weapon can turn out to be extraordinarily skilled drone operators, those with a talent for electronics, radio and signals work have a vital role to play in electronic warfare.

So this exercise by the government, probably long overdue, is about knowing who can do what and where they can be contacted.

Justin Crump, a former Army officer and now CEO of the business intelligence firm Sibylline, told the BBC: "Ukraine has shown us the importance of mobilising civilian skills and approaches in modern warfare. This is a first step, and an overdue one in many ways, with the effort likely to increase through early 2027. [It is] very much a part of deterrence and not an intention to use people".

He said veterans - a sometimes misleading term for men and women who are often in peak physical shape and fitness - that he has contacted have generally responded positively to the move. "After all", he said, "they signed up to help before, but want to make sure their enhanced skills and talents are valued".

The MoD's decision to contact ex-military personnel comes after news that the UK has signed an Â£8bn contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine fleet, which the defence secretary said would help get the country "warfighting ready".

Meanwhile, Streeting also praised the Duke of Sussex's "patriotic spirit" after the former Army officer said he would rejoin the armed forces again if needed.

Asked whether there could be a role for Harry, the defence secretary told Today: "I'm always happy to talk to him about how we can work together, whether that's through his Invictus Games, which does a brilliant job supporting our veterans and giving them opportunities to take part in those amazing and inspiring competitive sporting events, but he does have experience to bring to bear."

Streeting praised the "service he's given to our country" and the fact he had spoken about his "willingness and readiness to serve".

"I think that's exactly the sort of patriotic spirit we're looking for," he said.

"I think it's that sort of patriotic spirit we'll find throughout our strategic reserve."

Last week, Harry, who spent a decade in the forces and served on the front line in Afghanistan, said: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country, alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

News.title: Millions of people to see average monthly mortgage payments rise by £100
News.content:
More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

About 6.5 million owners are forecast to see their monthly repayment jump by Â£100 on average when they move onto their next deal by the end of 2029, new data in its Financial Stability Report reveals.

That is more the double the Â£45-a-month hike that the Bank estimated in its last report in July.

In the shorter term, about one million of those homeowners, who are on mortgage rates below 3% and due to refinance by the end of next year, will see an average Â£200 increase in their monthly repayments.

For borrowers, the interest rate on a fixed mortgage does not change until it expires, usually after two or five years, and a new one is chosen to replace it. The vast majority of homeowners and buyers have this kind of mortgage.

Since the Iran war began, global economic uncertainty has been pushing up the cost of deals, with the average rates on two and five year fixed mortgages at their highest for about three years.

On Thursday, the average rate on a two-year deal was 5.99%, and at 6% for a five-year deal, according to the financial information service Moneyfacts.

Analysts have described the situation as "brutal" for homeowners coming to the end of their fixed deals.

However, the Bank's report points out that the average Â£100 increase in monthly repayments was half the rise experienced by those refinancing during 2023 and 2024.

Dawn Fazackerley-King is a Pilates instructor who lives near Ipswich and has previously spoken to the BBC about her struggles with the cost of living.

She was on a five-year fixed deal at 1.4%, which she took out in January 2022. But the mother-of-two is about to refix for two years and the best deal she can find is a 5.69% loan. That will push her costs up by about Â£200 a month.

News.title: Princess of Wales drops in on arts project in the Borders
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has been in the Scottish Borders to see the work of an arts organisation that is helping to support projects across the UK.

It was her first engagement since two men were charged with trying to steal cufflinks and a clock from the royal couple's country home in Norfolk.

The Hugo Burge Foundation (HBF) which has three bases in the region - one of them on the Marchmont Estate near Duns - carries the name of the internet entrepreneur and philanthropist who died in 2023 aged 51.

The princess - who is known as the Duchess of Rothesay while in Scotland - got a glimpse of the work being carried out by the group.

News.title: Passengers hailed for ‘immense courage’ in facing down Huntingdon train attacker
News.content:
Passengers onboard the London-bound train attacked by a knifeman have been hailed for their “immense courage” as he was found guilty on 14 counts of attempted murder.

Anthony Williams, 33, carried out attacks on a LNER train between Peterborough and Huntingdon, where it made an unscheduled stop on 1 November last year.

CCTV footage from the train released by British Transport Police shows passengers attempting to subdue Williams using frying pans and toasters from the buffet car.

In a statement outside Cambridge Crown Court, CPS prosecutor Ben Samples praised the victims for showing “immense courage in defending themselves and others”.

News.title: Crystal Palace edge out 10-man Real Sociedad as Sunderland frustrated again
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Crystal Palace delivered Thomas Frank a first victory after they came back to beat 10-man Real Sociedad 2-1 in the Europa League.

Dean Henderson was kept busy in the first half, making several stops to ensure it was all to play for after the break in south London, where Frank took charge of a home game for the first time.

Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock in the 66th minute, but the contest turned on its head when Jon Martin was sent off with a second yellow card for tugging down Jean-Philippe Mateta six minutes later.

The Frenchman fired in the resulting penalty before second-half substitute Dwight McNeil tapped home from Jorgen Strand Larsen’s overhead kick.

Yeremy Pino had a chance to put the game away with a stoppage-time penalty but he was denied by Unai Marrero, and the hosts had to grind out a nervy finish, with Henderson producing his biggest save of the night to deny Orri Oskarsson at the death.

The result moves the Eagles into a play-off position, after starting the evening just outside of it, in 25th.

Sunderland were left frustrated again in their Europa League campaign after drawing 1-1 with Jagiellonia Bialystok at the Stadium of Light.

The Black Cats enjoyed the best of the first-half chances through Malick Fofana and Nilson Angulo, but the visitors had an opportunity when Robin Roefs saved Kajetan Szmyt’s free-kick.

Sunderland struck early in the second half through Timur Tutierov’s header, his second goal in the competition, but Kamil Jozwiak levelled only minutes later after capitalising on a mistake at the back.

A point means the Wearsiders stay in the knockout phase play-off places after being held to their second draw from five games in the competition.

open image in gallery Duran spared Celtic's blushes ( AP )

Camilo Duran came to Celtic’s rescue in Europe again after coming off the bench to head a late winner against Torreense in Portugal. The Colombian striker peeled off to the back post to meet a cross from fellow substitute James Forrest and send a downward header into the net in the 85th minute.

Duran’s 15th goal of the season earned a 2-1 victory over the Portuguese second-tier side and put Celtic on six points in the Europa League after his double off the bench inspired a comeback win over Besiktas last time out.

Celtic took the lead in the ninth minute when Javi Vazquez sliced Jota’s cross into his own net with Yang Hyun-jun right behind him.

But the Portuguese Cup winners levelled 10 minutes later after some sloppy defending. Both Kieran Tierney and Colby Donovan had chances to deal with bouncing balls after Alex Alfaro hit the bar from 22 yards but they could not clear and Haiti international Dany Jean volleyed home.

Celtic dominated second-half possession but clear chances were at a premium until Duran struck.

News.title: Tyson Fury’s Netflix documentary: Mental health battles, tragedy and family revelations
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

To make her new Netflix documentary, director Lucy Wilcox sat with Tyson Fury in nine three-hour settings. He never broke eye contact, she says.

That could surely feel like its own form of sparring with the former two-time world heavyweight champion and eponymous protagonist of Tyson Fury.

In the 90-minute film, we see archival footage and interviews with the British boxing star, his divisive father John (a travelling man and former bare-knuckle fighter), and Tyson’s wife Paris.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury in archival footage from the new Netflix documentary ( Netflix )

If you’ve seen Netflix’s reality TV show At Home With The Furys, you’ll know that Paris, Tyson’s childhood sweetheart, has the patience of a saint. If you’re a boxing fan, you’ll know almost all of what is depicted here – Wilcox confesses she knew nothing of the sport before making the documentary.

So, boxing fans may be disappointed, and they might realise halfway through that the climax will be Tyson’s first fight with Deontay Wilder. But there are still things to be gleaned here.

For example, Tyson has long said he is bipolar, but his admissions in this film touch on something even deeper and more troubling. He speaks of being hospitalised during his hiatus from boxing in 2016, hearing voices, and having a “full-on conversation with the radio”.

There was confusion around a schizophrenia diagnosis, with the film updated on the eve of its release to clarify comments by Paris, who originally suggested Tyson was officially diagnosed with the condition. He has never received such a diagnosis, all parties have now insisted, thus Netflix’s late amendment of the film.

“He’s a narcissist,” Wilcox tells The Independent and other publications, yet with no intent to insult. “We Googled it, and he was like: ‘Yeah, that’s me!’ But I do like him. He’s gentle, he’s quite camp, quite feminine. Not everyone’s gonna like Tyson, but I wanted people to understand him. I wanted to understand him, because I wasn’t sure if I liked him.”

The intimate access to the Fury trio is both an advantage and disadvantage. Wilcox says this is a “story about family, ultimately”, which explains the decision not to feature other talking heads, but a bit of distance might have helped at times.

Enjoy 185+ fights a year on DAZN, the Global Home of Boxing Never miss a fight from top promoters. Watch on your devices anywhere, anytime. Buy Now . If you sign up to this service we will earn commission. This revenue helps to fund journalism across The Independent.

open image in gallery Director Lucy Wilcox spoke to Fury in nine three-hour sittings – he didn’t break eye contact once, she says ( Netflix )

Still, Wilcox does well to get to the heart of certain matters with Tyson, given he can be as evasive in interviews as he can in the ring, and the boxer even tears up at times. “Tyson remembers what he wants to remember; Paris shines a light on him,” Wilcox opines.

Yet her greatest triumph is cracking open John, whose imprisonment for gouging out another man’s eye is covered in the film, as is his revelation to a young Tyson that he has secretly been the patriarch of two families at once.

“I wanted to break him,” Wilcox says. “He always says, ‘It is what it is,’ but I wanted him to see that it’s not what it is.” Indeed, in one scene, John reflects on Fury’s comeback to boxing in 2017 and says emotionally: “That’s what I call a man – not what I’ve been.”

As mentioned above, Tyson’s incomprehensible performance against Wilder in 2018 (in which he outboxed the American for the best part of 12 rounds, before miraculously rising from a brutal knockdown in the final frame) is an inevitable endpoint, given the target audience of this film.

open image in gallery Fury’s father John eventually makes some honest admissions in the film ( Netflix )

Also inevitable, however, is the heavy focus on Tyson’s prior absence from the sport in 2016. He was open at the time about his problems with drink and drugs, and his desire not to live anymore, as he put on a terrifying amount of weight.

Yet boxing hardcores still question whether a failed drug test, relating to the anabolic steroid nandrolone, caused Tyson’s spiral.

The film does not mention this, nor his link to the controversial management company MTK Global (whose boss was suspected Irish crime lord Daniel Kinahan). However, Wilcox insists: “We talked about all of it.” She adds that those elements would have remained if the film had been a series instead (it started off as a six-hour project).

Admittedly, these elements would have been more interesting to a different audience, and not the one that Tyson Fury is truly aimed at.

Still, we get other controversies, like Tyson coming under fire for sexist and homophobic comments, and again Wilcox’s insight is useful. “He’s not sexist, he’s not homophobic,” she says. “But when you question him on certain things, he doubles down, like my kids would.”

open image in gallery Fury’s wife Paris acts as a grounding figure in the boxer’s life ( Netflix )

We also get tragedies like Tyson’s uncle and trainer Hughie having his life support switched off, and particular focus on one of three miscarriages that Paris suffered.

Tyson decided to bring the baby home, burying them in the garden with the help of his brothers. “I found the deepest, darkest locker I could find in the back of my brain,” Tyson says of his method of dealing with the episode. He himself, somehow, was luckier when he was born, despite being eight weeks premature and “dying three times” in hospital.

But what of the future? When Wilcox interviewed Tyson, he was in the midst of his fifth and most-recent retirement, and his friend and fellow boxing icon Ricky Hatton sadly took his own life. This documentary will surely leave viewers pondering Tyson’s mental health going forward.

It is a sombre note to end on, but it highlights the complexity of Fury’s story. Wilcox and Netflix told a single but compelling chapter – one can only hope he has many more ahead.

‘Tyson Fury’ is available to stream exclusively on Netflix from 27 November.

Editor’s note: This story was updated on Thursday 26 November following Paris Fury’s statement of clarification that Tyson Fury has not received a medical diagnosis of schizophrenia.

News.title: Labour MPs warn Burnham not to approve Rosebank oil field
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Approving the Rosebank oil field would “permanently damage” the UK’s climate credentials and threaten Labour’s chances of re-election, backbench MPs have warned Andy Burnham.

In a letter to the Prime Minister, dozens of backbenchers urged Mr Burnham to refuse permission to develop the oil project 80 miles north west of Shetland.

Monmouthshire MP Catherine Fookes, who helped organise the letter, told the Guardian it had been signed by 92 MPs, enough to make it difficult to carry on Labour votes alone.

open image in gallery Catherine Fookes (House of Commons/UK Parliament) ( PA Archive )

In their letter, the group said they were “increasingly concerned that the approval of the Rosebank oil field would permanently damage our climate credentials as a party and as a country”.

They added: “Polling is clear – in order to stand a chance of winning parliamentary majorities, maintaining our ‘progressive electoral base’ is imperative… approving Rosebank risks becoming an irreversible ‘point of no return’ for the party’s climate credibility, and risks alienating members of the electorate who have put their trust in our message of hope and positivity.”

Following the collapse of the Cop31 climate talks in Turkey last week, the backbenchers said the UK “must be wary about what signals we are sending our counterparts about our commitment to transition away from fossil fuels”.

And they cast doubt on the argument that Rosebank would be a significant boost for the Treasury, describing it as “not a serious revenue raising measure” and claiming it would provide “less than 0.1% of our annual UK tax revenue”.

open image in gallery Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh (PA) ( PA Wire )

The Government is yet to say when Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh will decide whether to approve Rosebank, although one of the companies with a stake in the project has said it expects a decision by the end of the year.

The decision threatens to become a major political problem for Mr Burnham, who has already come under pressure from environmental charities to reject the project.

But the Conservatives have called for the Government to “get Britain drilling” and approve the project, claiming it would secure jobs, tax revenue and energy security.

Last month, the Government approved production at the Jackdaw gas field, also in the North Sea, despite opposition from environmental campaigners.

Writing in the Guardian, Ms Fookes said she and her fellow backbenchers had felt “uneasy” about Jackdaw but “understood the reasons for that decision” as it was a “relatively small, short-lived” project.

But, she added, Rosebank was “a different proposition” that would “do nothing to reduce energy bills for our constituents”, with the oil produced being sold “to the highest bidder”.

open image in gallery (PA Graphics) ( PA Graphics )

She said: “If Rosebank is approved, champagne corks will pop in the offices of oil companies. But it will not make an iota of difference to our constituents’ energy bills.

“And it will accelerate the climate crisis, which is already pushing up food bills, causing devastating floods in winter and in summer turning our green and pleasant land into a parched, burnt-out expanse.”

Green Party leader Zack Polanski piled pressure on to the Prime Minister, welcoming “the growing number of Labour MPs making a stand against Rosebank”.

He said: “The Prime Minister is giving every impression of wanting to see it go ahead – just over a year after he signed the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty.

“From cutting warmer homes funding to watering down electric vehicle mandates – this Labour Government cannot claim to be a climate leader while engaging in climate vandalism.”

A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said: “Any decision on Rosebank will be made through the quasi-judicial process, taking into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received as part of the regulatory process.”

News.title: Sunderland ‘disappointed’ after banned Jagiellonia Bialystok fans enter Stadium of Light
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Sunderland have expressed their disappointment after a number of Jagiellonia Bialystok fans gained access to home sections at the Stadium of Light during Thursday night’s 1-1 draw.

UEFA had issued an away supporter ban against Jagiellonia for Thursday’s match on Wearside.

However, police and stewards were called to handle a disturbance within a home area of the ground during the early minutes of the game.

A club statement said: “Sunderland AFC is disappointed that a number of Jagiellonia Bialystok supporters were present in home areas of the Stadium of Light during tonight’s UEFA Europa League fixture.

“Jagiellonia Bialystok were subject to a UEFA away supporter ban for tonight’s Matchday 5 fixture, following a disciplinary sanction imposed by European football’s governing body.

“In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and UEFA. Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.

“We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and will review the circumstances surrounding their entry to the stadium.”

open image in gallery UEFA had issued an away supporter ban against Jagiellonia for Thursday’s match on Wearside ( Getty )

Sunderland struck early in the second half through Timur Tutierov’s header, his second goal in the competition, but Kamil Jozwiak levelled only minutes later after capitalising on a mistake at the back.

A point means the Wearsiders stay in the knockout phase play-off places after being held to their second draw from five games in the competition.

Sunderland remain without the injured Brian Brobbey and Granit Xhaka, and Regis Le Bris made six changes from their goalless Premier League draw with Aston Villa on Saturday.

Jagiellonia showed an early flash of danger when Nik Prelec weaved into the box and played a low cross into the area, but Roefs held the resulting clearance.

Sunderland caused problems when Angulo found Enzo Le Fee and the midfielder had his strike deflected narrowly behind.

Slawomir Abramowicz was forced to push away Fofana’s menacing shot before the half evolved into a scrappy affair.

A sudden burst of energy from the hosts saw Trai Hume chip over and Le Fee was at the heart of another solid attack.

The Frenchman went around Abramowicz before playing a low ball across the box towards Angulo lingering in front of an open goal, but his strike from close range was blocked by Yuki Kobayashi.

open image in gallery Timur Tutierov opened the scoring for the hosts ( Getty )

An enforced change six minutes before the break saw Luke O’Nien introduced for Omar Alderete and moments later Roefs was called into action to palm away Szmyt’s free-kick just outside the box.

On the stroke of half-time, Jagiellonia struggled to clear their lines and Hume blasted wide of the upright.

Sunderland brought on Jules Ahoka and Thomas Meunier at half-time and just two minutes after the restart they went ahead.

A good team move stemming from Chris Rigg’s break down the middle resulted in the ball reaching Le Fee and his cross from the right was deflected by Taras Romanczuk in to Tutierov to nod home at the back post.

However, their lead was short-lived when Jozwiak pounced on a tame attempted back pass from Reinildo Mandava and rolled past Roefs in the 52nd minute.

Another sloppy defensive error allowed Jozwiak to again latch on to the ball, but Roefs tipped the resulting shot behind.

Sunderland’s frustrations continued when Fofana’s half-volley was stopped and Angulo blasted a free-kick straight into the wall before Rigg’s low shot was comfortably scooped up by Abramowicz.

Both sides went close in the 90th minute when Reinildo’s header was saved by Abramowicz, and Jeremy Agbonifo broke for the visitors but was denied by Roefs as the game fizzled into a draw.

Sports.title: Xabi Alonso demands immediate reaction from Chelsea flops as his future rests on winning Stamford Bridge culture war

XABI ALONSO is in the middle of a culture war at Chelsea — and his future will hang on winning it.

After back-to-back humbling defeats to Sunderland and Leeds, having also lost to Tottenham at home this season, the Alonso era is off to a stuttering start.



Add to that Cole Palmer angrily dismissing a team-mate and coach at full-time at Stamford Bridge on Saturday, plus Wesley Fofana making a fool of himself in a YouTube interview, and all is not well in south-west London.

Alonso was hired to set the club on the correct course after a season of turmoil and some very serious looking in the mirror by the ownership.



The Spaniard was brought in to raise standards, stop wasteful red cards and put an end to the petulance which has defined Chelsea in recent years.

There has been plenty of talk of process and progress, and steps to be taken.

Alonso is aware that nothing will change if he can’t correct the undercurrent of immature behaviour.

Are we seeing any signs of a change? Not at all — and Alonso knows he has a big job on his hands to alter the attitude of his squad.

He said: “We are in the process. Taking steps, taking a step forward, but until it is totally in the DNA of the team it takes time.

“The tendency is improving, but we have highs and lows. We knew that could happen, but when you feel it, it is not good.

“When you have that feeling like we had on Saturday, it is not good.

“Having lived that, we have talked about what we can do better and what we have to do better.

“There are no excuses not to do better. There are things that we all can do, even if you have a bad day in terms of feeling something you have to do at this level.”

Alonso’s firm belief is that culture and team spirit come before everything. A strong culture leads to good football and good results.

The lack of a culture or identity, then, must lead to what we are seeing now, where Chelsea are too easy to push off course and soft when they need to stand up.



Alonso is concerned his side were unable to deliver the basics against Leeds and says that at Nottingham Forest on Friday night, there is no excuse not to at least deliver on that.

He added: “The feeling of the last game is not good, but now it’s about looking forward and showing a reaction. There are no excuses.

“There are no ifs, no buts. Just certainties and things we have to do.



“After the result, we can’t control, but how you approach the game, how you focus on your priorities.

“We can define on the training and the messaging. We need to show that, not just talk. Talk is cheap. It’s about performing on the pitch.”

One reaction would be to start fighting back, rather than roll over.

Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey pushed the Blues’ defence around, before Dominic Calvert-Lewin did the same on Saturday. Now they face a similar challenge, with a familiar face in Liam Delap.

The former Ipswich striker, sold by Chelsea to Forest for £45million one year and just three goals after his £30m move to Chelsea, will be desperate to expose his old club’s shaky foundations.



Delap was not a success at Chelsea and it was a feat they still made a profit after a poor single season, but his journey underlines an issue Alonso also wants to address.

Under their American owners, the Blues have never shied away from buying and selling at a level not seen before.

Sports.title: How Mikel Arteta’s ‘tactical tornado’ can blow Man City away with Arsenal set to adopt new approach in attack

ARSENAL will be looking to give their hopes of retaining the Premier League crown a huge boost when they host Manchester City on Sunday.

The Gunners are six points clear at the summit despite being forced to settle for a draw at Newcastle last week.



And City have been struggling to rediscover their best form, with Erling Haaland admitting his team-mates are not on the same wavelength.

SunSport’s tactical expert Dean Scoggins broke down how Arsenal could get the better of their title rivals in the latest episode of Tactics Exposed.



ARTETA’S MUSICAL CHAIRS

I think Mikel Arteta is making a conscious tactical effort to give Arsenal more chances to score goals.

Some fans might say they look vulnerable, I say fun. Last season, they were the functional champions. But this season, I think they’re going to be more fun.



It’s musical chairs from Arteta, with there being a high number of rotations in the system.

The full-backs are really making that chaotic move. Arsenal are ending up with their full-backs in central midfield positions when they are on the attack.

It gives the opposition problems because the transitions make it very difficult to mark.

The right winger, who is expected to be Noni Madueke, also moves into the centre forward position and Viktor Gyokeres was running into the channels against Borussia Dortmund.

They continue rotating and that creates more areas to run in behind the backline.

There were times in the draw with Dortmund where Piero Hincapie and Ben White, who started at full-back, were the furthest men forward.

The full-backs are the disruptors in this system. They are not getting on the end of the chances.

City’s defenders could get drawn out of position and that will lead to plenty of space in behind.

But Arsenal’s attacking shape means they could get caught out on the counter-attack.



If they go seven-versus-six on one side of the pitch, there could be space for City.

It’s a bit of a tactical tornado from Arteta, where it’s much more organised chaos than pure structure.

RAY OF HOPE?

David Raya will be a big miss because he is a fantastic goalkeeper. Kepa Arrizabalaga is a decent stand-in.



But Raya is the start of the tactical trigger. He plays them out and decides when to go short or long, but Kepa hasn’t done that as often.

City had a different approach to pressing when Kepa was between the sticks in the Carabao Cup final last season – and that is what we will see in this game.

Under Pep Guardiola, City moved into a 4-2-4 block shape. They dropped back and let Kepa have the ball.

Kepa made no passes into midfield during the Carabao Cup final because of how City set themselves up.

We will see Arsenal’s defenders split and the full-backs push up high and wide in an attempt to give their keeper options.



The central midfielders will also come out of the middle of the park to allow a pass to be made between the lines and into the attacking players.

Kepa needs to be brave on the ball because City will try to make it difficult for him.

RUNNERS SET TO MAKE DIFFERENCE

Arsenal should target their runners, like Madueke and Gyokeres. It worked for Napoli during their Champions League draw at the Etihad.

Full-backs have been caught out at times this season, leading to their midfielders and centre-backs being split.

I think Madueke and Gyokeres are going to have a bit of a field day if City get their press wrong.

Sports.title: Premier League legend Fabrizio Ravanelli wins High Court battle over £340k tax bill linked to playing days
Sports.content:
Next

PREMIER League legend Fabrizio Ravanelli has won a High Court fight with the taxman over a bill linked to his playing days.

Italian striker Ravanelli, famed for his prematurely white hair, was one of the biggest stars in the early days of the Prem with Middlesbrough.



When he later moved to Derby County some of his earnings were paid into an “employee benefit trust”.

Tax was due when that was paid up — but the former player successfully argued it should not have included the £340,000 in National Insurance contributions as that was down to his old employers.



Mr Justice Eardley said: “I shall quash the decision refusing to reopen the settlement agreement.”

He added: “HMRC will need to remake that decision, this time without any reliance upon the erroneous view that, as a matter of substantive tax law, the trustee was liable to pay NICs.”



The judge said HMRC’s refusal was “vitiated by a material error of law” — though added it would be “jumping the gun” to order them to reopen the settlement or hand over the cash immediately.

During the hearing, Ravanelli’s barrister Tim Johnston told the court: “The NICs were not owed by or on behalf of Mr Ravanelli. They remained liabilities of the employer, who had ceased to exist.

“According to HMRC’s own guidance, no sums should have been withheld in respect of NICs when the distribution from the EBT was made to Mr Ravanelli.

“Mr Ravanelli’s case is that, as a matter of tax law, NICs were never due. As a result, no amount for NICs should have been deducted from the distribution out of the EBT.”



HMRC barrister Adam Tolley KC had argued: “When the trustee made the distribution, for the purposes of the relevant NICs legislation it did so as the deemed employer of the claimant and he received the distribution as the deemed employee of the trustee.

“As such, the trustee was liable to pay the NICs.”

Boro face bitter rivals Southampton for the first time on Friday since last season’s Spygate controversy rocked the football world.

Security has been ramped up on the South Coast ahead of the game, and Hellberg knows his table-toppers will be stepping into a cauldron. But he wants his players to enjoy every second and learn from it.

Sports.title: Emile Heskey, 48, now working new job selling controversial sweets after England cult hero’s split from wife
Sports.content:
Next

FORMER England star Emile Heskey is promoting a controversial CBD gummy.

The former Premier League star, 48, enjoyed a long career as a player, where he was best known for his time at Leicester and Liverpool.



Now, he is one of a host of celebs including Katie Price and former Arsenal midfielder Paul Merson endorsing Supreme CBD Gummies.

In a video posted to Instagram on October 26 Heskey stood in a warehouse surrounded by the products.



He wrote in his caption: “I swear by these products for my sleep.

“They have been fantastic for me for years now!”



Ex-Team GB Olympic boxer Anthony Fowler founded the company and has made unsubstantiated claims about their health benefits.

In 2024, the Advertising Standards Authority upheld a complaint after it was claimed SupremeCBD products could cure symptoms of anxiety and depression

The ASA noted: “We considered the ad made claims that implied SupremeCBD could be used to treat or manage chronic anxiety and depression.

“This included claims that SupremeCBD was more effective at treating those conditions than medically prescribed anti-depressants.



“Therefore, by marketing the product as a treatment for depression and chronic anxiety in direct contrast to prescribed medication, this discouraged essential treatment for those conditions.



“Chronic anxiety and depression were conditions for which medical supervision should be sought.

“Regardless of any evidence to support the effectiveness of CBD, any advice or treatment relating to those conditions should have been given under appropriate supervision.

“Whilst we welcomed Supreme CBD’s assurance that the ad had been removed, we did not receive any evidence which showed their advice and product was provided under the supervision of a suitably qualified professional.



“We therefore concluded that the ad discouraged essential treatment for conditions for which medical supervision should be sought and had breached the Code.”

In June, the ASA placed Supreme CBD Ltd on its public list of non-compliant advertisers for repeatedly breaking UK advertising rules.

The NHS acknowledges that CBD has some medical uses, but has warned that the “quality and content” of products sold online cannot be verified and some are “potentially dangerous.”



SunSport reached out to Heskey for comment via his management but have not received a reply.

Heskey split from his Real Housewives of Cheshire star wife Chantelle in July after more than 20 years of marriage.

They share four children together – sons Jaden and Reigen and daughters Milanna and Mendez.

Sports.title: Duran scores late Celtic winner to keep Europa League hopes alive
Sports.content:
Camilo Duran came off the bench to keep Celtic's Europa League hopes alive with a vital win against Torreense.

The Colombian striker peeled away to the back post to meet a cross from fellow substitute James Forrest, guiding a downward header into the net in the 85th minute.

Duran's 15th goal of the season secured a 2-1 victory over the Portuguese second-tier side and moved Celtic on to six points in the Europa League. His latest decisive contribution follows a match-winning double off the bench in the Hoops' comeback victory over Besiktas last time out.

Celtic took the lead in the ninth minute when Javi Vazquez turned Jota's cross into his own net, with Yang Hyun-jun lurking behind him.

Celtic dominated possession after the break but struggled to create clear-cut opportunities until Duran's late intervention secured all three points.

Sports.title: Bears stun Lions with TD in final seconds of NFL Thanksgiving epic
Sports.content:
The Chicago Bears scored the game-winning touchdown with just three seconds remaining to secure a stunning 39-35 comeback win over the Detroit Lions on Thanksgiving and claim first place in the NFC North.

Rome Odunze's second TD - a sensational toe-tap grab in the back of the end zone - clinched the victory and deny Detroit, who had led by 11 earlier in the fourth quarter after Jahmyr Gibbs ran in his third score of the game from 70 yards out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Detroit Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs scored an incredible 70-yard Touchdown during their game against the Chicago Bears

Chicago's lead secured right at the death was the first lead change in a game they've been involved with since they trailed the Carolina Panthers 7-0 in the first quarter of their opening game of the season. They had trailed the Lions for 53 minutes and 31 seconds of this match.

The Bears' dramatic win nudges them into solo first in the fiercely-fought NFC North, at 9-2 on the season, while the Lions drop to 8-3 with a first loss in seven.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports NFL's Ndamukong Suh and Jason Bell ate their Thanksgiving turkey live but one pundit was left far from impressed.

It also improves Chicago's record in the division to 1-2, with Detroit now 2-1, which could prove crucial should any potential playoff tiebreakers be necessary to separate the two teams - who meet again on the penultimate week of the season - or the Minnesota Vikings (7-3) and Green Bay Packers (6-5).

The game was initially slow to ignite, with only a Lions field goal to show from the first quarter, before Gibbs' first score to start the second lit the blue touchpaper.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Campbell's call to take the safety pays off, as the Lions then follow that up with a touchdown from Sam LaPorta.

The Lions continued to lead thereafter, until the Bears came roaring back in the final quarter. Caleb Williams firstly located Odunze deep down the field for a 41-yard TD, the QB ran in the resulting two-point play to cut the score to three, before Jared Goff threw an interception on the next series.

Chicago turned the ball over on downs, failing to convert on 4th and 3 just inside Detroit territory, but they got the ball back with just over two minutes to go, and this time marched down the field before Williams linked up with Odunze again for the game winner with seconds remaining.

Williams finished with 345 yards passing and those two scoring strikes to Odunze, while Bears running back D'Andre Swift had 162 yards from scrimmage and a touchdown. Gibbs had 20 carries for a massive 205 yards and three TDs for the Lions but it didn't prove to be enough.

Sports.title: NZ skipper Latham laughs off Pant dominating local cricket under false name
Sports.content:
New Zealand captain Tom Latham has laughed off India's Rishabh Pant dominating a local Christchurch cricket match under a false name, a day before their second Test.

On Monday, Daryl Mitchell and Glenn Phillips held firm for 43 overs to earn the Black Caps a hard-fought draw in Wellington after India posted a record score of 720-9d.

Pant scored 128 in that Test, with the second Test between the sides beginning on Thursday at Hagley Oval.

Yet, footage has since emerged of Pant playing for club side Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones on Wednesday, scoring 54 off 21 balls under the name 'Stan Stan' to seal a 16-run victory.

In an interview with The New Zealand Herald, Open House player Mohammad Safi said he had seen Pant on an electric bike in the city and asked if he would play, due to his club team being a player short.

"Did he play?! How'd he go?" Latham said at his New Zealand press conference. "That's brilliant!

"It's great. He's obviously a real character of the game, is Rishabh.

Image: New Zealand's captain Tom Latham (right) leads his side into the second Test after a gritty draw in the first Test

"It's great for him to be giving his experience back to LMS (Last Man Standing) teams!"

Pant has scored 3,853 runs in his 53 Tests for India, averaging just below of 45.

The 29-year-old also boasts a strike-rate of 74.43, which is bettered only by Virender Sehwag and Kapil Dev among players to have scored more than 2,000 Test runs for India.

Sports.title: Frank earns first Palace win with late comeback against Sociedad
Sports.content:
Thomas Frank earned his first win as Crystal Palace manager, coming from behind to beat Real Sociedad 2-1 in the Europa League.

The Dane lost his opening game to Coventry at the weekend, but saw the heart and fight he will need from his side as they picked up their second win in the competition this season.

Image: Thomas Frank applauds the fans after winning his first game as Crystal Palace manager

For 70 minutes, Sociedad dominated at Selhurst Park, with Dean Henderson needed to make a string of saves. They finally made the breakthrough when Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr tapped home from Job Ochieng's cross.

But the game turned out of nowhere as Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty and Jon Martin was sent off. He picked up a second yellow card for holding Jean-Philippe Mateta round the middle, with the striker expertly dispatching the spot kick to level for the Eagles.

Image: Jean-Philippe Mateta proved influential in masterminding Crystal Palace's comeback victory over Real Sociedad

The confidence surged in the hosts - backed by the famous atmosphere at Selhurst Park - and it was a well-worked second that put them ahead.

Yeremy Pino's cross was cleared to Jorgen Strand Larsen at the back post, who hit an overhead kick. It wasn't on target, but it did bobble into the six-yard box for the incoming Dwight McNeill, who slid to poke home.

Image: Jon Martin was sent off for Real Sociedad

Crystal Palace could have wrapped up the points in a topsy-turvy end after they were awarded another penalty. Carlos Soler was penalised for handball, but Pino's effort was well-saved by Unai Marrero.

The win catapults Crystal Palace into 12th place in the league phase table, just two from the top eight, and gives them a huge boost ahead of another key clash against Hull on Super Sunday. Real Sociedad have slid down into 27th.
