World.title: ‘Shocking’ decline seen in hep B vaccination against incurable virus, including babies with infected mothers
World.content:
Fewer newborns are being vaccinated against hepatitis B, an incurable infection that can lead to liver disease, including babies whose mothers are known to have the virus, a large new analysis has found.

As of June, just 66% of newborns got the hepatitis B vaccine within a day of their birth, down from 80% in 2022. The birth dose serves as a safety net especially for babies whose pregnant mothers are unaware they’re infected with the virus and unknowingly transmit it during childbirth.

Up to 90% of babies with the virus develop chronic infections, putting them at risk for liver failure and liver cancer later in life. Vaccinating them at birth dramatically lowers those odds.

The new study from Truveta, a health care and analytics company, included medical records from more than 1.3 million babies born in the United States from January 2018 through June this year.

During that time period, newborn vaccination rates increased from 76% in 2018 to 80% in 2022 before declining in mid-2023, falling to 66% by June this year.

“It’s shocking to see a nearly 15% decline in three years,” said Nina Masters, lead author and principal applied research scientist at Truveta. “Infants born to mothers with hepatitis B have a 90% chance of perinatal infection. That can mean a lifetime of chronic liver disease, cirrhosis and early death. This is a real preventable tragedy.”

The decline began before federal vaccine advisers voted in December to abandon a decades-old recommendation that all babies be vaccinated against hepatitis B at birth. (That decision was later halted by a federal judge in response to a lawsuit filed by the American Academy of Pediatrics. The block remains in effect.)

The findings mirror increasing trends in anti-vaccine behavior in general. A recent NBC News data investigation found three-quarters of U.S. counties that track kindergarten immunization rates no longer meet the minimum threshold to prevent measles outbreaks.

Now, measles outbreaks are popping up nationwide, with nearly 6,000 cases and at least 13 deaths, according to state health departments. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status Nov. 16, reversing one of the country’s greatest public health achievements this century.

“We talk about measles being the canary in the coal mine. We’re seeing those outbreaks,” said Dr. Richard Besser, a pediatrician and president of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. “This one — hepatitis B and the rise in unvaccinated newborns — these are the kinds of things that are silent, that you don’t see for years and years until these babies grow up and end up having liver disease.”

The study, published Tuesday in NEJM Evidence, also revealed that hepatitis B vaccination rates have fallen among babies born to mothers known to be infected with the virus. Up to 98% of those babies were vaccinated between 2018 through 2025. But between January and June, that rate dropped to 94%.

Cases of acute hepatitis B fell dramatically in children after the the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began recommending a universal birth dose in 1991, falling 99% from 1990 to 2019. A CDC analysis of children born from 1994 to 2023 estimated that hepatitis B vaccination prevented more than 6 million infections and nearly 1 million hospitalizations.

Last year, the University of Minnesota’s Vaccine Integrity Project published a review of more than 400 studies, finding no evidence of short- or long-term health problems from the hepatitis B shot after birth.

“Reversing the successes of previous public health programs puts individuals’ lives at risk,”

Dr. James Conway, a pediatric infectious disease physician and medical director of the UW Health Immunization Program in Madison, Wisconsin, wrote in an email. “It’s sad, tragic and preventable.”

World.title: Trump to visit Arizona manufacturer of semiconductor chips
World.content:
A White House official said Thursday that President Trump is planning to visit the groundbreaking of a Phoenix facility for a manufacturer of semiconductor chips, including for Nvidia, a trip that comes as the company is under increasing scrutiny for the president's involvement in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO after he had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

On Dec. 4, Mr. Trump will tour and deliver remarks at the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) facility in Phoenix, Arizona, a White House official confirmed Thursday. The Taiwan-based company has been expanding in Arizona since 2020, according to the company's website, and next week's visit will be to the latest expansion of its facilities.

The official said the new expansion is expected to fund more than 10,000 direct jobs and another 11,000 indirect jobs in the surrounding community.

It's unclear whether Arizona Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs or the state's Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego would attend the event next week.

The planned visit comes amid scrutiny of Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, with its high-powered chips emerging as integral to the race for AI dominance between the U.S. and China. Co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang earlier this month resigned after the news broke of his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former top executive at Singapore-based tech firm Megaspeed and who U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. China has denied it.

Mr. Trump advocated for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, with an official saying earlier this week that reinstating him would "preserve America's technological edge over China, strengthen our national security" and ensure the future of AI will be built in the U.S. Sources also told CBS News that Mr. Trump was privately concerned about the broader implications for the U.S. economy should Nvidia's value collapse.

Nvidia's board reinstated Huang on Monday, and Mr. Trump touted his return in a social media post shortly afterward.

World.title: Trump claims "fake economic numbers" were released before election
World.content:
President Trump is spending Thanksgiving in Florida, where he had a policy meeting early Thursday morning and then headed to his golf club nearby.

He and first lady Melania Trump, who are staying at Mar-a-Lago, are planning to call U.S. service members on Thursday evening.

On Thursday morning, Mr. Trump posted a holiday message on social media, wishing a happy Thanksgiving to the "American patriots who have worked so hard to make our country great!" He continued in the lengthy post to wish a happy Thanksgiving to several others with whom he has grievances, including the Commerce Department, immigrants, "the radical far left" and more.

Mr. Trump claimed that before the midterm elections where Republicans suffered heavy losses, there were "fake Economic Numbers" released. Mr. Trump cited the Commerce Department on Wednesday revising the gross domestic product in the third quarter to 4.3% on an annual basis, up from a prior estimate of 3.4%. The Commerce Department regularly updates its monthly economic data to improve its accuracy, including not just the GDP but also the monthly employment data.

Although he did not present any evidence, the president demanded an investigation.

Mr. Trump also wished a happy holiday to "all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left, those that are looking to change our Court System to that of Sharia, those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work."

The president continued his post with messages about the Somali community, deported immigrants and those who he believes do not appreciate the White House ballroom he is constructing.

Overnight, Mr. Trump praised the Army's controlled detonation of about five tons of degraded lead azide in Iowa, blaming former President Barack Obama for the situation and writing that no "carcinogens were released into beautiful Iowa air." Although Mr. Trump and other administration officials have praised the detonation, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News on Wednesday that prior to it, there was a chaotic lead-up inside the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner.

On Wednesday night, Mr. Trump met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and the pair issued a joint statement describing the meeting as "very impactful" and focused on Russia, Ukraine and Iran. The statement said they discussed "the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war."

Mr. Trump earlier in the week continued the annual tradition of pardoning turkeys, sending turkeys named Freedom and Feathers to live on a farm in Texas. Melania Trump, meanwhile, welcomed the official White House Christmas tree on Monday.

World.title: Fake online stores may fool AI shopping bots on Black Friday
World.content:
Scammers are using AI to churn out convincing copies of real online stores, and this Black Friday, the AI agents that many shoppers will rely on often can't tell the difference.

These fake sites pose a risk to the millions of Americans who are tasking their AI agents with making online purchases and transacting on their behalf.

"Artificial intelligence just makes building websites so much easier. You can upload anything into HTML and build a website very, very easily," Harrison Tang, co-founder of Spokeo, a data aggregator, told CBS News.

AI is enabling scammers to build what Tang described as convincing dupes of legitimate online stores in only hours, including copies of a brand's logo, marketing language and product images and descriptions.

"AI just makes creating these look-alike fake stores a lot easier, so there is a proliferation of them," Tang explained. "Platforms will try to catch them by not directing users there, but there are so many of them popping up all the time that they are hard to keep up with."

Research from Microsoft shows that criminals can use AI to set up fraudulent e-commerce sites in mere minutes rather than the days or weeks that were once required.

Spokeo identified copycat sites of dozens of popular brands, including UGG, L.L. Bean, Converse and Stella McCartney. As of Nov. 15, it had identified 65 distinct online stores that mimicked the legitimate sites of 60 brand names, according to its online shopping scam study.

L.L. Bean's copycat site lacks a corporate address and phone number. Spokeo

A deal that seems too good to be true is often a tip-off that a site is fake. Spokeo

The discrepancies between the authentic stores and the scam websites are subtle and require close examination.

The first place to look for proof of fraud, according to Tang, is in the online store's web address. For example, a fake Converse store uses the web address converseshop.us.com, whereas the real store's address is converse.com. The .us domain name is the top-level domain for the U.S. and is reserved for U.S. residents, but is commonly used for phishing attempts, according to Tang.

"It looks like an official website, but it's not, so if you don't pay close attention, it's easy to get tricked," he said.

AI agents need to get savvy

Bots aren't as well trained as some humans are at spotting phony websites, which can dupe even discerning shoppers because of how realistic they look.

Recent research from Podqi, a firm that monitors for intellectual property infringement, on AI search risks shows that AI engines can inadvertently direct shoppers to scammy stores.

The group asked popular AI tools, including OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Perplexity, questions about where to buy particular brands online. More than 18% of the AI bots' answers drew on a fake, infringing or invalid website.

For example, when asked where to buy clothing from Stussy, a streetwear brand, Perplexity referred to us-stussy.com, which it mistakenly identified as the brand's official website and "the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items." The web address us-stussy.com directs shoppers to a fake store. The real store's address is stussy.com.

Other brands with duplicate online stores include Figs, a medical scrubs maker; sock company Bombas; and dairy brand Fairlife.

World.title: Germany arrests 2 Iraqis allegedly tied to Iran-linked terror group
World.content:
Berlin — German authorities on Thursday arrested two Iraqi men on suspicion of terrorism. The suspects are alleged to be members of an Iran-linked terrorist organization that is said to have targeted U.S., Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe.

The men, who were arrested in Cologne and Heidelberg by the Federal Criminal Police Office, are Iraqi nationals Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., according to the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office.

The investigation centers on alleged links to Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya, a shadowy group that emerged to claim a series of sabotage, arson and violent attacks targeting Jewish institutions in Europe not long after the start of the U.S. war with Iran. The U.S. government has labeled HAYI a front for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iran-backed militia Kataib Hezbollah in Iraq. Britain has designated HAYI as a terrorist organization.

According to investigators, Mostafa Al-R. is alleged to have maintained contact with Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is currently facing criminal charges in the United States. Al-Saadi is considered a central figure within the alleged terrorist network.

As early as late 2025, Al-Saadi, Mostafa Al-R. and other individuals allegedly founded an independent group whose goal was to carry out terrorist attacks in Germany and other European countries, according to prosecutors. Ameer J. is also a member of this group, they said.

The group planned to target synagogues in Cologne and another European city, prosecutors alleged, saying unknown perpetrators traveled to the locations in March 2026 on behalf of the organization. The plans were not implemented for unknown reasons.

HAYI is also linked to attacks on Jewish institutions in the United Kingdom, France, Belgium and the Netherlands, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution said.

The suspects are accused of membership in a domestic terrorist organization under Section 129a of Germany's Criminal Code. The investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice had already issued the corresponding arrest warrants on Nov. 18.

Along with the arrests, extensive searches took place in Baden-Württemberg, Hesse and North Rhine-Westphalia. A total of 17 locations were searched.

More than 250 officers from the Federal Criminal Police Office, the Federal Police and the participating state police forces took part in the cross-state operation.

In Hürth, the investigative measures targeted another suspect, prosecutors said.

The proceedings were initiated based on information from the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution. The two detainees are scheduled to be brought to the presiding investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe on Thursday. The judge will decide on their pretrial detention.

The Federal Prosecutor's Office did not disclose further details regarding the length of the two Iraqis' stay in Germany, their immigration status or any other nationalities they may hold.

The investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Maps show where Thanksgiving storms are disrupting holiday plans
World.content:
Various types of severe weather are affecting large stretches of the United States, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving plans and hampering travel for Americans along both coasts and into the middle of the country.

A storm system that developed over Florida earlier in the week continued to pound that state and others in the Southeast, causing flooding that has impacted highways and flight schedules. About 1,300 flights into and out of the U.S. were delayed on Thursday morning, and another 400 or so had been canceled, according to the tracking site FlightAware.

Miami International Airport had canceled around 30 incoming flights and delayed around 50 following a brief ground stop Wednesday night after a FedEx cargo plane ran off a runway amid rainy conditions. No injuries were reported.

Meteorologists said they expected the storm to travel up the coast and move into the Northeast on Thanksgiving, with forecasts showing high winds and heavy rain across the region. Meanwhile, parts of the Midwest, including St. Louis, Missouri, could see snow around the holiday.

CBS News

About 80 million Americans were in the path of potentially severe weather on Thursday, and tens of millions had been placed under alerts, which included warnings for high wind, winter storm weather and flooding, depending on the region.

The weather service warned of powerful wind gusts, potentially as intense as 70 mph, brewing along a massive stretch of the East Coast, from South Carolina up to Massachusetts. Possible coastal flooding could make roads impassable in certain areas, it said.

In New York City, organizers of the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade announced the parade would be postponed until Saturday due to the storm. It's the first time in the parade's 100-year history that it's been postponed, although it was not held at all from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II. In 1971, the balloons were grounded due to strong winds, but the parade still went on.

CBS News

While the city isn't expected to get excessive rain, a relatively rare High Wind Warning has been issued for all five of its boroughs, along with nearby parts of New Jersey. The weather service in New York reported early Thursday that wind gusts reached 45 mph at LaGuardia Airport while emergency management officials said the state's monitoring stations recorded widespread gusts of up to 30 mph.

The wind warning will remain effective until Friday afternoon, according to the weather service, which said people within the alert area should prepare for destructive winds to down trees and knock out power lines, likely causing widespread outages.

"Travel will be difficult," the weather service said, "especially for high profile vehicles."

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Wednesday night declared a state of emergency for New York City, along with Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties.

"We're expecting heavy rain and strong winds that could create dangerous travel conditions," she wrote on social media.

In a separate travel advisory, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said forecasts indicated that the worst of the storm would likely hit the city beginning Thursday afternoon into late Thursday night.

CBS News

In addition to New York, other major cities like Boston, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Washington, D.C., would likely receive chilly rainfall on Thanksgiving, forecasters said, although they noted that most metropolitan hubs were expected to be spared from the highest amounts. They did warn that a combination of freezing rain and formidable winds, possibly gusting up to 75 mph, in D.C. could make any sort of travel difficult on the holiday.

Up to 5 inches of rain, or more, could fall in other places, especially in southeastern states like Florida and the Carolinas. They could also face damaging winds, tornadoes and, potentially, waterspouts as the storm system unfolds, forecasters said. The system already brought more than half a foot of rain to Miami by Thursday morning, resulting in significant flooding for some residents who woke to find roads and parking lots submerged in water.

CBS News

Interior portions of the eastern U.S. and some spots in the Midwest could receive their first measurable snowfall of the season around Thanksgiving. The weather service issued several winter storm warnings and winter weather advisories for parts of Illinois and Missouri, including St. Louis, through Thursday evening, as sections of both states brace for up to 6 inches, or even 9 inches in certain areas, of snow.

"Roads, especially bridges and overpasses, will likely become slick and hazardous. The weight of snow on tree limbs may down power lines and could cause sporadic power outages," the weather service in St. Louis wrote in a Wednesday advisory, which recommended that people delay travel completely, if possible.

World.title: FedEx cargo plane runs off MIA runway, causing brief ground stop
World.content:
A FedEx cargo plane ran off a runway at Miami International Airport amid wind and rain Wednesday night, prompting a temporary ground stop during one of the busiest travel days of the year.

According to an FAA advisory, departures bound for Miami were grounded until at least 9:45 p.m. Preliminary reports indicate a FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 cargo plane went off the runway, prompting the halt in incoming air traffic.

The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office said it responded to the runway at MIA at approximately 8:40 p.m. and found the cargo plane.

Neither of the two people on board was injured, and responding emergency crews from both the Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office and Miami-Dade Fire Rescue reported no signs of fire or smoke.

MIA posted on X, confirming the incident happened at Runway 26R and that all runways were closed except for Runway 9R.

A FedEx aircraft overran Runway 26R at Miami International Airport at approximately 8:40 p.m. All runways are closed except for runway 9R. @MiamiDadeFire units have responded, and there are no reported injuries. Passengers scheduled to travel tonight are encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport. We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations. — Miami Int'l Airport (@iflymia) November 26, 2026

Minutes before flights were set to resume, the FAA also posted on X about the incident, confirming that the FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 had departed from Frederick W. Smith International Airport in Memphis.

On Thursday afternoon, the National Transportation Safety Board posted on X and said it was investigating the "runway excursion at Miami International Airport."

Wet weather investigated as a possible cause for the incident



At the time of the incident, rainy conditions had reduced visibility to 7 miles, with a 13-mph tailwind reported at the airfield.

An airport employee who witnessed the aftermath and asked not to be named said the crew appeared to struggle to slow the aircraft on the wet pavement before it veered onto the grass.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," the employee said.

The worker noted that the overrun occurred on the airport's shortest runway, raising renewed concerns following a September Amazon cargo plane crash that killed five people.

The brief ground stop Wednesday left some Thanksgiving travelers waiting for hours before flight operations resumed.

"I'm kind of shocked," traveler Dennis Pastorizo said. "I didn't think that a delivery plane would cause a two-hour delay for a flight to the other side of the country, especially on one of the busiest [travel days] of the year."

FedEx issued a statement to CBS News Miami about the incident that says:

"FedEx Flight 910 from Memphis to Miami experienced an issue upon landing Wednesday evening at Miami International Airport. We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."

The FAA announced Wednesday night that it is investigating the incident.

World.title: Elon Musk doubles SpaceX share pledge for U.S. children
World.content:
Elon Musk is upping a pledge to kickstart U.S. children's savings.

On Wednesday, Musk and SpaceX said they will give every U.S. child two shares in the space exploration company, doubling a pledge the world's richest person made in October, which he said at the time would be the "first of many" planned gifts.

In the statement, SpaceX said it would give each child a newly issued share of its Class A common stock. The company will contribute the shares to U.S. kids' Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts the White House created to help American children build long-term savings.

Musk will personally match the number of shares SpaceX donates, according to Thursday's statement.

Additionally, SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell will donate more than 2 million SpaceX shares to U.S. children.

The total giveaway is worth about $18 billion, based on SpaceX's most recent stock price.

"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in announcing the donation. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."

There are roughly 70 million children in the U.S. who are eligible for a Trump Account. The Trump administration is automatically enrolling kids under eighteen with a valid Social Security number in the program. However, parents or guardians must still claim their child's account for it to be active.

As of Tuesday, friends and family members had contributed more than $1 billion to individual Trump Accounts, according to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

Additionally, philanthropists including Michael and Susan Dell and other donors have made major gifts, bringing the total assets deposited in Trump Accounts to over $9 billion.

World.title: High school band raises $350K to stay for Macy's Thanksgiving parade
World.content:
One high school marching band from Texas says it has raised $350,000 to cover the cost of its 500-member group remaining in New York City after the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was rescheduled until Saturday due to a potentially historic storm hitting the region on Thursday.

"It's been exhausting and emotional to figure this out, but it has been incredibly humbling to see an outpouring of kindness," Ryan Demkovich, the director of the Pride of Pearland Marching Band at Pearland High School in Texas, told CBS News about raising the funds required to cover the extended trip.

Other marching bands that traveled to New York from across the country are also raising money to cover the cost of their extended stays. For many of the high school musicians, the parade is a once-in-a-lifetime chance to perform for millions of spectators along the route and watching at home, and the postponement has made the trip significantly more expensive.

"This was quite a challenge for us, and there was a very frantic and large call to action to our community to let the kids stay here and finish it out," Demkovich added.

By Thursday, the band had raised enough money to pay for two extra nights at a hotel and to charter buses back to Texas after the parade on Saturday. One logistical challenge: They'll have to relocate from the Marriott Marquis in Times Square, which is booked for the weekend, to a hotel near the Meadowlands Sports Complex in New Jersey.

And they'll travel home by bus on Saturday because flights are booked until late Monday or Tuesday, Demkovich said. The donations also cover extra meals for the ensemble.

The parade's delay also scrambled plans for tourists and family members who had traveled to New York to see the parade on Thursday. Among them was the Sims family, who traveled from Florida to see their daughter perform as part of the Great American Marching Band.

"We came up to see her. It's our first time in New York City," Dustin Sims told CBS New York. "We've had a great week, but now we gotta decide whether we're gonna stay another day or not."

Outpouring of support

Demkovich told CBS News that the group's fundraising push quickly spread across social media, soliciting contributions from Pearland businesses with a history of charitable giving and from strangers alike.

Several Texas businesses, including Gringo's Mexican Kitchen in Pearland and Houston's Mattress Mack and CenterPoint Energy, opened their wallets by making generous donations through a fundraising link on the marching band's website.

Eight other marching bands are scheduled to perform on Saturday. The Dobyns-Bennett High School Band from Kingsport, Tennessee, also issued a plea on social media, calling on its community to help defray the cost of the band staying in New York through Saturday.

"While we are grateful that our students will still have the opportunity to perform in this historic 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade during the Dobyns-Bennett Band's own centennial year, this unexpected change presents significant logistical and financial challenges for our program," the group said in a post on social media on Wednesday.

"Extending our stay in New York City means additional expenses that were never anticipated in our original trip budget, including extended charter bus rentals, additional nights of hotel accommodations, and meal stipends for our students," the group added.

By Thursday morning, the Dobyns-Bennett Band said it had met its undisclosed fundraising goal and that the band would be staying in New York through Saturday to perform in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

"We have secured the necessary funding for the band to stay the extra night and to pay for the extended bus contract to get the kids home on Saturday!" the group said in the post.

World.title: Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate
World.content:
Congo Ebola outbreak reaches 12,000 cases as some responders evacuate

toggle caption i Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP

BUNIA, Congo — The fast-moving Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo has topped 12,000 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, as fighting between rebels and the army disrupts efforts to contain the spread of the disease.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and nearly half the 12,021 people confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from Congo's Ministry of Health. It is also the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.

The outbreak declared in May is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Response teams are battling armed conflict, poor roads and violence from residents fueled by mistrust and misinformation.

Sponsor Message

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of people who are sick or have died from the disease. Containing the disease requires quickly identifying and treating patients in isolation, monitoring people who may have been exposed and safely burying the dead.

Fighting between the army and the Convention pour la révolution populaire rebels resumed Thursday morning in Iga-Barrière, a mining town about 25 kilometers (15 miles) north of Bunia in eastern Congo, sending new waves of displaced people toward the city. Bunia is the capital of northeastern Ituri province and a major hub for the Ebola response.

CRP is one of more than 100 armed groups in eastern Congo, where conflict has created one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The group was founded last year by former warlord Thomas Lubanga, who was convicted by the International Criminal Court in 2012 of recruiting children under 15 and using them in fighting.

Fighting between the army and the rebels earlier this week had already prevented teams from reaching some communities, disrupted monitoring of people exposed to the virus and left some treatment centers with fewer staff, Dr. Catherine Smallwood, the World Health Organization's Ebola incident manager, said Wednesday.

Sponsor Message

Smallwood said that about a dozen people, including two WHO personnel and Congolese health officials, were evacuated to Bunia on Tuesday after three full days trapped in a hospital in Akwe, northeast of the provincial capital, amid intense crossfire.

World.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
World.content:
North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture

toggle caption i Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring U.S. President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.

Experts say Kim likely wants to show off his evolving nuclear arsenal, the backbone of his authoritarian rule, and reaffirm his rejection of any future talks on dismantling his nuclear program.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.

Sponsor Message

KCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.

North Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defense capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment." He accused the U.S. of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said.

"The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.

Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.

Sponsor Message

"Trump has talked about a willingness to meet Kim Jong Un, but the basic U.S. position that North Korea must denuclearize remains unchanged. So Kim Jong Un wants to say 'Look at how powerful we are. Don't talk about denuclearization if you want to meet us,'" said Moon Seong Mook, an analyst for the Seoul-based Korea Research Institute for National Strategy.

Moon said Kim's visit to the nuclear facilities was also likely meant to check on how state objectives on the nuclear program have progressed this year and what future goals must be set ahead of a year-end Workers' Party conference.

South Korea's Defense Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the U.S. South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the U.S.

Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.

In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there … There'll be a time when we meet … It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."

Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."

Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.

Sponsor Message

Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."

Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

World.title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says
World.content:
Storms disrupt Thanksgiving travel. And, FCC violated ABC's free speech, judge says

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Severe storms sweeping across the nation threaten to cause widespread travel delays today, as millions of people gather with their loved ones. New York City officials announced that the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been rescheduled to Saturday due to the threat of powerful wind gusts that could reach up to 60 mph. This year marked the 100th procession, and the first time the iconic event is being postponed.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

🎧 Something is happening across almost every part of the country right now, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Extreme high tides are affecting the West Coast, snow is expected in parts of the Midwest, and in the South and Southeast, a major storm is advancing up the East Coast. Meteorologist Richard Bann with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center tells Lonsdorf the East Coast storm is the primary concern. Bann says the storm will become better organized throughout the day, bringing strong winds and heavy rain that could lead to coastal flooding. The good news: Forecasters expect the East Coast's major storm to move on, mostly wrapping up by Saturday, Lonsdorf says.

Sponsor Message

The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs targeting goods from 14 major U.S. trading partners, including China, Japan and the European Union. Administration officials argue the measures counter unfair foreign trade practices, though critics question their ultimate effectiveness. Proposed rates may reach 40% on Chinese imports, 35% on Vietnamese goods, and 20-25% on products from other targeted nations. Additional tariffs on Brazilian sugar and aircraft are also being suggested.



🎧 U.S. Trade Ambassador Jamieson Greer said that new tariffs could take effect within a couple of months. For each country, the White House has listed a "proposed" rate and a "deal" rate, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben says. For example, if talks with China progress positively, they may receive a deal rate of 20%, which is different from its proposed rate of 40%. Although the Supreme Court overturned President Trump's previous tariffs, the new ones fall under Section 301, a law meant to counter unfair trade practices. The administration says these countries exhibit "structural excess capacity" in various manufactured goods, a situation caused by policies that lead to overproduction, which can distort the global market.

Federal scientists are testing the air, soil and water in Eastern Iowa for lead contamination after the U.S. Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown yesterday. Officials said the controlled explosion was the only safe way to dispose of the bomb-making compound.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio says the major concern is the potential release of lead into the air from the explosion. She adds that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has tested the area since the detonation and hasn't found lead in the air. The EPA has deployed around 300 people to sample the air, ground and nearby water. Lead is a neurotoxin that especially endangers children and pregnant people because it can impede childhood development. After a week and a half of delays and inconsistent communication from the Army, residents have grown hesitant about the Army and the EPA's initial findings, Billingham says. Residents want independent monitoring and the University of Iowa and the University of Illinois are conducting regional sampling. Results are expected in a few days and should show if their measurements align with the EPA's data, Billingham says.

A federal judge has blocked Trump from challenging the ABC television network's broadcast licenses. U.S. District Court Judge Loren AliKhan ruled that the president retaliating against satire and commentary he dislikes is unconstitutional. AliKhan issued the preliminary injunction yesterday and dismissed the administration's request to throw out ABC and Disney's lawsuit challenging the review of the local license. Licenses typically last eight years and are rarely revoked. AliKhan's decision drew heavily on Trump's public statements and social media posts against ABC and Disney, as well as comments from Brendan Carr, the president's pick for chair of the Federal Communications Commission.

Life advice

toggle caption i J Studios/Getty Images

Holiday shopping season is in full swing. Before you spend, consider if you actually need what's in your cart. Sales are exciting because our brains are wired to seek newness. Retailers capitalize on that urge. To escape the cycle of constantly wanting more, shop intentionally and appreciate what you already own, says Eric Athas, author of Saying No to New. He shares his insights on breaking this cycle and finding joy in your current possessions with Life Kit.

Sponsor Message

🛒 Delete the app or remove your credit card info if you have one-click checkout with a company.

🛒 Add an item to your online shopping cart and leave it for 24 hours. Research shows that delaying a purchase decreases your interest in it.

🛒 Make intentional choices. Don't reject all new things. After you understand this, you can learn to say no to the wrong items and yes to the right ones.

🛒 Revisiting old things can provide you with untapped enjoyment in them, research has found. You can apply this by rereading a book or by traveling to a city you have visited before.

For more guidance on how to reclaim joy without seeking newness, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

Picture show

Andrea Starr

Apple farmers across the Pacific Northwest are ripping out thousands of acres of orchards and grinding trees into mulch because growing the fruit no longer pays. Many say they're being crushed by soaring labor and equipment costs and international tariffs. Even multigenerational growers are leaving land unused rather than hemorrhaging money. Thousands of acres of fruit have been left to rot unpicked on branches, pushing some well-established farms into bankruptcy. Federal farm relief has also largely failed to reach specialty-crop growers. Take a look at photos and videos of affected farms, and read more about how the region that supplies the majority of the U.S.' fresh apples is handling the challenge.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Emilee Chinn/Getty Images

The Pittsburgh Steelers have cut quarterback Aaron Rodgers after he claimed in an interview that the team's head coach sleeps in meetings. The Ariston Cafe opened in 1924 along Illinois's Route 66, serving classic American diner fare. The National Register landmark attracts international travelers and hosts local milestones, from wedding proposals to 65th anniversaries. In this week's Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Emily Feng brings readers views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro. She was able to see it during a camping trip at altitude.

Sponsor Message

World.title: At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course
World.content:
At Albuquerque's Indian Pueblo Kitchen, Native American dishes are the main course

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

There are plenty of kitschy diners and barbecue joints along Route 66, but just a couple of miles off the highway in Albuquerque, N.M., Native American dishes are the star at Indian Pueblo Kitchen.

Late on a weekday morning, the restaurant was already starting to fill up. Most of the tables were taken up by locals, like Merlyn Liberty and Rolf Pendall.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

"I started with breakfast dessert. The blue corn waffles. And now I'm finishing up my sweetheart's plate of enchiladas and pinto beans," Pendall said.

The restaurant is attached to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a museum and cultural center founded in 1976 by the 19 Pueblo tribes of New Mexico.

Sponsor Message

The center sits on land where the Albuquerque Indian School operated. Open from 1881 to the early 1980s, it was one of the hundreds of federally funded boarding schools designed to strip Native American children of their family bonds, languages, culture and spiritual practices.

The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center's president and CEO, Monique Fragua, said visitors can start in the museum's galleries and then visit the restaurant to experience Pueblo culture and hospitality.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

"Whether that's through our exhibits, or our food, or in our gift shop, we can celebrate the art of our Pueblo communities," Fragua said.

Museum cafés are not a typical destination for foodies, but this one is.

The menu is all Native American and Southwestern-inspired. Dishes include blue corn enchiladas that you can get "Christmas style," one with red chile sauce and the other with green chile sauce. There's a chile posole with beef short ribs served on the bone, as well as Indian tacos on homemade fry bread. Then there's a dish that's really popular on social media: pickles marinated in cherry Kool-Aid and then deep-fried and served with a green chile ranch sauce.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

Rita Toledo, from Jemez Pueblo, is Indian Pueblo Kitchen's star baker. One of her specialties is biscochitos — fragrant shortbread cookies spiced with anise and rolled in cinnamon sugar that are New Mexico's state cookie. Toledo has made some twists on the traditional biscochito, like making a chile pepper version that has just a little kick at the end with a nice balance of sweet and heat.

Sponsor Message

Indian Pueblo Kitchen's version of biscochitos is so popular that the restaurant also sells them at its café inside Albuquerque's airport. Toledo turns out at least 48 dozen biscochitos each week just for the airport location.

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

While we chatted, Toledo was wrestling to open a giant tub of one of her main ingredients — lard. These cookies can be made with butter or shortening, she said, but "lard's the only way to make good biscochitos."

Toledo said that she has been baking all her life and that her favorite part of her work is rolling out dough.

"It calms me. You know, your energy comes out on your dough," Toledo said. "I always tell my bakers, 'Come in happy and in a good mood. That way, your products will come out nice and everybody's gonna love it.'"

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

Along with locals flocking to visit, the restaurant is also a hit with tourists like Kathy Allio and Jeff Allen from Pennsylvania. While we chatted, Allio was finishing a bowl of bean chili with elk meat.

"The red chiles are just very flavorful without being hot," Allio said, "so it's delicious."

One thing Fragua, the center's president, is particularly proud of is that the Pueblo community can see itself reflected in the museum's galleries and programming and on the restaurant's menu.

"We're lucky to have that history here on our campus, that we've taken lands that were once created to really change the identity of Native people and change that story of who Native people are," Fragua said. "We've created a campus that's built on resilience, empowering our voices and truly telling the stories of who we are as Native people."

toggle caption i Adria Malcolm for NPR

Additional reporting by Jeanette DeDios of member station KUNM.

World.title: 'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII
World.content:
'Memories of a Good Meal': How food made a difference during WWII

toggle caption i Denny Culbert; June Hersh and Alon Shaya

NEW ORLEANS — Chef Alon Shaya believes there's power in a meal.

"It's always been the way that I can start a conversation, build a relationship, disagree about things, but still be able to come together and break bread," Shaya, of the acclaimed Crescent City restaurant Saba, said one recent afternoon. "When you share a meal with someone, a lot of those barriers get broken down."

The Israeli American chef also believes food can be a source of inspiration even in the darkest of times. A few years ago, he spearheaded the Rescued Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and that got him digging deeper into the role that food played during World War II.

Sponsor Message

Now, he's collected those stories and the dishes they inspired in a new historical cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.

Shaya hopes home cooks use the recipes to inspire dinner table conversations about the deeper stories behind them.

"I want people to gather and cook and eat and put their phones down, and share a meal and recount these miraculous stories of survival, resilience and heroism," he told NPR.

Stories like that of Roddie Edmonds, a U.S. Army master sergeant, whose unit was captured in the Battle of the Bulge and imprisoned in a German POW camp. (Edmonds posthumously won the Congressional Medal of Honor earlier this year for his refusal to turn in his Jewish troops to be sent to concentration camps.)

One of the ways Edmonds and his fellow prisoners distracted themselves from the horror of the camp was to talk about the foods that reminded them of home, be it Sunday spaghetti sauce, hot cakes or cherry pie.

"They're eating up this idea that they were going to go home," Shaya said. "They were going to be free, and they were going to be able to sit around and dig into that filet mignon with creamy mushroom sauce."

Sponsor Message

The servicemen sketched out detailed plans for a dreamed-of restaurant called the Jolly Chef. There, they would serve all those yearned-for dishes, including candied yams with pecans and whipped marshmallow — one of the recipes in the new cookbook.

Another chapter highlights Polish partisan fighters who lived in underground bunkers and sabotaged the Nazis by derailing trains and blowing up ammunition plants. In a nod to the fire that ensued, a recipe from their chapter also includes smashed potatoes flambéed in vodka.

"Vodka was a form of currency for them," Shaya said. "They would use it to barter. They would use it to celebrate. And so each moment of that recipe helps to really tell the story of what they were going through."

The book has stories from around the world – Hungarian Jews whose non-Jewish cook salvaged the treasured family cookbook as they were being sent to Auschwitz; a French village that took in Jewish children and hid them from the Nazis; Navajo code breakers who changed the course of the war; and Japanese Americans, convicted of no crimes, who were incarcerated in military-style camps in the U.S.

June Hersh, a food historian and writer who worked with Shaya on the cookbook, said remembering and talking about favorite recipes was a form of resistance – turning a tragic situation into something triumphant.

"You can put me in a uniform, you can make me do hard labor, you can shave my head, you can starve me if you want, but I'm not going to let go of my food memory," she said. "It's something you can't take away from me."

World.title: A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty
World.content:
A dish with a story, Thanksgiving with culinary historian Michael Twitty

toggle caption i NPR

This Thanksgiving, Morning Edition host Leila Fadel left the studio for her kitchen, where she was met by the two-time James Beard Award winner Michael Twitty, who came with a spice blend, fresh sage, fish peppers and onions from his garden.

His book, The Cooking Gene, planted him as one of the nation's foremost chronologists tracing his ancestry through African American culinary history.

Kush, the forerunner to Southern cornbread dressing

Kush is one of Twitty's most beloved Thanksgiving offerings and one he's been making since he was a teen. The name and the ingredients show the way food became a tool for the enslaved in the Americas to preserve their cultures.

Sponsor Message

"The name comes from Hausa, the language of West Africa. They are a predominantly Muslim people, but Muslim in the way that West Africans do Islam – which is Islam with a lot of the influence from the traditional culture and spirituality," he said on the origins of the side dish. "And so the name Kush, it's like, couscous," he added.

toggle caption i

The dish is one that connects Twitty to his ancestry.

"There was a time when I couldn't tell you what particular African ethnic groups I came from, but now that I know that I'm part Wolof, Hausa, Fula, and Serer and so many others," he said. "Now, I know this dish has a connection to who I am and my roots and where I came from."

In the making of this dish, Twitty also shared his work documenting the ways African American Jewish people create hybrid dishes in the kitchen.

"It's Matzah ball gumbo, and it's black-eyed peas and quiche," he said of his Black and Jewish identity. "It's a lot of dishes that were from North Africa or from Ethiopia, it's kosher jollof rice and Shito. Shito usually has shellfish in it – we don't put that."

What Thanksgiving and this dish mean to Twitty

The author of four books tracing the deep roots of the foods he loves says for him it's less about the lore of Thanksgiving, and more about the people the day brings together.

Sponsor Message

"I have to say that along with a lot of other African Americans, not everybody, but a plurality of us, Thanksgiving, as it's been expressed, means very little," he said of the holiday. "Which means we're not attaching ourselves to the myth of Thanksgiving, we don't really care for that. But we do love tradition, we love cooking, we love food, we love gathering."

And in that spirit, Kush in particular, remains one way for him to taste history.

"It means I haven't forgotten who I come from. And it means I haven't forgotten that I have a legacy to leave," he said.

You can find the recipe for Twitty's Kush in his book, Recipes from the American South.

World.title: Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid
World.content:
Court lets Puerto Rico governor fire firm that runs the island's troubled power grid

LUMA Energy took over the electric grid five years ago. The court's ruling nullifies its contract, and gives the government a year to find a new operator.

Transcript

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

Puerto Rico's supreme court has ruled the island's governor can kick out the private company that's been running its troubled power grid for five years. The decision could have huge consequences for electric service in Puerto Rico. Here is NPR's Adrian Florido.

ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: After Hurricane Maria flattened Puerto Rico's already rickety power grid in 2017, the island's government privatized it. It gave a company called LUMA Energy, based in Canada and Texas, a 15-year deal to take over the power lines, promising that LUMA would rebuild the grid stronger and improve the notoriously unreliable service. LUMA took over in 2021. But things have not gone as planned.

Blackouts are still a constant fact of life. LUMA has come in for harsh criticism from customers and officials. Last year, Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez-Colon filed suit to nullify LUMA's contract. Yesterday, the Puerto Rican Supreme Court ruled in her favor that LUMA must go.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

JENNIFFER GONZALEZ-COLON: Today is a day of celebration on the island.

FLORIDO: This is the governor speaking after the ruling. She said LUMA has not lived up to its promises.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GONZALEZ-COLON: More outages on the island, more shutdowns on the island. They have not fulfilled the requirements of the contract.

FLORIDO: In fact, the island's supreme court ruled on procedural grounds, saying officials had not followed local requirements when approving agreements with the company. The court gave the local government a year to put a new operator in place. The governor said the work to find a new private company will start immediately.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

GONZALEZ-COLON: It's going to be a good transition. We're going to make it in a year. And I hope that all companies that are interested in participating in this process will fulfill and follow the process of law. And we're going to be opening that process for public bid.

FLORIDO: The court gave LUMA Energy 10 days to request a reconsideration of its ruling. In a statement, LUMA said it is considering its legal options. The company has long argued that the grid it took over was in awful shape and that it is not fully to blame for the blackouts. A new operator will need approval from both the local government and a federal oversight board that Congress put in place 10 years ago to get Puerto Rico out of bankruptcy. In a statement, that board criticized the governor for ending LUMA' s contract without having a new company ready to go. It said it's worried about the continuity of service on the island. In her remarks yesterday, the governor said she has a plan in place and will reveal it soon.

Adrian Florido, NPR News.

(SOUNDBITE OF TOBACCO'S "BACKWOODS ALTAR")
