World.title: Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed
World.content:
Powerful storms disrupt holiday travel, as Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is postponed

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

Tens of millions of people are bracing for delays at airports and highways across the country on Thursday, as powerful storms across the United States threatened to disrupt travel for the Thanksgiving holiday.

On the West Coast, high tides have flooded streets along California's shorelines and knocked off a part of Pacifica Pier. The floods have also prompted evacuation warnings. On the East Coast, authorities are preparing to weather the impact of a storm making its way up into New England from the southeast with strong winds and heavy rain. Snow was also forecast in parts of the Midwest.

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

Some 81.5 million people in the U.S. are expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA .

Sponsor Message

Hundreds of flights had already been cancelled or delayed by early morning Thursday, particularly on the East Coast, where authorities have warned people to stay home as the storm barrels through. The majority of people are expected to travel by car for the holidays, and the winter weather could affect their plans due to visibility issues on the road.

toggle caption i DANIEL SLIM/AFP via Getty Images

Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center, told NPR that the East Coast storm remained the main concern, calling it a "multi-hazard" storm.

"It's going to be getting better organized as we go through the day, and it'll be spreading a considerable amount of wind, heavy rain. The real concern with this thing is going to be coastal flooding," Bann said.

Meteorologist Matthew Cappucci with The Washington Post and MyRadar told NPR the storm's magnitude at this time of the year was "unusual."

"We would expect this in deep winter," Cappucci said.

The storm in the East Coast, however, is expected to mostly clear out by Saturday, easing weekend travel for those returning from Thanksgiving gatherings.

Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City delayed

Beyond travel, several Thanksgiving parades have also been affected by severe weather.

Sponsor Message

The incoming storm is expected to cause high winds in New York City, prompting Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday to delay the city's famous Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade. Organizers were already inflating the iconic giant balloons for the parade on Wednesday when officials announced the decision.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

The parade, which is now expected to take place on Saturday, will be the city's 100th, and while it was cancelled before during World War II, this is the first time that it's been postponed in the last century.

The parade's organizers said it took two years to prepare the elaborate celebration, which includes over 11,000 participants and volunteers, thousands of high school marching band musicians from across the country and hundreds of balloon handlers. In previous years, up to 2 million spectators have attended the parade.

"Safety is and will always remain our top priority, and this will be a heavy storm," Mamdani told reporters.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images

He urged the city's residents to prepare for extreme weather conditions. He said the city expected sustained winds between 30 and 40 mph and possible gusts as high as 65 mph, with resulting floods and flash floods.

"Generation after generation has watched Spongebob and Spiderman soar down our streets and has taken in Garfield floating down 6th Avenue. And I know this change of plans will cause inconveniences," Mamdani said. "Yet safety has to come first."

Philadelphia also grounded all balloons for its parade this year due to winds.

Steve Kastenbaum contributed reporting for this story.

World.title: Ford says he wouldn't hesitate to shoot a home invader, encourages Ontarians to 'fight back'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he wants to see legal changes to address a spate of home invasions, and in the meantime is advising people to "use anything you can to protect your family."

Ford says he is a legal gun owner and wouldn't hesitate to use it on someone trying to break into his home, advising people without guns to use knives or baseball bats to protect themselves and their children.

"I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back," Ford told reporters at Queen's Park on Thursday. "Not hide, but fight back."

"Someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up, I'll blow the guy right through the front door. You'll look like Swiss cheese by the time he's done."

The premier was reacting to the fatal shooting of a 39-year-old musician during an overnight home invasion in an affluent midtown Toronto neighbourhood on Wednesday.

It happened nearly a month after a violent home invasion and shooting in the Bridle Path neighbourhood left a family of four adults injured.

WATCH | Victim in fatal home invasion was Toronto musician: Victim in fatal home invasion was Toronto musician | Duration closed caption 2:41 Police have identified the victim of a shooting during a home invasion in midtown Toronto Wednesday as Michael Eckert, 39. As CBC’s Dale Manucdoc explains, police are seeking at least one suspect.

Police suggest contacting 911 first

Toronto police said in a Wednesday news conference that people facing home intruders should contact 911 first.

"The Toronto Police Service provides the very best that it can in terms of public safety services," said Det. Sgt. Alan Bartlett. "I would encourage people to contact 911 to tell people what is happening."

Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said he trusts police.

"I would call 911 and make sure my family is safe and allow the police to do their job," he said. "I think it's incredibly dangerous to suggest to people that they should be shooting other people."

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said Ford should be looking for ways to ensure people feel safe in their own homes, not telling them to arm themselves in order to protect their families.

"Doug Ford, he's really good at writing letters and coming out with outrageous statements, but the truth is that he can control some things in the province of Ontario," she said.

"For example, we have absolutely overloaded courts right now in the province of Ontario. We are letting the bad guys out too soon because of these packed courts, and he can do something about that and refuses to take responsibility.

"He has the power as the premier of Ontario to be able to protect Ontarians, and instead he's saying, 'You're all on your own. Protect yourselves.' That is unacceptable."

Past comments on Ford's take on crime

It's not the first time the premier has advocated for a violent approach to crime.

At an unrelated news conference in June of last year, Ford told a story about masked men who had tried to steal a vehicle overnight from his home, saying that if they came back, he would "take care" of them better than the police.

At the same news conference, he said a man charged by York Regional Police for allegedly shooting a gun in the air during an attempted vehicle theft deserved a medal.

A few months later, the premier spoke about threatening to beat up a Home Depot shoplifter.

Earlier this year, he said a York Region resident who shot and injured an alleged home invader "should have shot him a couple more times."

"Congratulations," he said. "I'm glad you shot the guy."

WATCH | Ontario Premier Doug Ford praises homeowner who shot intruder: Ontario Premier Doug Ford praises homeowner who shot intruder | Duration closed caption 2:06 Ontario Premier Doug Ford congratulated the homeowner who shot and injured an alleged home invader north of Toronto, saying he 'should have shot him a couple more times, as far as I'm concerned.' Opposition leaders denounced the comments as irresponsible.

Premier calls for legal change on federal level

Ford says he is directing his attorney general and solicitor general to look at legal changes that could bring the province "right up to the edge" of so-called castle law.

Ford has previously mused about introducing the castle doctrine, laws in some U.S. states that allow people to use reasonable force, sometimes including lethal force, to protect themselves in their homes.

Attorney General Doug Downey says there are already rules around self defence, but that they will examine whether the line is in the right spot.

Ford also called on the federal government to strengthen bail laws and increase mandatory jail time for violent offenders, which federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre echoed.

"This unfortunately has become an all-too-common story," he said in Ottawa. "Canadians are literally afraid to go to sleep at night."

The federal government's Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, or Bill C-14, received royal assent in June. It makes over 80 changes to the Criminal Code, Youth Criminal Justice Act and the National Defence Act to make bail and sentencing laws tougher for repeat and violent offenders.

Meanwhile, criminal lawyers and justice advocates have said that the changes could put more pressure on an already backlogged court system while doing little to address the factors that lead people to commit crimes.

Home invasions hit a 10-year high in 2024, before dropping in 2025 and then rising again at the beginning of this year in Toronto, according to CBC News analysis of Toronto police data. Affluent areas with large detached houses and driveways were among the hardest hit.

World.title: 12 First Nations in B.C. buy stake in Coastal GasLink pipeline
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A group of 12 First Nations in British Columbia is buying an indirect ownership stake in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, backed by a $168-million loan guarantee from the federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program.

On Thursday, CGL First Nations Limited Partnership (CGL FNLP) announced an agreement to purchase an economic interest in an entity owned by TC Energy that holds the company's 35 per cent limited partner stake in the pipeline.

This deal marks the second Indigenous equity partnership to buy into TC Energy's stake in Coastal GasLink this fall, following a $65-million announcement in October for a separate, five-nation coalition.

Together, 17 First Nations along the route now hold an equity interest in the project.

"Our government is building a Canada where Indigenous Peoples are true partners, with the resources and opportunity to pursue their own ambitions and play a leading role in shaping the path forward. That is what meaningful reconciliation looks like in practice," said Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty in a statement.

Coastal GasLink is a 670-kilometre pipeline that carries natural gas from near Dawson Creek in northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada export facility in Kitimat. It is owned by Coastal GasLink Pipeline Limited Partnership, with TC Energy as the operator.

It is the only direct path to the West Coast for natural gas to be liquefied and shipped to Asian markets.

The 12 nations part of the deal include: Cheslatta Carrier Nation, Kitselas First Nation, Lheidli T'enneh First Nation, Nadleh Whut'en First Nation, Nee Tahi Buhn Indian Band, Saik'uz First Nation, Skin Tyee Nation, Stellat'en First Nation, Ts'il Kaz Koh First Nation, Wet'suwet'en First Nation, Witset First Nation and Yekooche First Nation.

The terminal served by the pipeline, LNG Canada, is planning a major Phase 2 expansion, doubling its capacity from 14 to 28 million tonnes a year, putting it on the trajectory to become one of the largest LNG facilities in the world.

The pipeline still faces some First Nations opposition, including from hereditary leaders who had fought its construction through blockades and other protests.

In a statement, Wet'suwet'en and Gitxsan leaders said the existing Coastal GasLink pipeline did not obtain free, prior and informed consent of all impacted nations, nor has the expansion project.

"We respect every nation's right to self-determination, and the reality is this project destroyed our lands without our consent. CGL was built despite Canada and B.C. recognizing in a memorandum that Wet'suwet'en rights and title are held by the Wet'suwet'en Houses under their system of governance," said Wet'suwet'en Hereditary Chief Na'Moks.

The federal Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program provides up to $10 billion in loan guarantees to reduce borrowing costs so Indigenous communities can buy equity stakes in major projects.

World.title: After nearly 6 decades on the job, this retired CBSA officer shares stories from 'the booth'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Windsor Morning 11:17 Customs worker retires after 55 years on the job

Anne Marie Handsor wasn’t quite 18 years old when she was hired to help secure the border between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Mich.

Most of her time with the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) was spent on the front lines at the Ambassador Bridge.

Fast forward 55 years and she's finally leaving the customs booth with lots to reflect upon after retiring last week.

Not quite 18, Handsor was hired to work for Canadian customs in 1971 in Windsor. (Submitted by Anne Marie Handsor)

Handsor, a Windsor native, began her career as a customs officer in 1971 when there weren't many women working for the border agency in the region.

“I do know I was the only young female officer at that time — there were five older women,” she told CBC Radio’s Windsor Morning host Amy Dodge.

“The funniest thing that used to happen to me, when people would pull up to my booth and they would go, 'It's a female.' And I go, ‘Yeah, so what's with that?’"

She said they would then reply with, "'Well, we don't like female officers because they're too thorough,’ because they thought we asked too many questions — and we did."

WATCH | Windsor, Ont.'s Anne Marie Handsor just retired after 55 years at the CBSA: After nearly 6 decades on the job, this CBSA officer shares stories from 'the booth' | Duration closed caption 3:31 Anne Marie Handsor started working with Canada Border Service Agency when she was 18 — now, after 55 years with the agency, she's retiring. She spoke with Windsor Morning host Amy Dodge about how the job changed over her years of service and some of her favourite memories.

The union representing Canada’s border employees called Handsor “an officer at heart.”

“She loved her job and interacting with the travelling public,” said Lisa Howe, Customs and Immigration Union (CIU) Windsor branch president.

“She was always full of stories and had so many pioneering experiences with the agency through her 55 years … and helped pave the way for women in the agency when there were very few women working at the border.”

Handsor holds a picture of herself, during the start of her career as a Canadian customs worker in the 1970s. The Windsor native recently retired after 55 years on the job. (Leandra Vermeulen/CBC)

The CBSA calls Handsor’s 55 years of service one of the longest tenures in its history.

Spokesperson Maria Bohotineanu said Handsor's career demonstrated an exceptional commitment to border security and serving Canadians.

“The CBSA is grateful for her decades of dedication, professionalism and contributions to the organization,” said Bohotineaunu. “We congratulate her on this extraordinary career milestone and wish her all the best in her well-deserved retirement.”

What’s changed over the years?

When I started, all we had was a pen and a badge, and there was no protection at all. If somebody ran the port, meaning that they didn't stop at the booth, we'd have to shout, ‘Stop at the name of the Queen,’ three times — and then we could try to catch them. Well, nobody ever caught them. Anne Marie Handsor, 55-year Canadian customs officer

“When I started, all we had was a pen and a badge, and there was no protection at all. If somebody ran the port, meaning that they didn't stop at the booth, we'd have to shout, ‘Stop at the name of the Queen,’ three times — and then we could try to catch them. Well, nobody ever caught them, but that was just something that happened.”

The fallout of Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks invoked more change for customs than any other one thing or event, according to Handsor.

“That was a frightening day that day because so many people [Canadians] work over there [Michigan]. Nurses, doctors, teachers — they were all coming back home. It was a very bad day. I'll never forget that day because we realized …. right around that time that the public … was different. The public was more dangerous than in the past. The public, they saw your uniform and they they were respectful. But that's all changed. Having the tools that we do have now, it's very necessary.”

Handsor said a “multitude” of guns are coming across the border to this day — with “five, or six or more” at a time. As for drugs, she said, they’re predominantly being hidden in commercial trucks.

Human smuggling is also frequently discovered, according to the recent retiree.

“We've seen people being smuggled underneath, holding on to tractor-trailers, coming over the bridge. That's how desperate people are to get into Canada. But this … one I'm thinking of had 11 people underneath, but they did get caught.”

Vehicles move along Windsor's Huron Church Road, which leads to the Ambassador Bridge. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

Handsor said that when she worked at the Ambassador Bridge and specifically during her time manning the truck lane, the fumes were bad.

“I had a light blue shirt. Everyone of us at the end of the day, the black soot from the trucks that were coming out every day, our collars at the back were just black — like, you had to wash those.”

Emotional COVID-19 crossings

During the peak of COVID-19, the land border was closed between Canada and the U.S. for roughly a year and a half.

Handsor said she felt for the roughly 1,500 Canadian nurses who crossed into Michigan for work each day during the pandemic — especially during what she referred to as the “worst period.”

“When everybody was dying and they were putting the bodies into refrigerated trucks, the nurses would pull up to the booth and they would literally start crying because they were exhausted and they've never seen anything like this.”

A Gordie Howe bridge finale

Before she put a wrap on her nearly six-decade career, Handsor asked — and was granted — permission to work one shift at the new Gordie Howe International Bridge on her last day.

“It was nice. It was a gift to me. It is really high tech. It's really good. It's clean right now. It's a beautiful bridge. The booths are a lot bigger than the ones at the [Ambassador] bridge are, and they're clean.”

Handsor got her wish granted at the end of her career to work one shift at the Gordie Howe International Bridge, shown in this drone view with transport trucks and cars entering Canada. (Carlos Osorio/Reuters)

Handsor says she contemplated retiring five years ago but wanted to wait for the new crossing to open first.

“That was what my goal … and then it was a disappointment because we were going to have an honour guard. I was part of the honour guard. Then because of Trump … not letting the U.S. open the bridge, it was scaled down. We were all hyped up … it was supposed to be like a big happy celebration.”

Her share of celebrity encounters

Handsor said she had the privilege of meeting then U.S. President George W. Bush and Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chrétien roughly one year after 9/11 — an encounter she’ll never forget.

“My boss had told me, he said, 'Be prepared because George W. Bush is known for turning around and mingling with the workers.' And sure enough, he turned around, and he took my hand and he shook it. And he said to me, ‘Thank you for the work that you do, officer.’ And I said nothing. No words came out of my mouth. I don't think I talked for two days because I was in [awe]. I just wish that I could have met [U.S. President Barack] Obama, too.”

Other well-known people she encountered were musicians Smokey Robinson, Kid Rock, Bob Dylan and Alice Cooper.

Retirement plans: Good health, good garb

Now that she has finally entered the next chapter of her life at age 73, Handsor said her focus is clear.

“I hope for good health.”

Handsor looks at photos of her time working for the CBSA. (Leandra Vermeulen/CBC)

She also said she wants to give more attention to her wardrobe, now that she doesn't have to worry about wearing her work uniform five days every week.

“It was a good career. And I never actually minded ... I never didn't want to go to work.”

World.title: So, your personal info was hacked in a breach. Here's how scammers use it against you
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The hacks just keep coming.

Canadians have been hit with a string of data breaches recently, with companies and organizations such as Bell, Staples Canada's printing website, KPMG, Pattison Food Group and Toronto's Hospital for Sick Children all reporting cybersecurity incidents in the last few months alone.

In many cases, personal — but not financial — information was accessed by unauthorized third parties. Bell and Staples Canada both confirmed no financial information was exposed in their recent breaches.

While it may come as a relie f to those affected that their credit cards and bank accounts, at least, haven't been compromised, information such as mailing addresses, passwords and phone numbers were.

That's enough to increase the risk of falling victim to identity theft or a financial loss, according to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.

WATCH | Fears AI is making data breaches easier: Bell cyberattack raises fear AI is making data breaches easier | Duration closed caption 1:49 Bell Canada has confirmed that an ‘agentic’ threat actor breached its systems on Nov. 17, which may have exposed personal information belonging to customers of Bell, Virgin Plus and Lucky Mobile.

When companies say that no financial data has been stolen, or that the breach was small, people tend to think the breach wasn't that serious, said Ali Dehghantanha, a professor in the school of computer science at the University of Guelph and a Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity and Threat Intelligence.

But he said criminals can stack and merge the personal information taken from multiple breaches — a piece here from Bell, a piece there from Staples — and use it to try to access your finances, often with the help with AI.

"Once you stack them up, it becomes much easier to scale your attack and targets a much wider and bigger audience," Dehghantanha told CBC News.

"Companies judge each breach alone. But criminals add all of them up. And that's what gives the criminals the upper hand."

How hackers use personal data

While companies at the centre of some of the most recent breaches, such as Bell, said no financial information was compromised, our identity alone can be linked to financial information, said Jeff Horncastle, an outreach officer at the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

"They can potentially have enough information to be able to compromise existing accounts, get into existing accounts or apply for new credit with the information that they've gained," he told CBC News.

"And if they're missing any information, they may be behind a different type of fraud where they're phishing for the information that they're missing."

Scammers can use the information they've accessed from breaches to trick victims into handing over their own financial information on scam calls, Dehghantanha said.

Bell's leak, for instance, included the date and amount of customers' last payment, which call centres use to verify their identities.

People walk bast a Bell store in downtown Montreal on May 7, 2025. Bell is one of several Canadian companies who recently warned customers their personal data had been accessed by hackers. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

If someone has access to a bill you've paid recently, they now have your phone number, and can call you and say your payment for a specific amount on a specific date failed, Dehghantanha said.

If the small pieces of information they repeat to you seem legitimate, they might convince you to give them your card information.

"These bills that have been leaked, have been stolen, are now the gateways," Dehghantanha said.

The scam can also go both ways. Criminals can call companies pretending to be person whose information they now possess, and ask to have their phone number moved to a new SIM card.

So, next time you log into your bank and it texts you an authentication code, the scammer will get it instead, giving them access to your account, Dehghantanha explained.

What to do if your data was breached

Business are required to notify affected customers of a breach.

If you receive a notice about a data breach, contact the organization directly using its official website or phone number, Horncastle said, because sometimes fraudsters will pretend to be a breached company. (Fraudsters have even been impersonating the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre for years).

You need to be suspicious for at least a year, not a week. Ali Dehghantanha

If your information has been exposed, Horncastle says you should change your passwords and contact your financial institution if needed. Some companies will offer credit protection through either Equifax or TransUnion, but he strongly suggests using both.

Try to find out what information was accessed and be cautious for how it may be used, Dehghantanha said. In the recent Staples breach, for example, order summaries and encrypted passwords were accessed by an unauthorized third party.

A customer shops at a Staples Canada store in Richmond Hill, Ont. on Nov. 17, 2026. Staples Canada said there was a 'security incident' on its staplesprint.ca website in early November, which saw a third party get unauthorized access to certain customer data. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

That could mean criminals now have access to your print orders, which might include wedding invitations, or funeral programs, or job applications, making you vulnerable to scams that target newlyweds, grieving families and job-seekers.

It's also important to keep in mind that most personal information doesn't have an expiry date, and criminals can wait a long time after the initial data breach before they attempt to use it.

"You need to be suspicious for at least a year, not a week," Dehghantanha said.

How can people protect their information?

Horncastle said you should use strong, different passwords for each of your accounts, turn on multi-factor authentication, and regularly monitor your bank and credit card statements, and credit reports, for unusual activity.

In addition, he suggests always independently verifying the source of an email or text message, no matter how legitimate it looks. When possible, log into your accounts using official apps and websites — avoid clicking on links through messages.

"Never share your passwords, banking information or verification codes with anyone over the phone, especially when you receive that contact unexpectedly," he said.

Always be careful about any personal information you choose to share online, he added.

"It may be the missing piece of information for the puzzle."

Dehghantanha suggests contacting your phone carrier to lock your number from being transferred to a new SIM card, if that's a service they allow, and setting a unique a pin representatives are required to ask before they can make account changes.

And don't just rely on text messages for authentication, since scammers may be able to access those, he added. Enable the call-back option, or combine the text message verification with another method, such as the unique pin, or your fingerprints for touch ID, Dehghantanha said.

WATCH | Cellphone number transfer security risks: Cellphone number transfer highlights potential security risks | Duration 2:55 Huijun Long received a notification on the Virgin Plus app that her service with the company had been cancelled. Turns out, her phone number had been “mistakenly transferred” to a Bell Mobility account. Angela MacIvor has the story.

Dehghantanha also suggests every family has their own unique code word, because AI has made voice-cloning technology so convincing that people are often tricked into thinking they're getting a call from a loved one in distress — commonly known as a grandparent scam.

"If a conversation is uncommon, just quickly ask, 'What is the code word?'" he said.

Finally, Dehghantanha warns people to never underestimate how quickly and convincingly you may be targeted after a breach.

"An AI intruder moves fast," he said.

World.title: A Boston man won $1M US in the lottery. Days later, ICE arrested him
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales held an oversized cheque for $1 million US and smiled in the photo posted Saturday by the Massachusetts State Lottery.

Local media described the Boston man as "all smiles," reporting that he planned to save and invest his winnings after matching 11 words on a $10 US scratch ticket. Lottery officials said it was the first puzzle he'd ever scratched.

A few days later, his photo was posted online again — but this time, by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which said it had arrested the "illegal alien from El Salvador" on Tuesday. Now, Velasquez-Morales will remain in ICE custody until he's removed from the U.S., the agency said in a news release.

The ticket "ultimately led to his arrest," ICE said, without elaborating how. CBC News has reached out to ICE and not yet heard back. Velasquez-Morales does not yet appear on ICE's Online Detainee Locator System, where members of the public can search for people held in the agency's custody.

“Looks like his luck ran out,” said ICE public affairs assistant director Micah Bock in the news release.

On Nov. 24, ICE Boston arrested Ariel Antonio Velasquez-Morales, an illegal alien from El Salvador, during operations in East Boston, Mass. Velasquez-Morales entered the United States illegally on May 15, 2013. He was ordered removed by an immigration judge on April 24, 2014. https://t.co/YieIbY7afF —EROBoston

"Welcome to the ERO [enforcement and removal operations] Boston lottery! Where illegal aliens and sanctuary politicians are out of luck, and the law-abiding citizens of New England are always the winners!" ICE Boston posted on X.

It's unclear if Velasquez-Morales has legal representation. CBC News has reached out to several Boston-area immigration lawyers and not yet heard back.

A woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's sister-in-law wrote on Facebook Wednesday asking for respect and empathy for him, his wife and children.

"There is a family waiting for him," she wrote in Spanish.

Another woman identifying herself as Velasquez-Morales's older sister commented on the same post, writing her wishes that he would soon be back home with his family.

CBC News has reached out to both women for comment and not yet heard back.

A photo of Ariel Velasquez-Morales posted by ICE in a new release on Nov. 25, announcing that ICE Boston had arrested the man a day prior. (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement)

Can you win the lottery if you're not a citizen?

Velasquez-Morales illegally entered the U.S. in 2013 through the Texas border, according to ICE. An immigration judge ordered him removed in 2014, the press release noted, but "he illegally remained in the country."

While ICE posted on social media that "th e rights and privileges reserved for American citizens are for American citizens," state lotteries typically do not require citizenship or residency — if you meet the age requirement and are physically present in a participating jurisdiction when buying the ticket, you can play.

CBC News has reached out to the Massachusetts State Lottery and has not yet heard back. But its website help desk notes that anyone age 18 and up who is physically present in the state can buy lottery tickets at retail locations and win prizes. The Boston Globe reports that the lottery also doesn't require winners to have social security numbers, but that non-resident winners often face higher federal taxes on their winnings.

Some U.S. states allow lottery winners to remain anonymous no matter the amount, others depend on how much a person win, but many — including Massachusetts — do not let winners claim prizes anonymously.

"The Massachusetts State Lottery treats a winner’s name, town and prize as public information and releases them," explains the Massachusetts Legal Resources website.

WATCH | ICE arrests passengers boarding plane in Seattle: 'They're taking my dad:' Masked ICE agents arrest passengers at Seattle airport | Duration closed caption 2:00 New video showing masked, plainclothes ICE officers detaining Sofia Hernandez Mejia and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport is sparking backlash from various politicians and protesters. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security says Mendoza overstayed his visa and will be deported to Mexico.

"The lottery’s position, and the state’s, is that publicity is part of the game: It demonstrates that real people win, and it deters fraud in the claiming process."

Michael Baker, a Massachusetts attorney who works with lottery winners, told the Boston Globe that immigrants may not realize how much exposure winning the lottery can bring them.

"I’m sure people, when they play, they’re not expecting being at risk of being arrested," he told the media outlet.

World.title: KDgate for Montreal mayor continues with website mocking Kraft Dinner comments
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The controversy over her Kraft Dinner comments is sticking to Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.

The City of Montreal unveiled a budget that featured a property tax average increase of 9.8 per cent — about three times the inflation rate – on Tuesday.

The budget is due to be adopted in mid-December.

But an ill-timed Kraft Dinner comparison over budget choices has been haunting the mayor, giving rise to a website created by a Montreal software developer presenting the city budget on KD boxes.

There is also a protest outside city hall later Thursday afternoon.

The landing page for the website, kdgate.ca, alludes to the mayor's comments. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)

Martinez Ferrada’s comments during an interview with French-language media outlet Quartre95, a personal finance site, following the budget rollout compared creating a municipal budget to decisions taken at home.

"We're going through every service to see what we can save. It's like when you make your personal budget: if you know you'll have less money one year, then, you have to make choices," she said.

"Sometimes, you'll have to eat a little more Kraft Dinner because you can't afford filet mignon."

The comments were walked back by Martinez Ferrada on Wednesday morning in an Instagram story where she described the comparison as “clumsy.”

"What I meant was that when we make choices, the city is the same as when we make personal choices," she said.

The website, kdgate.ca, includes a rundown of the city budget listed in a way that mirrors the nutritional facts on the back of a food item. (Submitted by kdgate.ca)

But not before it unleashed a torrent of backlash on social media, framing her remarks as out of touch with the reality of Montrealers dealing with higher cost-of-living.

On Thursday morning, a website, kdgate.ca, was published outlining a municipal budget in the form of nutritional information on the packaging of the popular comfort food.

Niko Draca, the Montrealer behind the site, told CBC News about what prompted him to create the site.

"I saw a lot of outrage over the comment and I wanted to turn it into something positive and really get people looking at this data," Draca said.

"These documents are usually quite long and dry, so I figured a fun way to visualize could help, basically using the KD comment as a hook."

Meanwhile, a “Soraya Dinner” is planned for Thursday afternoon in front of Montreal’s city hall.

Organizers are inviting demonstrators to bring a pot, a portable stove and their own ingredients.

World.title: Ex-Conservative MP sues Liberal volunteer over alleged election campaign interference
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A former Conservative MP is suing a Liberal volunteer, accusing the man of creating fake websites in a "malicious" and "calculated" plan to interfere with his re-election prospects during the 2025 campaign.

One-time Bay of Quinte MP Ryan Williams alleges Steven Solarz — who had ties to the Liberal campaign that year — defamed him when he set up websites to make it appear like the Conservative camp was behind "deceptive" tactics.

Williams, who was elected in 2021, lost to Liberal candidate Chris Malette by 3,700 votes.

According to documents filed as part of the lawsuit, Williams alleges Solarz set up multiple websites associated with Malette's campaign. At least one of them, chrismalette.ca, redirected visitors to Williams's official campaign website, said his statement of claim.

Williams's case alleges Solarz was trying to create confusion and wanted the Conservative side to "be blamed, criticized or publicly associated with deceptive campaign tactics."

After the election, the former MP got a court order to compel the domain registration company GoDaddy and the Canadian Internet Registration Authority to disclose who was behind the websites. Solarz's name was on the domain registries, the documents show.

"[Solarz's] conduct was intentional, malicious, high-handed and calculated to cause harm to Williams and to interfere with his campaign and electoral prospects," his claim says.

"The defendant's conduct occurred during an active federal election campaign in which Williams's public reputation, credibility and trustworthiness were central to his candidacy and electoral prospects."

Williams is seeking $1.5 million in damages.

The lawsuit was filed earlier this year but has recently nabbed local attention. None of the allegations have been proven in court.

Solarz denies allegations

In his statement of defence Solarz denies he participated in the publication of a false or defamatory matter concerning and argues Williams's claims are based on "speculation" and "inference."

His lawyers have asked a judge to dismiss the matter, suggesting Williams's case is a strategic lawsuit against public participation (SLAPP) intended to interfere with Solarz's rights including freedom of expression.

In a statement through his lawyer, Solarz said he only got involved with the Liberal Party in 2025, ran for the nomination in March of that year and volunteered on Malette's campaign during the final two weeks of the campaign. He said he has no personal relationship with Malette.

"I welcome the opportunity to address Mr. Williams's claims in court," he said.

"I recognize that this has been an unfortunate situation. However, because the matter is before the courts, I am unable to comment further at this time."

Malette's office said he "unequivocally condemns the alleged actions and reiterates that this kind of behaviour has no place in our democratic process."

His office said the MP would not comment further while the matter is before the court.

Williams told CBC News he also lodged a complaint with election authorities.

The Office of the Commissioner of Canada Elections said in a statement on Thursday it was aware of the case but "generally does not confirm whether it has received a complaint or whether an investigation is underway regarding a particular matter."

Poilievre accuses Liberals of 'dirty trick'

During a news conference in Belleville, Ont., Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said it appears the Liberals played a "terrible, dirty trick."

WATCH | Conservative leader comments on lawsuit: Poilievre says Liberals might have played 'dirty trick' on former Conservative MP's campaign | Duration closed caption 1:05 Opposition Leader Pierre Poilievre vouched for former Conservative MP Ryan Williams on Thursday. Williams is suing a Liberal volunteer, alleging the man created fake websites to interfere with the former MP's campaign during the 2025 election.

"I hope that they answer for what happened here and that there is justice," the leader said.

"It should never be allowed to happen in our democracy. We welcome competitive elections that are hard fought, but there should not be this kind of fraudulent activity."

World.title: N.L. apologizes, says it now accepts Innu history dates back more than 300 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” said Grand Chief Jodi Ashini live on Facebook on Thursday. She read a letter Premier Tony Wakeham had sent her in which he apologized and said he regretted past tensions when the province refused to acknowledge that Innu had been in the province longer than 300 years.

The Grand Chief of the Innu Nation says Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham has apologized following a months-long controversy over the Innu's history in Labrador.

"Newfoundland and Labrador accepts the position that the history of the Innu in Labrador goes back to the time of immemorial, prior to the arrival of Europeans," Jodie Ashini said on a Facebook livestream Thursday.

Ashini was reading a letter written to her by Wakeham dated Thursday.

The controversy has been making headlines since June, and boiled over when it was revealed that, according to the Innu, the province's archaeology office only considered the history of the Innu to go back 300 years — which Ashini has called "a theory."

The tension between Ashini and Wakeham boiled over in September, when Ashini walked out of a meeting with Wakeham and later committed that the Innu Nation would not vote to support the new Churchill River deal with Quebec unless the province changed its tune on the Innu's history.

The pair held a nearly three-hour meeting earlier this month. Wakeham had previously committed to an independent audit of Innu records held by the archaeology office.

“I regret the length of time the controversy around the 300-year issue has taken to resolve. I apologize for the problems which arose from the province's position," Wakeham's letter, shared with CBC News, said.

WATCH | Breaking down the dispute between the N.L. government and the Innu Nation: Why is the Innu Nation upset with the N.L. government? | Duration closed caption 8:03 A conflict has erupted between the Innu Nation, The Rooms provincial museum and the provincial archaeology office over the First Nation's history and a planned exhibit. The CBC’s Leila Beaudoin takes this look at Innu history and what could be prompting the controversy.

Speaking with reporters late Thursday afternoon, Wakeham said he had an emotional conversation with Ashini on Wednesday.

"To be brutally honest, it was emotional for both of us," Wakeham said.

"It caused me a lot of grief … trying to get to the bottom and understand all of it. And yeah, it was a lot of grief, I think, especially for the Innu Nation."

Federal clarification was what N.L. needed to hear: Wakeham

Wakeham was hesitant to take a stance on the timeline in the months during the dispute, often saying he wanted to wait to get the facts before making a judgment.

On Thursday, Wakeham told reporters he got those facts in October.

As part of land claim negotiations between the Innu, the provincial government and the federal government — which have been ongoing since 1977 — Wakeham said the federal government clarified that Innu have history in Labrador since time immemorial.

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham says the federal government clarifying to the province that the Innu have been in Labrador since time immemorial was what he needed to be able to move forward in addressing the wrongs felt by the Innu Nation. (Terry Roberts/CBC)

Following that clarification, Wakeham said he felt comfortable to move forward.

"Clearly, I don't see as a province how Newfoundland and Labrador cannot be on the same side as the federal government in acknowledging the Innu. And I spoke to the Grand Chief about that," Wakeham said.

"[I] apologized for the length of time that it had taken and regret the grief that it had caused the Innu Nation.”

Ashini wiped away tears several times throughout the livestream, expressing thanks for the support from "every single Innu."

“I don’t know if I thought this news would ever come, honestly,” Ashini said.

“I’m proud to bring you this letter that our history will forever be recognized that we were here longer than 300 years … and they’re not going to erase our grandparents and they’re forever marked."

Wakeham said he hopes the province and the Innu Nation can continue to work toward reconciliation.

"It was important for me to try to mend that relationship. None of us want to be at odds, and I think for both myself and Minister [Lela] Evans, that was important."

World.title: Vast Majority of Women Suffer Violence Without Reporting It
World.content:
Actress Samantha Ruth Prabhu is participating in a campaign to end violence against women in India. Globally, only a very small percentage of women seek help or report the physical or sexual violence they have experienced to the authorities, and legal cases often fail to result in convictions or sentences. Image: UN Women India

By IPS Correspondent

HAVANA TIMES – Only seven percent of women who experience physical or sexual violence report it to the police, and barely 23 percent seek help from family members, their communities or authorities, according to a UN Women report released on Monday, November 23.

The study by the United Nations agency, based on data from 54 countries, estimated that worldwide, 840 million women and girls – nearly one in three – have experienced physical or sexual violence at some point in their lives.

Published ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, November 25, the report notes that even when women decide to come forward, justice is far from guaranteed.

Sexual violence crimes are among the least likely to result in a conviction.

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that “too many justice systems around the world are failing women and girls who experience violence. Cases go unreported, trials fail to move forward, and rulings go unenforced.”

“Justice cannot be achieved when women and girls have no access to it or when the law fails to protect them. We must work to ensure that justice systems fulfill their fundamental responsibilities to protect survivors, uphold their rights and prosecute perpetrators,” she added.

The UN Women study reveals a system in which silence is the norm, accountability is the exception, and perpetrators are far more likely to go unpunished than women are to obtain justice.

Many women remain silent, not by choice, but to protect themselves from the risks associated with speaking out. That is why barely seven percent of victims report acts of physical or sexual violence to the police, despite it being one of the most widespread human rights violations.

Women who report abuse may lose their homes, their children and their income. They may face abandonment by their families, exclusion from their communities and threats from the perpetrators they identify.

When women decide to come forward – sometimes years after the crimes were committed – they are all too often punished for speaking out and blamed for having waited. Some are murdered by their abusers simply for seeking help.

The number of women survivors of violence seeking help is declining in most countries that track such data.

In Asia, according to UN Women, only 16 percent of survivors seek help. In Africa, the figure is 31 percent, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, 40 percent.

In European Union countries, while 64 percent of survivors speak about the assault with someone close to them, only 14 percent go to the police.

According to research cited in the report, between 63 and 97 percent of complaints worldwide do not result in a conviction. Cases get lost in the justice system; survivors are subjected to repeated questioning and intimidating situations, and perpetrators may never be brought to trial.

All too often, perpetrators in positions of power are never convicted of the crimes they commit, fostering a culture of impunity.

The same pattern is repeated in the digital sphere. Only 25 percent of women involved in public life who experienced online violence filed a complaint with the police.

It is not the perpetrators who are penalized, but the women, who are silenced and excluded from digital spaces and prevented from exercising their right to participate freely in public life.

Against this backdrop, Bahous stated that “progress is possible. Today there is greater recognition of violence against women and girls, more laws protecting survivors, and more perpetrators behind bars.”

She emphasized that “the protections women have today are the result of the struggles of generations who dared to speak out. Now we must honor their courage by delivering justice, ensuring that every law provides safety, every promise translates into protection, and every word into action.”

“Until every woman and every girl can live free from violence, without fear and without having to prove that she deserves to be believed,” the UN official added.

The theme of this year’s International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women is “UNiTE to End Violence against Women and Girls.”

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

World.title: Cuban Regime Punishes Jailed Journalist Henry Constantin
World.content:
and also his partner with three months without visits

Although authorities allege a violation of prison regulations, the journalist interprets the measure as further retaliation against her and her partner/ Facebook

HAVANA TIMES – Alejandra García denounces that prison authorities sanctioned her for trying to deliver water, food, and books to the journalist, who has been imprisoned since September.

Cuban authorities have added a new measure of punishment against independent journalist Henry Constantín, director of La Hora de Cuba, who has been imprisoned in Camagüey since September 16. This time, the sanction falls on his partner, fellow journalist Alejandra García, whom the Kilo 7 prison administration has banned from visiting him for three months for attempting to deliver drinking water, food, and books. The items never even made it into the prison.

The complaint was published by La Hora de Cuba in a video in which actress and independent journalist Iris Mariño interviews García about what happened. According to her testimony, she received a call from prison officials asking her to come in on Thursday, November 19. After waiting several hours without being seen, she was told to return the next day. On Friday, she was informed that her visits to Constantín were suspended for three months.

The alleged reason given by the authorities was that she had tried to deliver items to the inmate outside of designated visiting hours. García explained that the water, food, and books were rejected by the officials. Despite this, the prison administration decided to impose a sanction that will keep her separated from her partner for three months.

“Another injustice is being committed right now,” La Hora de Cuba reported when publishing the testimony. “Everything has been arbitrary, everything is unjust; it has all been pressure, aggression, and threats,” García stated.

The new measure adds to a series of incidents denouced since the journalist’s arrest. He was initially accused of disobeying a police summons, which he maintains he did attend. After being detained at Villa María Luisa, the State Security headquarters in Camagüey, he was transferred on September 24 to Kilo 7, where he remains in pretrial detention.

Since then, his defense has denounced obstacles to accessing the court file, procedural delays, and the refusal to modify the precautionary measure. A habeas corpus petition filed to challenge the illegality of his detention was rejected.

The persecution denounced by his family and friends is not limited to the legal proceedings. On October 15, Constantín was sent to solitary confinement after officials claimed to have found a homemade knife among his belongings. The journalist denied that the weapon was his and maintained that it had been deliberately planted to frame him.

In addition to the accusations, there are complaints about his conditions of confinement.

In a statement published by his own media outlet , García questioned the circumstances of the search and claimed that no fingerprints had been taken from the object. The incident resulted in 15 days of isolation and a second criminal case for alleged disorderly conduct and possession of weapons in prison facilities.

In addition to the accusations, there are also complaints about his prison conditions. García stated that Constantín had lost about eight pounds and was being pressured to leave Cuba. She also reported that he was not receiving all the medications and food sent by his family.

The journalist described hygiene problems, the presence of mosquitoes and bedbugs, as well as difficulties accessing drinking water. In an article published after her first conjugal visit , held on November 12, she recounted the conditions of the cellblock and reported that prison authorities had threatened her because of her writings about Constantine’s imprisonment.

The ban on visits comes, therefore, after García made those allegations public. Although the authorities cite a violation of prison regulations, the journalist interprets the measure as further retaliation against her and her partner.

Constantin’s imprisonment comes amid a repressive escalation against the independent Cuban press.

The legal situation also appears to be stalled. According to García, Constantín’s lawyer informed him that the case for disobedience is now before the Camagüey Municipal Court, under the abbreviated procedure. However, a trial date has not yet been set.

The case has prompted statements from international organizations. The Inter-American Press Association (IAPA), whose Committee on Freedom of the Press and Information Constantín serves as regional vice president for Cuba, demanded his release and described his imprisonment as extremely serious. Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists have also called for his freedom, while the Cuban Observatory for Human Rights has requested guarantees for his physical and psychological well-being.

Constantín’s imprisonment comes amid a repressive escalation against the independent Cuban press, marked in recent months by arrests, interrogations, threats of imprisonment, and restrictions on movement. In November alone, police detained reporters Adelth Bonne and Camila Acosta, while Yoani Sánchez, director of 14ymedio , was held for nine hours by State Security.

More recently, Acosta denounced that the authorities intend to charge her with assault . The Inter-American Press Association (IAPA) had already warned in October about the intensification of police and judicial harassment against those who practice journalism outside of official media outlets, in a country where the independent press still lacks legal recognition.

Translated by Translating Cuba.

World.title: Havana Weather for November 26 to December 2
World.content:
Photo at a Havana bakery by Juan Suarez

Change in weather in western Cuba with rain followed by a drop in temperatures, bringing cooler conditions toward the weekend…

By Adrian Fuentes

HAVANA TIMES – The approach of a trough and the advance of a cooler air mass over western Cuba will bring an increase in rainfall in Havana over the coming hours, followed by a slight drop in temperatures toward the end of the week.

In the capital, rain and thunderstorms were expected to continue on Wednesday the 25th. A cold front will arrive between Wednesday night and the early hours of Thursday the 26th. Beginning Thursday, rainfall will gradually decrease, with partly cloudy skies and cooler conditions. Stable weather will prevail on Friday the 27th and Saturday the 28th, with temperatures slightly below normal for this time of year. Starting Sunday the 29th, temperatures will gradually rise again, although variable cloud cover will persist.

Winds will be from the southwest and west before and during the passage of the system, subsequently shifting to the northwest and north at speeds of between 15 and 30 kilometers per hour, with potentially stronger gusts associated with thunderstorms. Relative humidity will remain high during the first half of the forecast period, potentially exceeding 90% during rainfall, before decreasing slightly toward the weekend. Maximum temperatures will range between 24 and 29°C (75 and 84°F), with the lowest expected on Friday and Saturday, while the lows will range between 20 and 23°C (68 and 73°F). Sea surface temperatures will remain at 26 and 27°C (79 and 81°F).

According to the National Hurricane Center, the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season recorded 10 named storms and only one hurricane (Isaias), with activity well below average. No additional tropical cyclone development is expected in the basin before the official end of the season on November 30, and there are no active systems posing a threat to Cuba.

World.title: Anti-Feminism as an Electoral Force for Brazil’s Far Right
World.content:
Newly elected state legislator Eduarda Campopiano, a young rising star of Brazil’s far right, at an election campaign event in São Paulo in October. Fighting feminism is the main rallying cry of this new lawmaker, who rose to fame as a social media influencer. Photo: Rafa Neddermeyer / Agência Brasil

By Mario Osava (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – At just 23 years of age, anti-feminist activist Eduarda Campopiano is Brazil’s new electoral sensation, espousing a cause that has become a powerful electoral rallying cry for the far right.

She received 1,956,238 votes to win a seat in the São Paulo State Legislative Assembly, presenting herself as “the greatest enemy of feminists” in that southeastern Brazilian state.

In the October 4th general elections, only two men surpassed her in the number of votes received: Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, both from the same far-right Liberal Party (PL) as Campopiano. The two male candidates received more than three million votes each to win seats as federal deputies in the states of Minas Gerais and São Paulo, respectively.

Another candidate who is also a leading anti-feminist crusader is Ana Campagnolo from Brazil’s southern state of Santa Catarina. Campagnolo was elected to that state legislature with a record 387,522 votes. The 36-year-old historian wrote the book Feminism, Perversion and Subversion, which seeks to provide a theoretical foundation for anti-feminism.

In percentage terms, she was Brazil’s most-voted candidate, securing 9.07% of the valid votes (out of an extensive list of candidates) in her state, which has 8.3 million inhabitants. Meanwhile, Campopiano received 8.4% of the valid votes a field of 20 candidates in São Paulo, the country’s most populous state, with 44.2 million inhabitants.

The presidential, federal and state legislative, and gubernatorial elections held in October resulted in a 21% increase in female representation in both the national legislatures and in the 26 states plus the Federal District of Brasília, according to electoral authorities.

The number of women elected to legislative bodies rose from 308 in 2022, to 373 in October.

The most significant increase was seen in Brazil’s senate, where two-thirds of its 81 seats were up for grabs. Of the 54 newly elected or reelected senators, 12 are women, three times the number in 2022, when only one-third of the seats were contested.

In the 513-member Chamber of Deputies, the number of female representatives will increase from 90 to 109, a rise of 21.1%.

The new legislatures will be inaugurated on February 1, 2027, while governors will take office on January 6, and reelected president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, will be sworn in a day earlier.

A demonstration by the Mujeres Vivas [“Women Alive”] movement in Rio de Janeiro in July 2026, urging both chambers of Congress to approve a law against misogyny and femicide. It now appears unlikely that any legislation against gender-based violence will be approved by Brazil’s new Congress, dominated by far-right forces. Photo: Tomaz Silva / Agência Brasil

The rise of the far right a blow to feminism

However, the far right was the political force that made the greatest gains in both legislative chambers. The Liberal Party, which encompasses most of the extremists, will have three new female senators, increasing its number of female deputies from 17 to 22. Its congressional delegations will occupy 28 of total 81 Senate seats, and 121 of 513 seats in the Chamber of Deputies.

These figures dampened feminists’ celebrations over the increase in the number of women in the legislative branch. Moreover, conservatives as a whole strengthened their majority in the bicameral National Congress.

There are fears of a rollback of some hard-won women’s rights, given that the PL’s far right, known as Bolsonaristas for their allegiance to former President Jair Bolsonaro, has allies in other parties considered right-wing or center-right.

The strong presence and mobilization of women on the far right is nothing new. It occurred during the years of of “historical fascism in Germany and Italy,” as well as in Spain with the “blue women” of the Civil War (1936–1939), and in Portugal under the dictatorship of António de Oliveira Salazar (1933–1968), recalls Sonia Correa, coordinator of the Sexuality Policy Watch.

In Brazil, the so-called Integralismo movement, a far-right group of the 1930s, had a broad female base. In 1964, a series of demonstrations called the “March of the Family with God for Liberty”, spearheaded by women, paved the way for the military coup that same year and served as an example for similar mobilizations in the United States and Chile, the researcher added.

From the grassroots to leadership

“One difference is that in historical fascism, women were mainly in the movement’s grassroots, or served as mid-level cadres in the Italian Fascist Party, the Nazi hierarchy, the Spanish Falangist movement and the rise of Portuguese dictator Salazar. Today, they are leaders, aspiring to and attaining leadership positions,” Corrêa explained.

The winners of the 2024 European Parliament elections included Marine Le Pen (France), Giorgia Meloni (Italy) and Alice Weidel (Germany), far-right figures who subsequently won other victories, she noted.

In Brazil, conservative women such as Damares Alves, minister of Women, Family and Human Rights during Jair Bolsonaro’s administration (2019–2023), have risen to prominence, along with deputies Bia Kicis (Brasília) and Caroline De Toni (Santa Catarina), elected in 2018 and reelected in 2022.

All three will now hold Senate seats: Alves was elected in 2022 and the other two in October 2026. Together they make up the female leadership within the Bolsonarista movement, alongside the former president’s wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, who was also elected senator for Brasília.

Alves, the former minister and now senator, is not a member of the Liberal Party like the other three, but rather of the Republicans Party, an example of how Bolsonaro supporters are spread across several right-wing political organizations.

One similarity between the women recruited by historical fascism and those on the far right today is that both have benefited from feminist struggles begun in the 19th century, and spearheaded by progressive movements, Corrêa pointed out.

“The reactionary women aligned with the fascist camp today are clear beneficiaries of what is known as the fourth wave of feminism – that of my generation – in terms of access to the workforce, education and, above all, political participation,” she said in an interview with IPS in Rio de Janeiro.

Ana Campagnolo, the newly elected state legislator from Santa Catarina and an active proponent of Brazilian anti-feminism, at a hearing in the City Council of Itajaí, a city of 302,000 inhabitants and an important export port in southern Brazil. Photo: Davi Spuldaro / Itajaí City Hall

A backwards step for civilization

In Brazil’s specific case, one significant aspect of the rise in women’s anti-feminism, alongside the macho far right, is “the expansion of fundamentalist evangelical sects, whose main audience is women, especially poor women,” she stressed.

“Ultra-Catholicism” also contributes to shaping this political current, but “evangelical Christianity creates a favorable environment, not only because of its economic dimension, the so-called prosperity theology and its emphasis on entrepreneurship, but also because of its agendas concerning sexuality,” the researcher emphasized.

“Gender and sexuality issues are not peripheral. They are not merely moral issues or a smokescreen to deceive people but long-standing central pillars of the political project of the reactionary camp, as well as of the new right,” she clarified.

Far-right women deny the benefits of feminism. Ana Campagnolo, for example, attributes women’s suffrage, which was not introduced in Brazil until 1932, not to feminist struggles but to a concession made by men. Only those who held power could extend that right to others, she argues in her public statements.

Campopiano, the youngest star of the Bolsonarista movement and a follower of Campagnolo, rose to popularity as a social media influencer by espousing thoroughly backward-looking ideas, going so far as to claim that the Christian conversion of Indigenous peoples prevented them from continuing to practice cannibalism and burying children alive.

In her view, femicide is an invention, and it is not enough to eliminate the legality of abortion in cases of rape or when the mother’s life is at risk, both of which have been legal in Brazil since 1940; rather, abortion must be made “unthinkable,” unacceptable under any circumstances.

She opposes racial quotas for admission to universities, public service and other activities, and advocates expanding the right to carry firearms, including for women, as a way to defend themselves against violence.

Campopiano dropped out of her political science studies in her second year at a private university and acknowledged having been an “agnostic” until the age of 20, when she converted to Catholicism.

In addition to social media, she spread her beliefs through a traditional radio network. In 2024, she was elected to the City Council of Praia Grande, a city of 371,000 inhabitants located 77 kilometers from São Paulo. This marked the beginning of her precocious political career, and another example of how Brazil’s far right is renewing its leadership.

“There is an obvious contradiction in women occupying positions of political power thanks to rights historically won by feminist movements, while at the same time rejecting feminism and advocating social roles of submission and devotion to the domestic sphere for other women,” warned Leticia Vella, a lawyer and sustainability director of the Feminist Collective for Sexuality and Health.

But exposing these contradictions and debating the meaning of feminism is not enough. “We need to understand how anti-feminist narratives manage to connect with women’s anxieties, expectations and aspirations, and how to build alternative narratives based on those experiences,” she acknowledged in remarks to IPS from Brasília.

A major challenge is changing the way a segment of the population perceives feminism, which requires reassessing strategies for communication, mobilization and dialogue with society, Leticia Vella concluded.

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more feature articles here on Havana Times.

World.title: The Grocery Combo: Cuba’s Pantry Is Paid for Abroad
World.content:
Products paid for abroad and delivered to homes.

By Safie M. Gonzalez

HAVANA TIMES – On an iron chair and a blue sofa with worn upholstery, survival is displayed in plastic. A tray of thirty eggs, bottles of cooking oil, bags of powdered milk, Yeya pasta, Rios rice and canned goods form a pyramid that, at first glance, looks like a middle-class family’s groceries for the month. To one side sits the coveted La Excelencia toilet paper, Fox detergent and Coolwhite soap. On the floor, green mesh bags reveal malanga, sweet potatoes and plantains.

This is not the bounty from a miraculous ration store, nor the result of a carefully planned shopping trip to a local market. It is a supermarket package paid for abroad.

The transaction did not take place in Havana. It happened through a screen in Miami, Madrid or Santiago de Chile. A click, a credit card, a Zelle transfer or a cash payment at a shipping agency. Across the sea, a relative or friend put together the package, selected the brands and paid in foreign currency so that, days later, a “mule” or a delivery truck would drop off this shipment of food and hygiene products at the doorstep of a Cuban home.

This is the new anatomy of Cuba’s basic basket of goods: a household economy no longer governed by state salaries, but by the wallets of the diaspora and the exchange rate.

The Luxury of Basic Necessities

This type of grocery combo package is a barometer of the crisis. A decade ago, a shipment from abroad usually included clothes, shoes, perfumes or household appliances. Today, the priorities are eggs, cooking oil and toilet paper. The diaspora has become the de facto “Ministry of Food” for thousands of households, sending what cannot be guaranteed locally.

The irony lies in the brands. Products such as Yeya rice or La Excelencia toilet paper are notorious among Cuban consumers for their poor quality or local packaging processes. Yet when included in a package paid for abroad, they acquire the status of a privilege. Having a pantry stocked with these products means having a relative who makes sacrifices, working overtime abroad to ensure that detergent or powdered milk does not run out back on the island.

The Divide of Plastic and Cardboard

This reality also illustrates the social inequality eating away at the island. While packages of pasta and canned goods pile up in some households, in others survival depends on the informal market, where prices are beyond people’s reach.

The grocery package paid for abroad is a lifeline, but also a marker of social class. For those who receive it, it offers the peace of mind of knowing that their protein and hygiene needs are covered for a month. For those who have no one abroad, it is a reminder of their economic isolation. In Cuba today, family solidarity crosses oceans, but it also leaves many stranded on the shore.

The Business of Survival

Behind this domestic scene lies a commercial machinery. Shipping agencies have perfected the model of grocery packages known as “combos” (Combo A, Combo B, Executive Combo). They offer emigrants the convenience of choosing a preassembled package—with eggs, grains, cooking oil and hygiene products—and paying for it securely.

This model has transformed consumption. Families in Cuba no longer ask for what they need; they adapt to what the package offers. Standardization has turned grocery shopping into a lottery in which those who pay get to choose, and those who receive make do with what they get.

In the middle of the living room, the package waits to be unpacked. Every can, every roll of toilet paper is a reminder of distance and of love packaged for delivery. But it is also evidence of a country where daily survival has been outsourced abroad, and where a packet of detergent or a simple bag of root vegetables and plantains has become the most precious of treasures.

Read more from the diary of Safie M. González aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba Restricts Food Rations to Only the Most Vulnerable
World.content:
An employee distributes rationed food to a customer inside a nearly empty state-run grocery store in Havana. Food distributed through the ration booklet is being restricted to people in the most vulnerable situations. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

By Dariel Pradas (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – Most Cubans, except for the oldest generations, were born into a system with a ration booklet, the hallmark of a state-subsidized and rationed distribution system for food and other basic goods to which all inhabitants had access.

Today, however, almost all the bodegas, the local name for state-run neighborhood stores where these goods were previously sold, remain closed. A few are now responsible for distributing food as social assistance to the most vulnerable, while others have been leased to the private sector.

“Look, I haven’t received rice in months. Nor sugar, coffee, or beans. As for chicken, not since 2025, if I remember correctly. Now people are saying they’re going to eliminate the ration booklet, but I think that in practice they had already eliminated it,” Carlos Garrido, a 63-year-old construction worker living in Havana, told IPS while showing his household’s ration booklet.

This distribution system was established in 1962 to overcome shortages generated, among other factors, by the position taken by the United States, then the country’s main supplier, which, dissatisfied with the direction of the Cuban Revolution, severed all kinds of relations with this Caribbean island nation.

Rice, chicken, sugar, milk, eggs, cooking oil, beans, spaghetti, and cooking gas were sold through the ration booklet until about five years ago.

After the COVID-19 pandemic, as Cuba’s multidimensional crisis intensified, with rising inflation, economic contraction, and a failed monetary reform, the number of products offered through the ration booklet steadily dwindled.

In 2026, the oil blockade and new financial sanctions imposed by the United States on the island exacerbated the crisis and rations at state-run grocery stores were reduced to a bare minimum.

Cubans, who previously met part of their calorie needs through the distribution of subsidized food, now have no choice but to face the high prices of a predominantly private market governed by supply and demand, without the government-imposed price caps previously used in unsuccessful attempts to contain price increases.

The ration booklet “has disappeared in practice; it could be said that it has become extinct, and among the approved measures it is indicated that in the future it will focus exclusively on vulnerable sectors of the population,” economist Omar Everleny wrote in an article for IPS.

On the radio program *Haciendo Radio*, Marpessa Portal, general director of Merchandise Sales at the Ministry of Domestic Trade, announced that “1,913 bodegas had been selected to serve people in the most vulnerable situations,” out of the 12,000 existing nationwide.

According to Everleny, this new approach “would require the State to define who is and who is not vulnerable, so the necessary clarification must be made in this regard.”

During an IPS tour of several bodegas that remain operational, each was found to be responsible for distributing products within a community, either free of charge or at a cost of one US cent or less, mainly to recipients of social assistance or people of retirement age, which is 60 for women and 65 for men.

To a lesser extent, beneficiaries also include children with chronic illnesses or low body weight, women with high-risk pregnancies, female heads of households with more than three children, and other specific cases.

According to the store managers, who gave similar accounts, the census to identify these individuals was conducted with social workers from the Ministry of Labor and Social Security, local political delegates, and health and education authorities.

Under the new system, a person can receive rice, beans, sugar, and even sunflower oil every month, the latter being highly sought after and expensive on the private market. The World Food Program (WFP) provides that oil and other imported products, which are distributed every two months to vulnerable individuals.

Many people are therefore eager to be included on these lists of vulnerable individuals at a time when survival is becoming increasingly difficult for most of the population.

A mother of three who benefits from the new system and preferred to remain anonymous when interviewed by IPS lied during the census, claiming that she was raising her children alone when, in fact, she lives with her husband and receives his financial support.

“I had to say I didn’t have a husband because things are really bad. Our money isn’t enough for anything. The other day we couldn’t eat until we picked up the package of subsidized products at the bodega,” she acknowledged.

Customers line up outside a state-run bakery that sells rationed bread rolls to the population in Havana. Photo: Jorge Luis Baños / IPS

The Long-Standing Debate Over Eliminating the Ration Booklet

There had been talk of eliminating the ration booklet for many years.

In 2011, at the Sixth Congress of the Communist Party of Cuba (PCC, the only political party permitted in the country), former Cuban President Raúl Castro (2008–2018) already spoke of eliminating universal assistance and focusing it on the most vulnerable, advocating a policy of subsidizing people rather than products.

The then-president even reduced the number of items available through the ration booklet in an effort to eliminate extensive subsidies that, as late as 2012, represented an annual expenditure of more than US $1 billion, with only 12% of the actual value of the products being recovered.
