World.title: Apartment conversions offer lifeline for vacant Tallinn offices
World.content:
Tallinn's oversupplied office market is prompting developers to consider converting older office buildings into rental apartments as demand for traditional office space declines.

Vacant office space in Tallinn has grown from 50,000 square meters a decade ago to 130,000 square meters this year. The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for property owners, said Eduard Sorokin, a commercial real estate broker at Uus Maa.

The amount of available office space began increasing during the coronavirus pandemic in 2020. Since then, the market has also been affected by the full-scale war in Ukraine, rising energy prices and, more recently, the growing use of artificial intelligence.

"We are only now reaching the point where the effects of COVID are fully being felt, because office leases were typically signed for five years. In reality, many leases signed at the start of the pandemic or before it are only now expiring. The new leases these companies and tenants are signing usually cover significantly fewer square meters. Companies are taking smaller spaces, teams are smaller and remote work is common. Only now is the impact of COVID truly reaching the market," Sorokin said.

According to him, there is a distinction between official and unofficial statistics in commercial real estate. The difference lies mainly in how actual occupancy levels are reported.

High rise and older buildings in central Tallinn. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"Commercial real estate assets are valued based on income. Property owners find it extremely difficult to honestly acknowledge and often even disclose their true occupancy levels because it directly affects the market value of their assets," Sorokin explained.

The market value of office properties also affects owners' credit lines and loans. Real estate is such a capital-intensive business that most assets have been purchased with borrowed money. According to Sorokin, current vacancy rates and the resulting lower rental income often mean that a property's real value is lower than its declared value.

"This trend is continuing," Sorokin said.

The total amount of office space has nevertheless increased significantly over the past decade. At the same time, tenants' preferences have changed. Integrated business districts have become more attractive than standalone office buildings, said Andrei Kokk, head of real estate at commercial property company Kapitel Tallinn.

"New buildings often emerge in locations where favorable conditions for similar businesses already exist. Examples include the Ülemiste and Rotermanni districts, among others. That is an additional reason why newer and more modern buildings remain more popular among tenants," Kokk said.

Signage at entrance to the Ülemiste City development in Tallinn. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

One option for attracting tenants to older office buildings is changing the building's purpose, said Roman Raivet, head of corporate banking credit analysis at Luminor.

"For example, ground-floor premises can be converted into retail space or accommodations. In Tallinn, tourism and hospitality are doing well. As a result, an office building can be converted into short-term accommodation if circumstances allow," Raivet said.

Finding a new purpose for office buildings can also mean a complete conversion into residential units.

"There are already examples in Tallinn where former office buildings are being converted into apartments. I expect this is a trend that may become even more pronounced over time," Kokk said.

Sorokin also predicts that a large share of currently planned office projects will ultimately be developed as residential real estate. He is referring to rental apartment buildings built on commercial land rather than traditional apartment blocks on residential land. As a prominent example, he cited Endover's recent purchase of City Plaza at Tartu maantee 2.

"Golden Gate" development near port of Tallinn. Source: US Real Estate

According to Sorokin, the developer is acquiring an entire tower in central Tallinn and plans to convert the relatively new office building, approximately 12 to 15 years old and currently home to LHV's headquarters, into apartments.

"It will remain on commercial land. The apartments will not be sold to private individuals but will remain a rental project. Rental buildings are the direction in which we are moving," Sorokin said.

In his view, many office and commercial projects currently planned for the coming years will eventually have their purpose changed and become apartment buildings rather than office developments.

At the same time, office construction continues. Roughly 127,000 square meters of office space was under construction in Tallinn during the third quarter of this year, with completion expected between 2026 and 2028.

"I do not believe these projects will ultimately be completed as office buildings in their current form because there simply is no market or demand for traditional office space. In A++ office buildings, you can charge €25 per square meter, even €30 per square meter per month. Those are premium prices. But if you look at everything below A+ level, namely B-class office buildings, which are abundant throughout Tallinn, including along Pärnu maantee and elsewhere in the city center, rents have fallen by at least half over the past five years. Offices that rented for €12 per square meter in 2019 are now being publicly advertised at €5 per square meter," Sorokin said.

World.title: Dead body found in Tartu hostel may have been there '2 or 3 weeks'
World.content:
The body of a man who had been dead for several weeks was found in a room last week at the Hektor Hostel, Tartu Postimees reported .

The Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) confirmed they received a report at around 11:30 a.m. on November 16 that a man's body had been found at the hostel on Riia tänav, near Tartu's Aparaaditehas cultural hub.

The PPA ruled out foul play and sent the body to the Estonian Forensic Science Institute, which will identify the individual and determine the cause of death.

A guest found the remains after an odor had spread to other rooms, Õhtuleht reported, and the guest also told the newspaper the body had been of a young man, with speculation having it that he may have lain dead in the room for two to three weeks.

Rait Sinimäe, CEO of Hektor's hotel and accommodation services, confirmed the death to Õhtuleht but declined to discuss the details. He added that the PPA had ruled out foul play and that the Hektor building remained safe to stay in.

Tartu Postimees said Sinimäe asked them to submit further questions in writing.

World.title: Europe-wide money laundering investigation culminates in raid in Estonia
World.content:
Twenty-one suspects were detained in Germany, Estonia and Belgium in raids linked to a Europe-wide money laundering scheme.

The criminal police in the German state of Thuringia said Thursday that the suspects are believed to have laundered at least €120 million.

More than 300 premises were searched across 12 countries as part of the police operation. One of the operation's main targets was the German state of North Rhine-Westphalia where more than 100 searches were carried out.

The suspects are accused of providing money laundering services through an elaborate VAT fraud scheme and a shadow banking system.

The criminal gang allegedly controlled at least 22 shell companies in Germany.

The companies issued invoices for services that were never provided and improperly charged VAT. Large amounts of cash, luxury cars, watches and jewelry were seized during the searches, along with evidence including documents and digital storage devices.

Tax losses in Germany alone are estimated at at least €18.9 million.

Money transferred to the shell companies was allegedly withdrawn in cash, with some of the funds returned to the companies and individuals who had purchased the fraudulent invoices.

World.title: Study: No good solutions for insulating fieldstone walls from the inside
World.content:
Insulating old fieldstone walls from the inside can preserve a building's historic facade but risks causing long-term moisture damage, according to new research from the Estonian University of Life Sciences.

"Fieldstone walls are quite common in Estonia. Perhaps less so in northern Estonia, but on the island of Ruhnu, for example, a remarkably large number of fieldstone buildings have survived," said Kadri Leiten, a lecturer at the Estonian University of Life Sciences who recently earned her doctorate. On Ruhnu, for example, people primarily use fieldstone buildings as summer homes because the walls get too cold in winter.

Anyone wishing to use a fieldstone building year-round, however, might want to insulate it somehow. "If you don't want to hide a beautiful facade, you need to find an alternative way to keep the building comfortable inside during the winter months," Leiten explained. In some cases, this means installing insulation on the interior side of the walls.

In her recently defended doctoral dissertation, Leiten assessed how advisable this approach is. Using a wall of the stable at Mooste Manor as a case study, she investigated whether and how an old fieldstone wall could be insulated from the inside using reed or wood fiber boards combined with clay plaster. "Insulating from the inside makes it possible to preserve the exterior facade, but a safe insulation solution has yet to be found," the lecturer noted.

Moisture damage accumulates over time

The fieldstone masonry Leiten studied was at least half a meter thick. Insulating such a wall from the inside makes the masonry colder. "Adding an internal insulation system restricts the flow of heat from the room into the wall," the lecturer explained.

If heat cannot penetrate the insulation attached to the wall, the fieldstone masonry remains cooler. Moisture can gradually accumulate inside the cold wall because the material covering its interior surface prevents the masonry from drying inward. "This can lead to more freeze-thaw cycles, as materials that are already damp are more susceptible to cracking when they freeze," Leiten explained.

In her research, she tested two domestically produced materials for insulating the stable's fieldstone wall: reed boards and wood fiber boards. She used clay plaster as a leveling layer. Short-term experiments indicated that mold might not develop immediately between the masonry and the insulation boards.

Over a five- to seven-year period, however, the model indicated that moisture could still accumulate in the insulated wall. "Unfortunately, based on the results of my research, I cannot currently say that this is a particularly safe method of insulating walls from the inside," Leiten acknowledged.

Old linen warehouse in Puka. Source: Tibukonn/CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The wall she studied, however, has now been insulated for four or five years. According to Leiten, the coming years will reveal whether moisture actually begins to accumulate as predicted by the model.

"The next step is to investigate what methods could be used to reduce moisture accumulation in the wall. One approach used elsewhere in the world is water-repellent treatment," she said. In Belgium, for example, masonry walls are treated externally with water-repellent coatings, allowing buildings to be insulated from the inside. However, Leiten noted that the climates of Belgium and Estonia are not comparable.

Wetter climate on the way

To assess the climate resilience of wood fiber and reed boards, Kadri Leiten used models developed for the climate of the Vantaa region in Finland. These are also suitable for northern Estonia, as Vantaa's climate is expected to resemble northern Estonia's future climate. "Under an extreme scenario, we would rarely see subzero temperatures in winter anymore. Estonia's long-term climate projections also indicate that temperatures will fall below freezing much less frequently by 2100," the lecturer said. In other words, it makes sense to start designing both stone walls and all other types of walls in Estonia with the expectation of more moisture and rainfall.

Salts can also accumulate in old stone walls, particularly in buildings that have previously served some agricultural purpose. As part of her research, Leiten therefore also investigated how these salts could be removed using clay- and lime-based sacrificial plasters. "The wall is plastered and the plaster is essentially sacrificed. Liquid water containing dissolved salts moves from the masonry into the plaster, which is then removed from the wall," Leiten explained.

Nearly all the sacrificial plasters tested in her study removed salts from the stone masonry. However, another important consideration, according to Leiten, is how easily each type of sacrificial plaster can be removed after use. "Compared with lime-based plaster, clay plaster was generally easier to remove from the wall," she noted.

Leiten advises readers who want to use their fieldstone buildings year-round to exercise caution when insulating them. According to the lecturer, natural materials are not particularly well suited to the task. "Nothing may happen in the first five years after you insulate with clay or reeds. You may simply not be able to see what's happening between the layers inside your wall over the course of 20 years," she warned.

Another option is simply to leave an aesthetically pleasing old stone wall uninsulated. "You might put on some wool socks and a sweater and you'll be fine. For now, leaving the wall uninsulated is a safe option, provided it can dry both inward and outward and the room has ventilation," Leiten said.

Polli Manor stables. Source: Kadri Kroon/CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Kadri Leiten, a doctoral student at the Estonian University of Life Sciences' Institute of Forestry and Engineering, defended her doctoral dissertation, "Long-Term Evolution of Moisture Regime and Damage Risks in Internally Insulated Massive Masonry Walls under Changing Climate Conditions," on November 12. Her dissertation was supervised by Marko Teder, Ph.D. The opponents were Associate Professor Evy Vereecken (KU Leuven, Belgium) and Simo Ilomets, Ph.D. (Tallinn University of Technology, Estonia).

World.title: Watchdog warns bosses not to monitor staff with cameras non-stop
World.content:
Employers cannot use cameras to monitor workers continuously or check their duties, the Data Protection Inspectorate (AKI) warned amid rising workplace complaints.

AKI officials said bosses must disclose camera rules, ban audio or break-room recording and set short deletion limits to meet personal data and defense-of-privacy rules.

Maire Iro-Miller, public relations adviser with the AKI, said workplace cameras have long drawn top inquiries from staff and employers.

"Because the inspectorate receives more complaints every year, we are also seeing quite a few cases involving the use of cameras," Iro-Miller said.

One recent complaint saw a firm using surveillance to track staff continuously, check tasks and verify attendance, without explaining why.

Lawyer Jekaterina Aader said identifiable camera footage counts as personal data processing and so requires a clear lawful purpose and signage.

"Cameras cannot be used for continuous real-time monitoring of employees, to check whether they are at work or to monitor how they carry out their duties," Aader said.

Changing rooms, break rooms, toilets and showers are off-limits, while audio recording is rarely lawful, she noted

"The Data Protection Inspectorate also points out that recording audio in the workplace is even more intrusive and generally does not comply with data protection requirements," Aader continued.

Recordings must be deleted promptly, with justifications growing stricter once 72 hours have elapsed since the recording was made. Access logs and computer-tracking rules also apply.

Europe-wide, video should normally be deleted within days of being captured.

"The European Data Protection Board takes the view that video recordings should in most cases be deleted after a few days, ideally automatically," Aader added.

Workers who suspect unlawful monitoring can file a complaint with the AKI.

World.title: French sports media: Estonian rally driver Robert Virves signed for M-Sport Ford
World.content:
Estonian rally driver Robert Virves has reportedly struck a deal with M-Sport Ford for next season, according to renowned French motorsport magazine Auto Hebdo.

Virves and co-driver Jakko Viilo were crowned world champions in WRC2, the second-tier of the World Rally Championship, this year. Competing in a Škoda Fabia for the Toksport team, the pair contested seven rounds, winning four and finishing second twice.

"In 2026, Robert Virves secured the WRC2 title for Škoda, but according to our information, the Estonian has decided to go his own way and join the M-Sport Ford project," Auto Hebdo wrote Wednesday. "This would be one of the biggest stories of the winter transfer season."

M-Sport would be familiar territory for Virves, who also competed for the team in 2023. It was his debut season in WRC2, during which the Estonian contested six World Rally Championship rounds. His best result was a sixth-place finish in his class at his home event, Rally Estonia.

Robert Virves talking to ERR. Source: Siim Lõvi/ERR

M-Sport, which at the top-tier WRC level has been much smaller than the dominant Toyota and Hyundai, has yet to confirm its driver lineup for next season, but has previously indicated that three seats should be available. This year, the team's drivers were Irishmen Josh McErlean and Jon Armstrong. The team will compete in the Ford Fiesta Rally1 Kit, a modified Rally2 car eligible for Rally1 competition.

Virves won the 2022 Junior World Rally Championship and became the first Estonian driver to capture the WRC2 title in 2026 while driving for Toksport WRT. He previously spent a 2023 WRC2 stint with M-Sport Ford and claimed his first WRC2 victory at Rally Estonia in 2025. A move to M-Sport Ford would mark his return to the manufacturer's lineup ahead of the new era.

Norwegian-Swedish driver Oliver Solberg won the overall Rally Estonia in July 2025 while he was still a WRC2 competitor. In Estonia he raced in a one-off Rally1 appearance, before stepping up full-time to Toyota's top-tier lineup for 2026.

Virves' fellow Estonian Ott Tänak is also returning to the senior WRC with Toyota in 2027 after sitting out the 2026 season. The 2019 world champion drove one season for M-Sport Ford too, in 2023, winning two races, in Sweden and Chile.

World.title: Video: Fox found at Tallinn Airport, safely returned to the wild
World.content:
A fox that wandered into Tallinn Airport last week was caught by rescuers and released back into the wild.

"It is true that in the early morning of November 16, a young and apparently quite travel-hungry fox was exploring the baggage area of Tallinn Airport. This time, however, it did not get to take a flight. With help from the Rescue Board, the four-legged travel enthusiast was caught and safely returned to the wild. The fox's little airport adventure ended happily for everyone involved," said Tallinn Airport marketing and communications manager Margot Holts.

A wild fox at Tallinn Airport. Source: Tallinn Airport

Holts said that this time the fox was wandering around the airport's baggage handling area, and at that hour there were no arriving passengers it could have encountered.

She added that the fox entered from the airfield side, not through the main entrance.

Holts said the movement of birds and animals is closely monitored in aviation because their presence in operational areas can pose risks both to flight safety and to the animals themselves.

"From time to time, an uninvited guest finds its way onto our grounds, and young animals in particular may not always be able to find their way back out. In such situations, our goal is to ensure flight safety while also making sure the animal can continue its journey safely," Holts said.

A fox climbed onto a baggage conveyor belt at Tallinn Airport. Source: Majaka - Tallinn FB group

The video source is footage from Tallinn Airport's security cameras, provided to ERR by the airport.

World.title: Thousands protest in Irbil as Baghdad moves to seize Kurdish oil and border control
World.content:
IRBIL, Iraq: Thousands of demonstrators gathered Thursday in Irbil, the capital of Iraq’s semiautonomous northern Kurdish region, protesting a move by the federal government to take control of oil operations and border crossings previously run by Kurdish authorities.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi announced the measures Tuesday, describing them as steps to address oil smuggling.

The decision marked a new escalation in a long-running power struggle between the central government and Kurdish authorities and spurred rival Kurdish parties to come together in opposition to Baghdad.

Al-Zaidi — who took office earlier this year with the backing of US President Donald Trump — has been trying to assert authority on several fronts, including sending security forces into an area long controlled by a powerful Iran-backed militia last week.

A move to consolidate control

Tuesday’s decision brings official and unofficial border crossings in the Kurdish region under federal government management. It places approval for oil exports from the region under the authority of the federal oil ministry and transfers the management of oil fields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces to it.

Al-Zaidi also dismissed Kirkuk’s operations commander and police chief and the head of the Border Ports Commission. He said the measures reflect Iraq’s “independent national will.”

Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court on Wednesday backed Baghdad’s move and ruled that federal authorities may deploy troops to secure all of Iraq’s international borders, “including the borders located within the territories administered by the Kurdistan Region.”

Defense Ministry spokesman Maj. Gen. Yahya Rasool said Wednesday evening that Al-Zaidi, who is also commander in chief, had ordered the deployment of military units to Kirkuk and other provinces and had ordered dirt roads used for oil smuggling to be blocked.

A long-running power struggle

Iraq’s Kurds have governed themselves since 1991, and the 2005 constitution recognized the Kurdish region and its government. But since 2003, Irbil and Baghdad have struggled for control over land, oil and money.

The Kurdish regional government’s cabinet said Wednesday that Al-Zaidi’s order “violates both the Constitution and the constitutional rights of the Kurdistan Region” and represents “an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime.” It accused Baghdad of using “military rhetoric and threats” to carry out a “premeditated, long-standing plan directed against the constitutional structure of the Kurdistan Region.”

The Federal Supreme Court said the Kurdish regional government’s authority covers only the land it administered on March 19, 2003, the day before the US-led invasion that unseated Saddam Hussein. Kurdish peshmerga forces moved into many disputed areas after 2003, including the oil fields covered by this week’s orders.

The Iraqi constitution’s Article 140 was meant to settle the fate of the disputed territories, a band of land from the Syrian to the Iranian border that is home to Kurds, Arabs, Yazidis, Assyrians, Turkmen and other communities.

The article called for reversing Saddam-era policies that expelled Kurds from the area and moved Arabs in. It also called for a census and a referendum by the end of 2007 on whether the areas would join the Kurdistan Region. Neither was held.

Peshmerga forces took control of oil-rich Kirkuk in 2014, when the Iraqi army collapsed in the face of an offensive by Daesh militants. Iraqi forces pushed them out in October 2017, weeks after the Kurdish region held an independence referendum that Baghdad called unconstitutional.

Oil at the center of disputes

The disputes between Baghdad and Irbil have largely centered around oil exports and revenues. The country relies on oil revenues for about 90 percent of its budget.

In 2014, Baghdad suspended federal budget transfers to the Kurdish region amid a dispute over oil exports. Disagreements over oil revenues and budget allocations have since repeatedly delayed salary payments for public employees in the region.

In 2022, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court ruled the Kurdish region’s oil and gas law unconstitutional. The following year, oil exports through Turkiye were suspended after an international arbitration ruling found Turkiye had violated its pipeline agreement with Iraq by allowing independent Kurdish oil exports. Exports resumed in 2025 under an agreement placing sales under federal government oversight.

The Kurdish region’s own politics are also in turmoil.

On Nov. 5, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan quit the government led by the Kurdistan Democratic Party, calling it “failed” and threatening to form a parallel administration.

No new cabinet has been formed since October 2024 regional elections, and the legality of the current government is being challenged at the Federal Supreme Court.

World.title: Ukraine has ‘no intention’ of spreading war to Libya: minister
World.content:
KYIV: Ukraine was not attempting to spread the war with Russia to Libyan shores by attacking two Russian ships off the coast of Benghazi, Kyiv’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on Thursday.

In a post on X, Sybiga said he had called his Libyan counterpart Al-Taher Al-Baour to explain that “none of Ukraine’s actions have ever been directed against Libya or the Libyan people, only against Russian military objects directly serving Russia’s war.”

“We have no intention of extending Russia’s war against Ukraine to Libya or any other country,” he added.

On Monday, Kyiv claimed responsibility for attacks on two Russian ships — one of which was sunk — at the weekend off the coast of Libya, in what appears to be a spillover of the war between Kyiv and Moscow.

In his X post, Sybiga “reaffirmed Ukraine’s full support for Libya’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as for efforts to reunify the country.”

The incident has fueled concerns about its potential political and security repercussions in Libya, a country divided between the UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration based in Benghazi in the east.

The eastern administration is led by Khalifa Haftar, who maintains close military and strategic ties with Russia.

Tripoli had demanded explanations from Kyiv after the attack and denied any understanding with Ukraine, as speculation circulated about a possible role of the Tripoli authorities in the operations claimed by Kyiv.

The rival executive in the east has called for an international investigation into an alleged Ukrainian military presence in Libya.

The UN mission in Libya also condemned the attacks, calling for an independent investigation and urging respect for Libyan sovereignty.

World.title: EU leaders aim for budget deal before the end of the year, Merz says
World.content:
BRUSSELS: EU leaders will try to reach an agreement on the next long term budget for the EU this year, but will not reconvene for new talks on Friday, German chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday evening.

Merz said a day of talks between EU leaders in Brussels had brought “new movement” toward a reduction of the proposed size of the next budget, as demanded by Germany and other countries who are net contributors to the bloc’s finances.

The leaders will try to hammer out a deal during a two-day summit starting December 17, Merz said.

The German chancellor repeated his stance that all 27 EU members should contribute to aid for Ukraine, and said this would be discussed further during a last round of talks between the leaders on Thursday evening.

World.title: Letsch’s Al-Shabab keep revival going with Brownhill winner against Abha
World.content:
RIYADH: When Al-Shabab appointed Thomas Letsch in the summer, optimism within the ranks soared. Another student of the German game was on his way to the league, and maybe, this would mark Al-Shabab’s return to the summit.

Seven games into his stint at the club, alarm bells were ringing. The six-time league champions were winless in the league and had been eliminated early from the King Cup at the very first hurdle. Eleven weeks later, however, Al-Shabab look a very different side under the German.

Granted, a 1-0 win over bottom-placed Abha is hardly one for the highlight reel, but it is Al-Shabab’s fourth victory in six games, and they remain unbeaten in that spell, which includes a historic 6-1 drubbing of Al-Ahli.

Their only goal against Abha came in the 39th minute, when Daniel Podence slipped past left-back Mohammed Al-Zaid with a smooth dribble before releasing Josh Brownhill in the box for the finish.

The victory lifts Al-Shabab back into the top half of the table, with the club now in ninth place on 17 points. Should the good run of form continue, there may be talk of a top-six finish and a spot in a continental competition for next season.

Elsewhere, Mourad Batna was the hero for Al-Fateh once again, delivering another trademark scorcher in the 70th minute to give his side a 1-0 win over Al-Riyadh. The victory, Al-Fateh’s second of the season, lifts the club to 16th place, just one point from safety.

In Sudair, Al-Faisaly mounted a late comeback from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 with Diriyah in new head coach Mohamed Dahmen’s first match at the club. The Tunisian replaced Giovani Solinas, who resigned on Nov. 22, and will be encouraged by the response after Diriyah, who had been steadily climbing the table, looked to be heading for another win.

Saudi Pro League action resumes on Friday, with Al-Kholood hosting Al-Khaleej at 3:15 p.m., Al-Qadsiah facing Al-Fayha at 5:20 p.m. and NEOM traveling to Jeddah to face Al-Ittihad at 8:30 p.m.

World.title: The long road to a post-AI world
World.content:
In the 1980s, France’s Minitel system was a staple in many households, used for booking train tickets and searching phone directories. No one called it the “internet”; it was simply Minitel.

A decade later, the World Wide Web emerged, and “internet” became a household term. Then came smartphones, transforming the internet from a niche service into an integral part of daily life. Over time, people stopped discussing it as a standalone technology. It became infrastructure, much like electricity — a basic utility that businesses take for granted.

No one describes their company as “electricity-powered.” They simply operate, assuming the power will be there. This is the essence of “post-internet:” the technology fades into the background, becoming invisible yet ubiquitous.

Artificial intelligence appears to be following a similar trajectory, albeit at an accelerated pace. If the current rate of development, catalyzed by the 2022 launch of ChatGPT, continues, the era of “post-AI” could begin around 2040. This is less a precise prediction than an extrapolation of technological rhythms: a technology becomes infrastructure when it shifts from novelty to necessity, becoming embedded in economic and societal operations.

However, between emergence and maturity lies a less-examined phase: the “messy middle.” This is where the world currently stands. AI dominates public discourse and corporate strategies, yet it has not become a clear, sustainable driver of profit, trust or regulation.

A 2026 McKinsey survey of 1,719 respondents across 97 countries, representing a full range of regions, industries, company sizes, functional specialties and tenures, found that only 37 percent reported AI contributing to their operational profits.

This disconnect highlights a critical tension: while the technology is present, organizational structures and processes have not fully adapted. Many firms have adopted AI tools without overhauling legacy systems, expecting incremental additions to spark revolutionary change. True transformation demands redesigning workflows, retraining workforces and rethinking decision-making frameworks. This process takes time, as seen with the industrialization of electricity and the integration of computers into offices.

When returns lag, the question shifts to financing. Who underwrites the wait? By November 2026, the answer had become clear: capital markets, followed by trust and legal systems. Companies turned to debt and equity to fund data centers, chip procurement and computational infrastructure. In November 2026, the Federal Reserve’s biannual Financial Stability Report warned that advanced computing debt issuances had surpassed $680 billion by October 2026, five times the 2023 total, with infrastructure-linked liabilities potentially exceeding $3 trillion.

Nvidia exemplifies this dynamic. Traditionally a chip manufacturer, it evolved into a linchpin of AI infrastructure financing. In August 2026, Nvidia disclosed $105 billion in contingent liabilities tied to an Ohio data center leased by OpenAI, alongside a $6.3 billion compute capacity commitment to CoreWeave through 2032. Nvidia is no longer purely a chip supplier; it is entwined in a web of contracts, guarantees and investments that bind its fate to clients and infrastructure projects.

This interdependence was tested in November 2026, when Nvidia’s 33-year CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including one linked to a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. The stock plummeted 14.35 percent, wiping out roughly $600 billion in market value at its nadir.

A lawsuit filed by shareholders alleged mismanagement of risks tied to Huang’s personal conduct, further shaking investor confidence. The shock revealed that market enthusiasm had been predicated on fragile assumptions: sustained AI demand and manageable financial risks. Was this a bubble bursting? Not precisely. It was fragility exposed, not an implosion. Bubbles collapse internally when valuations and capital flows unravel together; fragility surfaces when a single shock reveals systemic dependencies.

As trust and capital wobble, legal pressures mount. When technology outpaces legislation, courts become arbiters of uncharted risks. In 2026, a landmark case in the EU challenged the liability of AI-generated content, setting a precedent for global regulatory debates. Lawsuits over AI model development no longer ask whether AI can be built, but under what conditions, who bears liability and who holds veto power. This marks a pivot from techno-optimism to institutional accountability.

Three pressures now converge: a leadership crisis eroding trust, financial warnings exposing fragility and legal challenges testing regulatory boundaries. This is the “messy middle” in microcosm. A 2026 IMF study quantifies the stakes: a sudden loss of access to advanced AI could shrink GDP by 0.2-0.41 percent, depending on substitutability. While modest, this underscores AI’s role as an economic input — not yet a proven profit engine, but critical enough that its disruption carries macroeconomic costs.

The post-AI era begins when AI shifts from product to utility, when “AI company” sounds as anachronistic as “internet company” does today. It arrives when the question evolves from “Does AI generate profit?” to “How do we manage an AI-dependent economy?” It also requires redundancy: disruptions become negligible because alternatives are plentiful, substitution is seamless and competitive catch-up is rapid.

Until then, the world remains in the “messy middle,” a phase marked by gaps between adoption and profitability, funding and fragility, and hype and governance. Yet the “messy middle” is not an endpoint. It is a stress test and a precursor to infrastructure. The internet took decades to vanish into omnipresence. AI will follow suit.

The question is: when will it become invisible because it is everywhere? The answer will likely come by 2040. This is a historically informed extrapolation. By then, AI will be pervasive, and we will have learned to live with its imperfections, finance its costs and govern its risks.

• Dr. Abdel-Hameed Nawar is an associate professor of economics at Cairo University.

World.title: Parents navigate the challenges of raising children in the AI age
World.content:
JEDDAH: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly embedded in education and everyday life, parents face a new challenge: helping children benefit from the technology without becoming overly dependent on it.

For some families, that means allowing children to explore AI independently. For others, it involves setting clear boundaries, supervising its use and ensuring that technology does not replace curiosity, critical thinking or human interaction.

Noha Al-Juhani never formally introduced AI to her nine-year-old son. He discovered it himself.

“He discovered it on his own, and afterward I showed him more about it,” the Jeddah-based mother told Arab News.

What began as a resource for schoolwork has since expanded into a range of interests. “At the beginning it was for school questions,” she said. “Now he uses it in many areas, mainly for his studies, but also food, general knowledge, plants and animals.”

DID YOU KNOW? Saudi Arabia introduced an AI curriculum for the 2025-26 academic year, targeting more than 6 million general education students.

Ninety-nine percent of people aged 15 to 74 in Saudi Arabia used the internet in 2025, according to GASTAT.

OpenAI requires users to be at least 13, or the applicable minimum age of digital consent in their country, to use its services.

Her son uses AI in Arabic, and his school has also adopted the technology. At home, she has not imposed specific restrictions.

“I haven’t set any rules,” Al-Juhani said. “So far the results have been positive.”

In Madinah, Lana bint Masoud has adopted a more supervised approach with her 15-year-old son, Qais Al-Ruwaili, allowing him to use AI for schoolwork only under adult oversight.

“He can use it for school tasks, but only when I am with him or when his tutor is supervising him,” she said. “I want to know how he is using it and make sure he is learning from the process.”

She welcomes the opportunity for her son to become familiar with emerging technologies but believes that guidance is essential.

“Technology is becoming part of his world, and I want him to learn how to use it. But at his age, I believe that should happen with guidance and supervision.”

The contrasting approaches highlight a growing dilemma for parents as AI becomes more accessible to younger users: how to encourage its educational benefits while safeguarding children's ability to think independently, evaluate information and protect their privacy.

Age requirements also differ across services. OpenAI’s terms require users to be at least 13, or the minimum age required in their country to consent to using its services. Those younger than 18 need permission from a parent or legal guardian.

For Andrey Sidenko, cyber literacy projects lead at cybersecurity firm Kaspersky, one concern is the tendency of AI tools to reinforce users' opinions rather than challenge them.

“AI systems are designed to be responsive and validate opinions rather than focus on objective truth,” he told Arab News, describing responses as “structured to maximize user satisfaction.”

“This can sometimes create an experience where children feel that the technology is always on their side.”

Such interactions can be particularly influential for children who are still developing their ability to assess information and consider different perspectives.

“For children who are still developing their judgement, constant validation can be problematic. Children need to learn that it is healthy to encounter different opinions and sometimes be told that they are wrong.”

AI, he added, “should be treated as a tool for exploring ideas, not as an unquestioning authority or a substitute for trusted adults.”

The risk of overdependence is also a concern for Masoud, who wants to ensure that instant answers do not come at the expense of independent discovery.

“I do not want him to become dependent on getting an immediate answer,” she said. “Sometimes a question should lead him to search, read and explore. If the answer is always given to him straight away, he may miss the opportunity to discover something himself.”

She added: “There still needs to be room for curiosity, especially at his age.”

She encourages Qais to research questions, check sources and assess what he finds before turning to AI.

“AI can help him along the way, but I do not want it to take over that effort.”

Sidenko acknowledged the technology's potential to support education, particularly by explaining difficult concepts and generating practice exercises in subjects such as mathematics and languages.

“AI can be extremely valuable when it helps a child understand something rather than simply giving them the answer,” he said.

The distinction, he explained, lies in whether AI helps children develop skills or simply completes tasks on their behalf.

“If a child asks AI to solve every problem, write every assignment or make every decision, they may complete the task without developing the underlying skill.”

Children still need “opportunities to struggle with difficult problems, make mistakes, research independently and develop their own ideas,” he added. “These experiences cannot be automated.”

Beyond learning, the growing use of conversational AI raises concerns about children's privacy, particularly when they begin treating these tools as confidants.

“When a child treats an AI tool like a confidant, they may not know what they should and shouldn’t be sharing: personal details, family circumstances, school information, emotions or private conversations,” Sidenko said.

“Children may not understand that these platforms collect, process and store data.”

He advised parents to teach children to think carefully before sharing personal or sensitive information and to seek human support when dealing with serious or emotional issues.

“When a child is dealing with something serious or emotional, an AI companion should never replace a trusted parent, teacher or qualified professional.”

The conversational nature of AI can also encourage emotional attachment, he warned.

“When an AI is conversational, responsive and always available, that relationship can feel very real to them.”

He added: “The more a child trusts a digital service, the more likely they may be to share information with it or accept what it tells them without questioning it.”

Language is another consideration, particularly for children using AI in Arabic, as Al-Juhani’s son does.

“AI models have been trained on very different volumes and types of information across languages, so the experience a child has in Arabic may not always be identical to what they would receive in English,” Sidenko said.

“For Saudi children, this makes verification particularly important.”

These concerns are gaining relevance as Saudi Arabia expands the teaching of AI in schools. A curriculum developed by the National Curriculum Center in collaboration with the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, and the Saudi Data and AI Authority was introduced for the 2025-26 academic year, targeting more than 6 million general education students.

Internet access is also widespread across the Kingdom, with General Authority for Statistics data showing that 99 percent of people aged 15 to 74 used the internet in 2025.

“The earlier children interact with powerful technologies, the earlier they also need the skills to use them responsibly,” Sidenko said. “AI literacy should develop alongside cybersecurity and privacy awareness.”

He stressed that ensuring children's safe use of AI requires a collective effort involving governments, technology companies, schools and families.

“It cannot be the responsibility of one stakeholder alone,” he said, adding that companies “need to build safety and privacy into their products from the outset.”

For Masoud, supervision is not simply about setting limits. It also offers an opportunity to explore the technology together.

“Sometimes we have fun creating images and designs when there is an artistic element to something he is working on,” she said. “We explore ideas together.”

Ultimately, her priority is to ensure that AI complements rather than replaces her son's independent thinking.

“I keep coming back to curiosity. He is 15, and he needs space to wonder about things, explore them and reach his own understanding. AI can support that, but I do not want him to depend on it completely.”

World.title: Levski Sofia coach says Marseille fan clashes ‘unacceptable’
World.content:
MARSEIILE, France: Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez said violent clashes between fans of the Bulgarian club and Marseille supporters ahead of their Europa League game on Thursday were “unacceptable for football.”

The lead-up to the match at the Stade Velodrome was marred by incidents in the stands between the two sets of supporters, including the throwing of projectiles and flares.

Several Marseille fans ran from the stand where they were situated about 10 minutes before kick-off, appearing to pursue a group of Bulgarian supporters.

They breached the stand designated for away fans, where around 500 Levski supporters were gathered.

Security personnel eventually managed to restore calm as the game kicked off on time.

“It’s a very regrettable episode — these are incidents which are unacceptable for football,” said Velazquez.

“I support the fans who were caught up in this incident. I hope nothing serious has happened. I’m very saddened by this situation.”

Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was “working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents.”

There were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break.

“We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable,” said Marseille coach Bruno Genesio.

The home team went on to win the game 1-0.

World.title: Thousands of protesters rally in Iraqi Kurdistan
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Thousands of protesters rallied in different cities in Iraqi Kurdistan on Thursday to oppose federal government moves to take over oil operations and international border crossings in the semi-autonomous region.

Crowds gathered near Erbil’s citadel and across Duhok waving Kurdish flags and banners rejecting federal interference in the region’s administrative and financial rights. Rival Kurdish political factions also united in opposition to the federal directives.

The protests took place after Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi decided on Tuesday to transfer control of all border crossings in Iraqi Kurdistan to Iraq’s federal Border Ports Authority.

The directives require the federal Oil Ministry’s approval for crude exports and transfer the management of oil fields in four provinces—Kirkuk, Diyala, Salah al-Din, and Nineveh—from Kurdish authorities to the federal government.

On Wednesday, Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court backed the measures, ruling that Baghdad has the constitutional authority to deploy federal forces along all international borders, including within the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

Al-Zaidi stated that the actions reflect Iraq’s independent national will and are part of a broader campaign to combat corruption and stop oil smuggling networks.

The move follows a separate federal crackdown the previous week against alleged oil smuggling by an Iran-aligned militia south of Baghdad.

The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) described the decisions as unconstitutional, arguing they represent an attempt to return Iraq to a centralized regime and criticizing the use of threats. The KRG’s prime minister, Masrour Barzani, stated that the measures are completely unacceptable.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate drops to 1,690 dinars in Iraq’s parallel market
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar slightly dropped on Thursday in both Baghdad, the Iraqi capital, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate declined in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,690 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,694.5 Iraqi dinars on Thursday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,695 Iraqi dinars and 1,685 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also declined, fluctuating between 1,694.5 and 1,693.5 Iraqi dinars.

US dollar exchange rates rose noticeably in the Baghdad and Erbil markets on October 7, following the cabinet’s decision to revalue the official rate of the local currency, causing turbulence and instability in the parallel market.

Iraq officially depreciated its national currency, with the baseline dropping from about 1,300 Iraqi dinars to 1,500 dinars per US dollar.

The Iraqi cabinet approved the structural adjustment, which marks a 14.5 percent decline compared to the previous official framework that had been in place since early 2023.

Following the announcement, parallel market rates in Baghdad and Erbil soared, with exchange shops reporting market gains of more than 1,700 Iraqi dinars per US dollar.

World.title: Iraq discusses raising overseas bank card usage caps for travelers
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Parliamentary Finance Committee discussed raising the spending limits on bank cards used by Iraqi citizens traveling abroad during a meeting with Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) officials in late November.

The committee hosted directors from key CBI departments—including investments, banking supervision, non-bank financial institution supervision, issuance, and treasuries—to review monetary policy plans.

Alongside raising overseas card usage caps for travelers, the discussions addressed expanding financial inclusion, increasing the number of exchange companies, ensuring adequate cash liquidity, and boosting state treasury revenues.

In mid-October, the CBI directed financial institutions to implement a monthly transaction limit for bank cards and to establish a maximum daily limit for purchases made at points of sale outside of Iraq.

The CBI underlined that the decision relates to point-of-sale transactions made outside Iraq, notably those that require the actual presence of the card with the merchant.

Holders of bank cards may use them for point-of-sale purchases outside Iraq up to a daily limit equivalent to $3,333 (or five million Iraqi dinars), provided that total monthly transactions do not exceed five million Iraqi dinars.

The measure replaces the previous daily limit of $333.3 (equivalent to 500,000 Iraqi dinars) specifically for this type of transaction.

World.title: Iraqi judiciary sentences 11 people to 15 years in prison for oil smuggling
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Central Criminal Court sentenced on Thursday 11 people to 15 years in prison each for smuggling oil to neighboring countries.

Reports indicate that the defendants were part of an armed group led by fugitive Ahmed Abdul-Wahid Shaya. This group smuggled oil from Basra province using boats and forged documents.

The court has ordered the confiscation of the boats involved, while authorities are actively pursuing the remaining members of the group.

The unanimous verdict credits the defendants’ time served in pre-trial detention between September 19 and November 25, 2026.

The ruling is subject to appeal and mandatory review by the Court of Cassation. Once finalized, harmed parties retain the right to seek financial compensation in civil courts.

The sentences coincide with an intensified federal campaign against fuel theft and illicit exports. Earlier on Thursday, Iraqi authorities began closing all unofficial border crossings with neighboring countries following a directive from Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi.

Earlier in November, al-Zaidi removed several senior officials and security personnel in connection with smuggling investigations at the state-run North Oil Company and pipeline-tapping networks in Babil province.

World.title: 10 French nationals sentenced to prison for joining ISIS
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Karkh Criminal Court sentenced on Thursday 10 French nationals to prison for joining the terrorist group ISIS.

Eight received life imprisonment, which equates to a 20-year term under Iraqi law, and two received 15-year prison sentences.

The 10 men are part of 47 French nationals transferred to Iraq from northeast Syria in 2025, whose trials in Baghdad began in September 2026 under Iraq’s anti-terrorism law.

Thursday’s rulings bring the number of convicted French citizens in this group to 26, as 16 had previously been convicted in earlier hearings. Another 10 defendants had their verdicts postponed to a later date.

Representatives from the French Embassy in Iraq and defense lawyers attended the hearings.

Iraq prosecutes ISIS members under its anti-terrorism statutes regardless of whether their alleged activities took place in Iraq or neighboring Syria.

France has repatriated hundreds of family members of jihadists while largely declining to bring back adult men accused of involvement.

Rights groups have criticized the pace and due process of Iraq’s terrorism trials, while Iraqi authorities continue processing thousands of detainees transferred from Syria.

World.title: Iraq in discussions with Apple to activate Apple Pay
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi authorities are holding official talks with Apple to introduce Apple Pay in Iraq as part of a broader push to expand digital payment services.

Head of the Communications and Media Commission (CMC) Baligh Abu-Kallal said in early November that Iraq is negotiating with Apple over launching Apple Pay, privacy policies, and gaming sector cooperation.

In August, Iraq accredited Apple as a verified digital platform, covering services such as the App Store, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts, Apple Arcade, and Apple Ads under local regulations.

Abu-Kallal stated that launching Apple Pay depends on completing technical, legal, and financial procedures, local news outlet Shafaq News reported.

Iraqi banks have also signaled interest in digital wallet expansion amid wider banking modernization and digital payment reforms.

Earlier in July, an Iraqi government source mentioned that the committee in charge of activating Apple Pay services met with Apple’s regional managers to make the service accessible in Iraq.

The initiative is part of the Iraqi government’s efforts to enhance the electronic payment infrastructure and boost the adoption of modern technology, thereby fostering financial inclusion and advancing digital transformation.

Iraq aims to make Apple Pay available to users, in accordance with the government’s strategy to expand the online payment sector and support the transition to a digital economy.

World.title: Iraq expands digital services for Iraqi Airways
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Transport has expanded digital services for Iraqi Airways to facilitate passenger travel and reduce airport congestion.

Travelers can complete check-in procedures and issue their electronic boarding passes online before arriving at the airport.

Passengers can also choose their preferred seats in advance during booking or check-in.

Users can now electronically change their flight schedules and destinations without visiting a sales office.

The airline enhanced its electronic reservation and online payment systems for both domestic and international flights.

A new pricing structure lets passengers select different fare classes with varying baggage allowances and modification terms.

Passengers can use these services through the Iraqi Airways official website or via the mobile app.

The step is part of the company’s strategy to grow its digital capabilities, improve passenger experience, and stay up with the latest standards in the aviation industry.

The service generally opens for check-in between 48 and 24 hours before the scheduled flight departure and closes up to two hours prior to takeoff.

World.title: Iraq’s judiciary rules that Baghdad can deploy forces along all borders
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Federal Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday that the federal government in Baghdad can deploy troops to secure all international borders, including those in Iraqi Kurdistan.

The decision backs Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s push to assert central control over border crossings and oil fields across the country.

The court affirmed federal jurisdiction over international borders, customs oversight, and the auditing of oil and gas fields, while allowing shared management with regional authorities and provinces.

Ali al-Zaidi ordered federal takeovers of Kurdish-run border crossings and disputed oil fields following an oil smuggling investigation. The Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) described the moves as constitutional violations and military threats, calling instead for dialogue.

The crackdown, which also targets militias with ties to Iran, is seen by analysts as part of Zaidi’s larger effort to consolidate power. As a result, the Supreme Judicial Council has called on all parties to uphold the 2005 constitution.

A day earlier, al-Zaidi ordered federal authorities to take control of all border crossings in Iraqi Kurdistan and directed the Oil Ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salah al-Din, and Nineveh provinces.

The KRG was instructed to approve crude oil and petroleum product exports only through the federal Oil Ministry.

The directives followed an investigation into smuggling at the state-run North Oil Company and a wider campaign against illicit oil networks—including alleged smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar linked to the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, which denied the accusation.

World.title: Judicial member must on bench to confirm PMLA attachment, says Supreme Court
World.content:
NEW DELHI: In an important insertion into the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, the

on Friday said the bench of the adjudicating authority (AA), tasked with deciding the confirmation of EDâs orders for provisional attachment of assets by terming them proceeds of crime, must have a judicial member.

Deciding a host of petitions questioning the competence of administrative members forming single-member benches to decide questions of law and conflicting judgements from various HCs, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said that to confirm confiscation of assets termed as âproceeds of crimeâ under Section 8 of PMLA, the AA is required to analyse legal provisions.

âThe presence of a judicial member on the bench undertaking the same ensures legal objectivity in the determination recorded by the AA. The lifetime of experience of the administrative and financial members in the AA would undoubtedly render them to be exceptional experts in their fields, but impartial and legally sound adjudication necessitates judicial temperament and training,â the bench said.

It added, however, that the judgment would operate prospectively and not provide grounds for the reopening of past decisions.

World.title: Bihar move illegal, says Supreme Court, quashes premature release of former MP Anand Mohan
World.content:
The state govt had amended prison rules to pave the way for Mohanâs release by removing the provision that disqualifies a person from remission if he is convicted of a public servantâs murder.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Quoting former US President Theodore Roosevelt to say justice consisted not in being neutral between right and wrong, but in finding out the right and upholding it, the Supreme Court Thursday quashed Biharâs decision to allow the premature release of former MP and strongman Anand Mohan in the 1994 lynching case of district magistrate G Krishnaiah.The state government had amended prison rules to pave the way for Mohanâs release by removing the provision that disqualifies a person from remission if he is convicted of a public servantâs murder. A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu quashed the amendment, saying it was indefensible and no rationale was given for changing the law. It directed Mohan to surrender within a month.âThe notification dated April 10, 2023, is declared unconstitutional, invalid and inoperative, and is hereby set aside. The order dated April 24, 2023, granting premature release to (Mohan), is hereby quashed,â the bench said.The court said the state government could initiate a fresh procedure to amend the remission policy. âIt is clarified that any future process to revise or amend Rule 481 shall not be initiated prior to (Mohan) surrendering within a month or being taken into custody, as the case may be,â it said.

World.title: Supreme Court to banks: Give nod to try officials in 7 days
World.content: Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati informed a bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalay Bagchi and V Mohana that in the 22 cases, HDFC, ICICI, Samman and PNB have granted conditional sanction for prosecution

World.title: 7 months on, mediation in Sunjay Kapur case hits deadlock
World.content:
Taking note of the report filed by the mediator, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran closed the mediation. âOne can never force a settlement,â it observed.

NEW DELHI: Seven months of mediation proceedings, which were conducted on the direction of the SC for amicable resolution of the property dispute between late industrialist Sunjay Kapurâs mother, Rani Kapur, and his widow, Priya Sachdev Kapur, fell flat, and the former CJI DY Chandrachud, who was the mediator, told the court Thursday that the mediation reached an impasse despite 15 sittings.He was roped in by the SC in May to settle the high-profile property dispute between them over Kapurâs Rs 30,000 crore estate.Taking note of the report filed by the mediator, a bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran closed the mediation. âOne can never force a settlement,â it observed.As the lawyers appearing for the Kapurs blamed each otherâs clients for mediation failure, the bench told the parties, âWhen you all decide to sit, talk, and try to find a way out, you need to show some flexibility, some understanding, and take a practical view of the matter... 15 sittings and you all couldnât reach a conclusion.âThe court said that it would pass a short order in the case.

World.title: Opposition worried, feels government won’t risk another defeat
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Despite repeatedly expressing apprehensions about a âsinister planâ behind the Modi government not proroguing the monsoon session for 106 days, the opposition was Thursday surprised by the BJPâs convening of the

, with the delimitation bill as the likely agenda. INDIA bloc is likely to meet Sunday to take stock of the situation.

There is uncertainty in the opposition about the numbers game given the buzz around NCP-SP that has made equivocal statements in recent days. DMKâs stance is also being watched with wariness, though it was against the bill in the past. There is a feeling that government will not risk a loss of face on the bill again, and the convening of Parliament has raised concerns.

The fate of the contentious legislation that would take the strength of LS to around 850 seats would depend on these two regional parties, strategists said.



Congressâs KC Venugopal said, âFor 106 days, they did not prorogue the monsoon session. There has been a complete lack of transparency... While the old delimitation bill was defeated, the new bill has not been circulated. Everybody is in the dark.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Amid speculation for more than three months over the delimitation bill, Congress spokespersons have been exuding confidence about the numbers, even vouching for DMK, which is not with the INDIA bloc anymore.





Many have pointed out that DMK is a signatory to the recent unanimous resolution of the Tamil Nadu assembly, which had demanded that LSâs strength be frozen at 543 seats.

Congressâs Jairam Ramesh said âthe fight is onâ, adding, âOn Constitution Day, after 105 days of Operation Lotus, Modi government announces a special session, hoping it will get its super-tainted two-thirds majority to pass an amendment bill. Can there be a greater insult to and assault on the Constitution?â

CPMâs MA Baby termed the delimitation bill as designed to carry forward the divisive agenda of BJP-RSS. âI was in Parliament for 12 years but had never witnessed such surreptitious methods being used to subvert democracy,â he said.

World.title: Special Parliament session from November 30; women’s quota on agenda
World.content:
Smarting under the govtâs first defeat on the floor of Parliament, BJP has since made determined moves to shore up its numbers, helped considerably by fractures in the opposition camp.

Shahâs assurance may be added to delimitation bill, Cabinet nod today

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Ending suspense, government Thursday moved to convene a short session of Parliament from November 30 during which it is expected to bring back the delimitation bills to implement the womenâs quota law from 2029, which would increase Lok Sabhaâs maximum strength to 850 from 550, reflecting confidence in NDA that it will muster a two-thirds majority this time to secure the billâs passage.Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju announced that government has requested Speaker Om Birla to reconvene Lok Sabha on November 30 and Rajya Sabha Chairman C P Radhakrishnan to call a sitting of the House on Dec 2 to transact âessential government businessâ.âSubject to exigencies of business, the sitting of both Houses may conclude on Dec 3, 2026,â he said, suggesting government is hopeful of concluding its agenda in four days.This is the second attempt by government to secure passage of its ambitious legislative agenda. If passed, it will mark the biggest realignment of Lok Sabha constituencies since Independence. A united opposition had thwarted the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill in a similarly convened session, of three days, from April 16.The move comes amid strong indications that government is confident of its numbers in the second trial of strength that the opposition is determined to force.In any case, it will be loath to risk another embarrassment; that too one during the build-up to assembly elections in UP and other states.Passage of the bill, which will ensure reservation of one-third seats in Lok Sabha and pave the way for a similar quota in assemblies, will give BJP a major campaign point in the upcoming polls to showcase its pro-women credentials.In an article on Thursday, PM Narendra Modi said the scuttling of the bill earlier this year âshould fill our hearts with shameâ, adding that a legislation aimed at giving adequate representation to women was prevented from being passed by one opposition party, in what was an attack at Congress.He assured women that âno force can prevent us from ensuring that justice is done to them.âLast time, among 528 MPs present in Lok Sabha, the bill had received support from 298 members while 230 opposed it, falling way short of the 352 needed for its passage.Smarting under the governmentâs first defeat on the floor of Parliament, BJP has since made determined moves to shore up its numbers, helped considerably by fractures in the opposition camp.The switchover of 20 of 29 Trinamool Congress Lok Sabha MPs to NDA has boosted its numbers. Going by the buzz within government, it is also counting on support of 22 DMK MPs and eight of NCP-SP, who had voted against the bill last time along with TMCâs entire lot.Lok Sabhaâs current strength is 540, with NDAâs tally at 321. The support of DMK and NCP-SP will take it to 351. The expected support from four YSR Congress MPs will take it closer to the 360-mark required in case all 540 MPs vote, which is unlikely as a few abstentions are expected to NDAâs advantage.Government has maintained secrecy about its potential new backers. DMK and NCP-SP have not announced support but have suggested that they can back the bill if states are not discriminated against â a threshold that government can easily meet by writing into the bill, which is already in Parliament, a clause providing for 50 per cent increase in seats across the board.Union minister Amit Shah had assured Lok Sabha in April that no state would suffer erosion in its relative strength in the lower House as the number of seats in each state would rise by around 50 per cent. The strength of state assemblies will be next to go up if the bill is passed. Shahâs assurance may be pencilled into the bill, which the Union cabinet headed by PM Narendra Modi is likely to clear Friday.A DMK MP told TOI that party chief MK Stalin will finalise their stand after looking at the bill, reiterating that southern states should not suffer. DMK has anyway drifted away from the opposition after Congress dumped it to align with CM Vijay-led TVK in Tamil Nadu.NCP MP Supriya Sule said âlet the bill be out firstâ, suggesting her openness to the proposal. She said the bill may be good and needed to be studied first, and that opposition and government had in the past supported decisions which were in national interest.The hard part for the government is in the Lok Sabha, as its numbers are more favourably aligned in the Rajya Sabha.

World.title: Supreme Court raps MNCs for ‘double standard’ on food quality
World.content:
NEW DELHI: The

on Thursday called out the âdouble standardâ of multinational companies in producing foodstuff for Indian consumers inferior in quality to what they did in Western countries, saying it was âdeeply troublingâ.

While directing

to enforce front-of-pack nutrition labelling (FoPNL) to make consumers aware of the contents of packaged food, a bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran deliberated on the dual yardsticks MNCs follow.

âConcerns have been raised that certain multinational FBOs operating in India adopt practices towards Indian consumers that differ from those they follow elsewhere, including in the composition of their products and in the information provided on their labels.



Such companies comply with, and in some instances voluntarily adopt, FoPNL requirements in other jurisdictions, yet resist similar measures here. If true, such double standards are deeply troubling,â the bench said.

Saying a consumer in India was entitled to âno less protection and no less informationâ than one in the US or UK, SC said, âWe would urge such multinational FBOs to adopt uniform standards across jurisdictions, and to extend to Indian consumers the same regard and respect for their health that they extend to consumers elsewhere.â

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines





It also directed FSSAI to ensure FBOs do not conceal or alter the composition of their products, or add additives, artificial preservatives, emulsifiers, etc, to soften the effect of FoPNL. âThe introduction of a warning label must not become an occasion for reformulation that is hidden from the consumer, or that places the consumer at comparable or greater risk,â SC said.

World.title: Pension, insurance for 15 lakh gig workers likely by year-end
World.content:
The National Social Security Board is expected to deliberate on contributory models, including a turnover-based model, where platforms or aggregators will contribute 2% of their turnover to the social security fund.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Government is likely to announce a pension scheme along with health insurance, maternity benefits and life and disability covers for the nearly 15 lakh gig and platform-based workers enrolled on the e-Shram portal by Dec-end, TOI has learnt.âWorkers who have been enrolled by platforms on the portal will be the primary beneficiaries. All leading platforms have already shared data,â an official said.The move will affect lakhs working with platforms like Swiggy, Zomato, Uber, Ola, Rapido, Pronto, Snabbit and Urban Company.The measures are set to be discussed in the maiden meeting of the National Social Security Board next month. It is expected to deliberate on contributory models, including a turnover-based model, where platforms or aggregators will contribute 2% of their turnover to the social security fund. The other possible model is payout-based, with aggregators contributing 2% of the transaction value.Ravindra Singh, regional secretary, Trade Union Co-ordination Centre and a member of the board, said workers must receive health and accident cover at the time of onboarding instead of waiting for the threshold set under the new labour codes.National Front of Indian Trade Unions president Deepak Jaiswal suggested government provide budgetary support to the social security fund.

World.title: Clashes at Besiktas match against Israeli club spark diplomatic row
World.content:
Istanbul club Besiktas's supporters unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during a UEFA Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia on Thursday (November 26, 2026), prompting a police response and sparking a diplomatic incident that led Turkey's foreign minister to contact his Georgian counterpart.

Also read | Irish athletes’ group urges national team to boycott Israel fixtures

Turkish football fans clashed with police in Batumi, temporarily halting the match, which had been moved from Istanbul over security concerns.

Images from the stadium showed Besiktas supporters displaying a banner reading "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine", waving Palestinian flags and chanting anti-Israel slogans before police intervened.

Georgia's Interior Ministry said in a statement that "three officers sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions", adding that 16 people had been detained.

It said some supporters had hurled stadium seats at officers and denied reports that police had used force in response to the display of pro-Palestinian flags and banners.

"We categorically deny these reports and emphasise that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," the Ministry added.

Police used pepper spray against fans, some of whom required medical attention, Turkey's private DHA news agency reported.

The match was suspended in the 26th minute because of disturbances in the stands, with Danish referee Morten Krogh sending both teams to the dressing rooms.

Turkey's football federation strongly condemned what it described as the "unacceptable" conduct of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters.

"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the UEFA Europa League match," the federation said in a statement.

‘Disproportionate use of force’

UEFA announced last month that the fixture would be moved to Georgia after Turkish authorities informed European football's governing body that, "for safety and security reasons", the match could not be hosted in Istanbul.

Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the outbreak of the Gaza war.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch supporter of the Palestinian cause, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza.

Pro-Palestinian banners and chants are seen or heard frequently at Turkish football matches, particularly since the start of the war.

Besiktas said they had lodged a complaint with UEFA over what they described as the "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.

"We have launched initiatives with our consulate general in Batumi and UEFA regarding the disproportionate use of force against our supporters by security forces," the club said.

Besiktas added that they would closely monitor the situation until all of their supporters had returned safely to Turkey.

Mr. Erdogan spoke by phone with Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali and said he was closely following developments, the club said.

Messages of support

After the match, which finished 2-1 to Besiktas, Hapoel Beer-Sheva posted a message on social media directed to their travelling supporters.

"Please act responsibly, show restraint and use your best judgement as you leave the stadium and make your way to your accommodation. Follow the instructions of the Georgian security forces, who are responsible for ensuring your safety," the club posted in Hebrew on X.

Messages of support poured in on social media from across Turkey, including from the Sports Minister and Ankara mayor.

Even Besiktas's traditional Istanbul rivals, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce, as well as Black Sea club Trabzonspor, condemned the incidents and expressed solidarity with the club.

A Besiktas club employee told AFP that five supporters were receiving treatment in hospital.

Besiktas supporters scuffled with police and hurled objects at officers as they attempted to make arrests, according to live television footage.

The incidents prompted Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to call his Georgian counterpart, Maka Botchorishvili.

"Officials from the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate general in Batumi are at the stadium," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.

"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights."

World.title: Leave aside any differences, remove BJP in U.P., says Congress chief
World.content:
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Thursday (November 26, 2026) in Lucknow urged party leaders and workers to strengthen the Samajwadi Party (SP)-Congress alliance and leave aside any differences in a bid to oust the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in Uttar Pradesh. “To win, we all have to fight together and leave aside egoistic talk. We have to strengthen the alliance and remove Modi-Yogi from power.
