World.title: Japan Tobacco studies deal for Imperial Brands
World.content:
Japan Tobacco is studying a potential deal for British cigarette-maker Imperial Brands, according to people familiar with the matter.

The Japanese group has been speaking with advisers as it evaluates a possible transaction, the people said. Japan Tobacco has been considering teaming up with a partner on an acquisition of Imperial and then splitting up the British company’s assets in different parts of the world, some of the people said.

Shares of Imperial have fallen about 5% in London trading this year, giving the company a market value of £22.2 billion ($29.1 billion).

Deliberations are at an early stage, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private.

Japan Tobacco markets Winston cigarettes across Europe and Asia, while Imperial sells the brand in the U.S. The British company’s other products include Kool menthol cigarettes and Rizla rolling papers. Japan Tobacco sells brands including Mevius, Camel, Benson & Hedges and Nordic Spirit in various geographies.

Tokyo-based Japan Tobacco has been weighing various deals around Imperial Brands on-and-off for years, and there’s no certainty it will decide to move ahead. Spokespeople for Japan Tobacco and Imperial declined to comment.

An acquisition of Imperial would mark the largest takeover of a publicly-traded U.K. company in more than eight years, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. The London market has been hit by an exodus of high-profile companies this year, with foreign buyers and private capital seeking to take advantage of lower valuations.

World.title: Vietnam must explain ‘abduction’ of activists: U.N. experts
World.content:
Vietnam must explain how three pro-democracy activists ended up in detention facing terrorism charges after being allegedly abducted from neighbouring Cambodia, United Nations experts said on Thursday.

Vietnam permits little to no dissent within its borders and critics say its security apparatus stretches abroad, with wanted dissidents previously abducted in Thailand and Germany.

The authorities in Hanoi confirmed in September they had arrested three men — an Australian, a Norwegian and a Vietnamese national — on charges of terrorism and forging documents.

“We urge Vietnam to disclose the circumstances and legal basis of the arrests,” said the experts, who are mandated by the U.N. Human Rights Council but do not speak on behalf of the United Nations itself.

They said Cambodia had a duty to investigate, while Vietnam must cooperate and detail “any involvement of its officials in the alleged abductions, transfers and enforced disappearances“.

“We are alarmed by these alleged transboundary abductions, which violate international human rights law,” they said.

Rights group Viet Tan raised the alarm in late September, saying two of its members had been abducted by Vietnamese authorities from across the border in Cambodia, forcibly brought to Vietnam and detained on “fabricated” terrorism charges.

Nguyen Duc Thuan, a Norwegian citizen, and Australian national Tran Hiep, also known as Ho Pham Hiep Huy, had been reported missing since Sept. 18.

Vietnam’s public security ministry later confirmed the pair had been arrested along with a Vietnamese man, Thai Cong Truong Son, who was not identified by Viet Tan as one of its members.

The terrorism charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in jail.

More than 160 political prisoners are detained in Vietnam, according to the NGO Human Rights Watch.

World.title: Japan firms say rate hikes are starting to bite, new study shows
World.content:
Japanese businesses are increasingly feeling the weight of rising interest rates, a new survey showed, sending a fresh reminder to the Bank of Japan of the need to keep a careful eye on financial conditions.

Almost 59% of companies said the negative effects of higher rates are greater than the positive ones, according to the survey released Wednesday by the Teikoku Databank. That’s an increase of 14 percentage points from the previous poll in December.

The BOJ raised its benchmark rate to the highest level in three decades in September and it’s widely expected to hike again next month. Gov. Kazuo Ueda’s board has raised policy rates six times since 2024, though its benchmark is still among the lowest among major economies at 1.25%.

The latest survey data shows the impact of those hikes is spreading across the corporate sector. It suggests the BOJ will continue to carefully watch both the accumulated impact of rate hikes and the upside risks to inflation, which has climbed above the central bank’s 2% target.

The Teikoku Databank found that some 48% of companies said their main banks had approached them about raising lending rates. Out of those firms, 29% said their rates had already been increased.

Average rates on new loans rose to 2.12% in September, according to a separate BOJ report released Wednesday, the highest level since 1996.

World.title: Nine hurt in huge explosion at Bangkok oil facility
World.content:
A huge explosion rocked an oil facility in Bangkok on Thursday, injuring nine people with three of them in a critical condition, Thai authorities said.

The blast was so strong that it rattled doors several kilometers away, according to reporters, who saw a column of flames above the site followed by thick black smoke.

Thailand’s Energy minister Akanat Promphan, visiting the scene, said the blast sparked concern as the sprawling Phra Khanong site in eastern Bangkok was “also a residential area.”

But he told reporters it appeared the fire broke out at a distillation tower, “which was at least 100 meters (330 feet) away from the oil depot,” limiting the damage.

Thai energy conglomerate Bangchak Corporation, which runs the site, said it brought the situation under control within 30 minutes.

The cause of the incident was under investigation, it said in a statement.

The firm later said “air quality monitoring around the refinery shows normal levels.”

Akanat said authorities tested for carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and other contaminants in a 1-kilometer (0.6-mile) radius around the facility and found no irregularities.

But the government was suspending production at the plant until the energy ministry was confident operations could resume without issue, he said.

Police said that students from nearby schools had been evacuated, and residents were also asked to leave.

The Erawan Emergency Medical Centre, which is operated by Bangkok city authorities, reported nine people were injured — three classified as critical, a change from its initial assessment.

Black smoke swept across the Thai capital’s skyline in the immediate aftermath of the blast.

A city-wide alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities urged people to avoid the area.

Bangchak Corporation’s website describes the site as a “modern complex refinery with a maximum capacity of 120,000 barrels per day.”

An explosion occurred at the refinery in July 2012, triggering a massive fire but no reported injuries. It was owned at the time by Bangchak Petroleum, which became the Bangchak Corporation.

The 2012 incident prompted questions about why such a large facility was located near a residential area.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said Thursday he was monitoring the situation, adding that it was too soon to apportion blame.

World.title: Designer baby toys and strollers drive South Korean retail boom
World.content:
South Korean entrepreneur Mah Seungeun rarely talks herself out of buying something for her 10-year-old daughter. With no siblings to share the family’s attention — or its spending — each childhood milestone feels like a one-time opportunity.

“Because I have just one child, I always think: ‘this is the last year my kid will be five, this is the last year they’ll be six.’ So even if I hesitate over a purchase, I end up buying it,” said Mah, 38. “The grandparents buy a lot of gifts, and so do the aunts and uncles.”

That impulse is turning South Korea, home to one of the world’s lowest birth rates, into an unlikely hotspot for premium baby goods. Its dwindling number of children are becoming what Korean marketers dub VIBs — “Very Important Babies” — showered with pricey strollers, designer clothes and toys by families determined to spare little expense for their only progeny.

World.title: Starbucks Korea sees profit return after ‘Tank Day’ backlash
World.content:
Starbucks Korea said it would return to profit in the fourth quarter, as the coffee chain shows signs of recovering from a public-relations crisis over the controversial “Tank Day” promotion that contributed to its first-ever losses earlier this year.

Rebuilding customer trust and preventing a repeat of the debacle have been top priorities, new Korea Chief Executive Offer Shin Dong Woo told reporters on Thursday at the opening of a sprawling new store at the landmark Namsan Seoul Tower. Since taking over, Shin has revamped internal reporting, created a team to vet marketing activities and continued employee training on social sensitivities.

“It would be presumptuous of me to declare that customer trust has been fully restored,” he said. “However, revenue has rebounded enough to absorb our cost structure, putting us on track for a bottom-line turnaround.”

Shin took the helm in June at SCK Company, which operates Starbucks in Korea, after his predecessor was sacked over the May “Tank Day” event that sparked a nationwide boycott, criticism from President Lee Jae Myung and a police raid on Starbucks Korea’s Seoul headquarters.

The campaign, designed to offer discounts on the company’s large Tank series tumblers, fueled public outrage as it coincided with the anniversary of a 1980 pro-democracy uprising that saw South Korea’s then-military junta deploy troops and tanks to crush protests, killing hundreds.

Shin previously held senior roles at Shinsegae Property, the real estate arm of retail conglomerate Shinsegae Group, which controls Starbucks Korea through its supermarket unit E-Mart.

South Korea is Starbucks’ largest market outside the U.S. and China, with more than 2,200 stores. E-Mart owns a 67.5% stake in Starbucks Korea, with the remainder held by Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC.

In May, Shinsegae Group Chairman Chung Yong-jin bowed repeatedly during a televised apology and took responsibility for the blunder, while U.S.-based Starbucks Corp. issued a statement calling the promotion “unacceptable.” Starbucks Korea also took the unprecedented step of closing all stores early in June for employee training on modern Korean history and social sensitivity.

The company posted its first quarterly loss in August since beginning operations in 1999 as boycotts mounted. E-Mart this month reported an earnings shock as Starbucks Korea’s third-quarter loss widened further.

World.title: Japan’s insurers have ‘given up’ on yen with record-low hedging
World.content:
Japan’s concerted push to bolster the yen is running into a major headwind, after the nation’s biggest life insurers slashed their currency hedging to a record low in the fiscal first half.

Nine of the largest life insurers collectively hedged 43.3% of their foreign-asset holdings with derivatives in the six months ended Sept. 30, according to analysis of their earnings reports. That’s the lowest-ever level based on data going back to 2011. The volume of currency derivatives fell 7.6%, outpacing a 1.5% decline in overseas securities.

The data serves as a reminder of the Herculean task confronting Japan’s authorities as they seek to prop up a currency that’s been buffeted by elevated crude prices and the nation’s wide interest-rate gap with the U.S.. The yen breached the closely watched ¥160-per-dollar level for the first time since September earlier this month, putting traders on alert for more intervention by policymakers.

World.title: U.S. chip curbs and distillation crackdown to impact Chinese AI model progress
World.content:
China’s Z.AI has fallen behind schedule on its next flagship artificial intelligence model, while rival Moonshot AI expects that the interval between major releases could double from six months to a year or longer if it loses access to overseas computing power, people familiar with the matter have said.

The previously unreported details show how efforts by U.S. AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic to prevent distillation, a technique in which developers train models using answers generated by more capable ones, have slowed Chinese AI development. Washington’s latest chip restrictions threaten further delays.

The measures jeopardize a key advantage that has helped Chinese AI companies challenge their American rivals despite years of export controls: the ability to develop competitive models at substantially lower cost.

World.title: Let’s keep doing lunch: Hong Kong exchange leans towards keeping noon break, sources say
World.content:
Lunch is likely to remain on the menu for Hong Kong stock brokers, as the city’s bourse operator leans towards extending trading hours at either end of the day while keeping the market’s traditional mid-day break intact, according to multiple sources.

Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) will not highlight the idea of cancelling the current hour-long noon break when it issues a discussion paper on its operating hours as early as next week, sources with knowledge of the matter told the South China Morning Post. Having the market open earlier or stay open later, or both, would be discussed, they said.

The paper, expected ahead of the Nasdaq’s extension to 23-hour trading on December 6, would elicit views on the overall direction of any change before a detailed consultation at a later stage, a source said.

World.title: Hong Kong lawmakers defend CUHK ordinance changes as move to boost governance
World.content:
Lawmakers have defended proposed amendments to the ordinance of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), saying the changes will strengthen how the institution is governed.

Legislators Jonathan Leung Chun and Bill Tang Ka-piu, who sit on the institution’s governing council, said on Thursday that much of the ordinance’s content had failed to keep pace with current societal and legislative changes, necessitating the amendments.

They also said the amendments aligned with the city’s ambition to become an international education hub.

World.title: Hong Kong signals route to ride-hailing licences for private car owners
World.content:
Hong Kong private car owners can apply for one of 10,000 ride-hailing vehicle permits under a quota system opening early next year, with higher chances given to those who have passed a combined driving test, already hold a ride-hailing driving permit, or have owned a private car for a designated period, according to transport authorities.

The Hong Kong Federation of Insurers also said on Thursday that 12 insurance companies would offer products for ride-hailing vehicles, with the premium for a private car insurance policy endorsement costing as little as HK$10,000 (US$1,280).

“The insurers will determine premiums based on individual risk factors, such as the car model, car age, driver age, driving experience, claims history and traffic conviction record,” the federation said.

World.title: Privacy watchdog urges firms to boost defences as cyber breaches hit over 1m people
World.content:
Hong Kong’s privacy watchdog has urged businesses to invest more resources in strengthening their information technology systems in the wake of a recent string of cybersecurity breaches that have affected more than 1 million users.

Privacy Commissioner Ada Chung Lai-ling said on Thursday that hackers were increasingly using artificial intelligence to launch attacks more quickly, as the technology eliminated the need for online testing and reduced the complexity and barriers to carrying out attacks.

She urged organisations to allocate more resources and hire cybersecurity professionals to better manage and safeguard their data security systems, saying they should take responsibility even when hiring a third party.

World.title: Tai Po fire: remembering the victims
World.content:
Hong Kong is still healing, one year after a devastating inferno engulfed Tai Po’s Wang Fuk Court residential complex. Survivors are trying to move forward while grieving loved ones – parents, spouses, siblings and children – whom they lost without the chance to say goodbye.

The South China Morning Post has created a full-page infographic to remember the 168 people killed in the fire . The petals symbolise the lives lost – people held forever in the hearts of their families, friends and the city.

World.title: Will Hong Kong’s expanded WinterFest this year boost the city’s retail spaces?
World.content:
Hong Kong’s expanded WinterFest is likely to boost the prospects of retail properties in the city’s core shopping districts of Causeway Bay, Central and Tsim Sha Tsui, according to property consultancy Cushman & Wakefield.

The city has spruced up its Christmas decorations this year with festive installations, which will run until January 5.

“We believe the city’s winter festival would become a signature seasonal event that appeals to both tourists and local residents,” said John Siu, managing director for Hong Kong at Cushman & Wakefield.

World.title: Hong Kong exports post fastest growth in 70 years on AI-related goods
World.content:
Runaway growth in Hong Kong’s exports, driven by demand for artificial intelligence-related electronic goods, continued into October, with shipments soaring by 65.6 per cent year on year, the fastest pace in more than 70 years, although fresh US tariffs have clouded the outlook.

Provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Thursday showed that the value of exports rose to a record HK$764.5 billion (US$98 billion) last month, while imports grew by 56.2 per cent to HK$783.8 billion, leaving a trade deficit of HK$19.3 billion.

Hong Kong’s export growth was the fastest since the 70.7 per cent increase recorded in April 1956. That monthly figure has never been breached since records began in January 1953.

A government spokesman said October’s historic high was marked by continued strong growth in exports of AI-related electronic products.

World.title: Up to 4½ years in jail for 6 men who had sex with 14-year-old girl they met on dating app
World.content:
A Hong Kong court has sentenced six men to between 20 months and 4½ years in prison for having unlawful sex with a 14-year-old they met through a dating app, with the judge sympathising with the teenager who turned to the internet to seek love and relationships.

Mr Justice Anthony Kwok Kai-on on Thursday sentenced the defendants for having sex with the victim between May and June 2023 after they had met her on Heymandi, a dating app which allows users to chat with each other anonymously.

Five of the defendants – teacher Tam Siu-chun, 28, civil servant Chan Ka-ming, 33, engineering apprentice Ng Kai-ching, 24, firefighter Tso Kit-ting, 31, and YouTuber Wong Pak-hong, 28 – earlier pleaded not guilty to having unlawful sex with a girl under the age of 16. They stood trial in the High Court and were convicted by a jury.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019331/Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
World.title: Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019331/Phones Banned, Chinese Students Turn to Paper Short Dramas
World.content:
Amid nationwide classroom phone bans, “paper short dramas,” half-meter-long printouts of scenes from short dramas folded into the shape of a smartphone, have recently surged in popularity among Chinese primary school students.

“The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” “Reborn as the Heiress of a Tycoon,” and “The School Bully Forces Me to Date Him” are just a few examples of the stories now stocked by school-adjacent stores and e-commerce platforms, selling for as little as 1 yuan ($0.14), domestic media reported Monday.

In 2021, China’s Ministry of Education issued a notice stating that primary and secondary school students should not bring phones into the classroom, and any phone brought to school must be kept by the school. The ministry tightened this in 2025, banning phones and other electronic devices in school classrooms as part of a student mental health initiative.

Paper short dramas’ accordion-style design allow them to be easily concealed and taken into school. They typically contain scenes from multiple episodes, pairing screenshots with written dialogue.

Despite often containing adult, vulgar, and violent content — in “The CEO’s Runaway Sweetheart,” for instance, a female character sleeps with a legendary CEO and becomes the envy of her peers — paper short dramas are marketed as toys, with some packaging citing toy-safety standards that are outdated or inapplicable to a paper booklet.

This marketing tactic allows sellers, who have not obtained permission from short drama producers to reproduce or distribute the content, to dodge copyright laws.

China’s short drama users reportedly reached nearly 664 million as of December last year. Industry estimates put the potential lost output value due to piracy at as high as 20 billion yuan.

In interviews with domestic media, some parents also reported concerns about the adult content in paper short dramas being available to children with no prior screening, saying that such stories might negatively impact their children’s values.

A hashtag related to paper short dramas on microblogging platform Weibo had garnered over 170 million views as of Thursday. Many commenters called the idea creative, terming it a “new kind of comic strip,” while others criticized it for exposing minors to harmful content.

“Products like this need tight control. Don’t let them poison kids,” one user wrote.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A box of different paper short dramas, each shaped like a smartphone. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
World.title: The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019319/The Costly Little Toys Taking Chinese Men for a Spin
World.content:
Zhong Weiting’s wife recently bought him a pair of trousers with four front pockets. They’re for the little metal objects he carries around — things that spin, slide, click, or flip open, some made from titanium and costing thousands of yuan.

Each day, he picks a few from a plastic organizer originally bought for socks. He plays with them in elevators, in his car, and at his desk, switching to quieter models when other people are around.

For Zhong, 32, they help relieve stress and keep his restless hands occupied. “I like the sounds they make, and knowing exactly how they’ll respond gives me a sense of certainty,” he tells Sixth Tone. “I feel a kind of electric tingling in my fingertips.”

For all their elaborate mechanisms, they’re just toys to fiddle with. And Zhong, an export salesman in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen who began collecting only in November 2025, already owns 25, including one he bought this month for 2,199 yuan ($330).

Across China, the toys have found a growing following under the name EDC, short for “everyday carry,” a term borrowed from an online subculture centered on practical gear such as pocketknives and flashlights. On social media, they’re also dubbed “cyber walnuts,” after the traditional Chinese pastime of rolling a pair of walnuts in the hand.

Among the most popular designs are sliders, known in China as “push cards,” whose metal plates produce a series of tactile clicks as they slide against each other. Some toys mimic the motion of revealing a playing card or recreate the sharp tap of a telegraph key, with adjustable resistance and sound on more elaborate models.

Basic models sell for less than 100 yuan, while stainless steel versions typically cost 300 to 500 yuan. Limited editions made from rarer metals or featuring elaborate designs can run into the thousands.

Between July 2025 and June 2026, online sales of EDC toys tracked by consulting firm Meritco Databank rose 55.5% to more than 45 million yuan, with nearly 500,000 toys sold, up 78% year on year.

The vast majority of the trade, however, still takes place within collector circles. While a few large brands sell openly on popular e-commerce platforms, smaller makers rely on private groups on Chinese super app WeChat to announce new releases, sometimes limited to just a few dozen pieces.

At an EDC exhibition in Beijing in October, organizer Fu Chunjun told domestic media that the community has a name for its growing obsession: the “men’s version of Pop Mart,” the Chinese collectible-toy company known for its blind boxes.

But when Zhong shows his latest purchases to friends, few understand the appeal. “They think, why should a plastic or stainless steel gadget sell for 500 yuan?” he says.

Idle hands

To buy a toy from one vendor at Shanghai’s EDC exhibition in April, Guo Songhao first had to draw one of two jokers from a deck of 21 playing cards.

He drew the big joker, securing a limited-edition knuckle roller, a small metal toy designed to be rolled and flipped between the fingers. “My luck was pretty good that day,” the 25-year-old Shanghai-based engineer tells Sixth Tone.

Organized by Laotiejiang, one of China’s oldest EDC brands, the exhibition brought together more than 100 brands and drew three times as many visitors as its 2025 debut. By the time Guo arrived that afternoon, many of the most sought-after toys had already sold out.

A friend who makes a living reselling EDC toys had traveled from northeastern China for the exhibition. After securing a 399-yuan VIP ticket through a lottery, he lined up for hours to get in half an hour ahead of regular visitors. When Guo caught up with him, his friend was carrying a bag containing more than a dozen toys worth tens of thousands of yuan. “He was there to stock up,” Guo says.

Guo first discovered EDC toys in high school but began collecting them in 2022. Still a student with little spare cash, he spent around 500 yuan on two spinners and a push card.

“I thought I’d stop after those three,” he says, even when the toys fell short of his expectations. “I couldn’t stop myself.”

Over the years, Guo estimates he’s bought and sold toys worth a combined 200,000 to 300,000 yuan, recovering what he spent on the hobby. One piece he bought for a little over 1,000 yuan later sold for 5,000 or 6,000 yuan.

Roughly 90% of those purchases took place in private WeChat groups, where Guo says some makers reserve new releases for repeat buyers, or give priority to collectors who already own all three of their earlier models.

While some brands increase production as demand grows, Guo says others deliberately restrict supply, leaving collectors who miss out on new releases facing higher prices on the secondhand market.

“Once everyone can buy it, people lose interest,” says Zhong.

Zhong recently tried to buy a slider he’d seen in numerous videos online. When he tried to add its maker on WeChat, the account had already been flagged for unusual activity following a flood of friend requests. Zhong eventually reached him and waited several more days to join the buying group, where nearly 1,500 people were vying for the first batch of just 200 toys.

He managed to get one, but no amount of adjustment produced a sound he liked. “The tactile feedback was atrocious,” he says. “It was really disappointing.”

He soon sold it on Xianyu, a popular Chinese secondhand marketplace, for 240 yuan, though he reckons it could have fetched more than 320. It was one of about 10 toys he recently sold, all priced below comparable listings.

Even secondhand, buyers expect these toys to look almost new, complete with their original boxes — a peculiar requirement for objects meant to be constantly handled. “I held on to the boxes, but my wife scolded me and told me to get rid of them, so I tossed them all out,” Zhong says. “That makes reselling things quite a hassle for me.”

After discovering EDC toys through online videos in 2025, Wang Yunfei, a master’s student at Shanghai’s Donghua University, began buying secondhand pieces to try different designs without losing too much money if he tired of them.

Over several months, he bought and resold toys worth a combined 2,000 to 3,000 yuan before growing weary of tracking new releases and prices. “I’ve archived those group chats,” he says, adding that he now rarely checks product announcements, spending more time on his studies.

Even Guo, after six years of collecting, has become harder to impress. He believes the market has expanded faster than the quality of its designs. “There are few people with real ideas, design ability, and taste,” he says.

During one spell of boredom, Guo switched to collecting actual walnuts, the traditional kind rolled in the palm. “I ended up buying a bunch of those, too,” he says.

New spin

Before founding 01EDC, now one of China’s leading EDC brands, Lin Tianfeng had simply set out to design a fidget spinner for himself.

In 2016, Lin, now 35, was repairing secondhand sweater-linking machines for his family’s business in southern China’s Guangdong province when he spotted a metal spinner on e-commerce platform Taobao and figured he could make one.

But factory after factory turned him down until a stainless-steel product manufacturer agreed to take his order. Lin commissioned a batch of about 20 three-bladed brass spinners, each weighing 120 grams — nearly three times the ideal weight.

Keeping a couple for himself, Lin tried selling the extras to fellow enthusiasts on Baidu Tieba, a Chinese discussion platform. “But nobody in China wanted these tie geda,” he says, using Chinese internet slang for EDC toys that translates to “little lumps of metal.”

A buyer in Singapore, however, spotted the spinners on Taobao and bought the remaining pieces. “He told me, ‘Your design is amazing. You’re a genius!’ I honestly thought he was trolling me,” Lin recalls. “But I figured, I’m not going to say no to money.”

Lin’s parents were less impressed. Unable to fathom why anyone would pay hundreds of yuan for a piece of metal, they stopped giving him money. At the time, he had just 75 yuan in his pocket.

Earning 10 yuan for every machine he repaired at the family shop, plus more for house calls, Lin managed to scrape together 3,000 yuan in less than two months. A business partner put up another 3,000 yuan, and with the Singaporean buyer’s help, Lin began reaching overseas collectors through Facebook groups.

“Our 6,000 yuan grew to over 10,000, then over 30,000, and then over 90,000,” he recalls. “It just snowballed.”

In his first year, Lin made more than 100,000 yuan in profit, mostly from spinners, all of which he gave to his family, plus an additional 10,000 yuan. “That’s when they believed I was building a business, not messing around,” he says.

Lin handled much of the work himself, sometimes spending 12 hours straight, from 2 p.m. to 2 a.m., meticulously cleaning brass spinners. And as collectors began favoring stainless steel and titanium alloys over brass, finding factories willing to work with the harder metals became increasingly difficult.

Of the seven factories Lin approached on one occasion, only one eventually agreed to take his order — after he spent hours drinking tea in its office. “They turned me down at first, as was to be expected,” he recalls. “I didn’t leave; I just kept sitting there until they finally agreed to handle one production run for me.”

For the first six years of his business, Lin had to keep finding manufacturers willing to take his orders. “It was a guerrilla-style operation, taking a shot here and a shot there, with no fixed base of operations,” he says.

In 2022, Lin finally bought his own machinery, set up a factory, and renamed his brand 01EDC. Most of Lin’s early customers were in the U.S. and Europe, though orders came from as far away as Brazil, where buyers were willing to pay $100 in shipping for a $60 toy.

“In China, the fidget-spinner craze of 2017 was followed by a second wave of interest during the pandemic,” Lin says. Videos demonstrating new designs on Bilibili and Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, drew more people into the hobby.

For men accustomed to collecting figurines or Gundam models, Lin says the pocket-sized toys had another attraction: They could play with them in public without attracting much attention. “Nobody thinks you’re childish,” he says.

Once reliant entirely on overseas customers, 01EDC — selling toys priced from 299 yuan to more than 3,000 yuan — now generates more than 70% of its sales in China, with Lin largely leaving exports to distributors. He estimates the number of Chinese EDC brands has grown from about a dozen in 2020 to more than 400 today.

“At home,” he says, “China alone is a whole world.”

Among his competitors are manufacturers selling near-identical designs under different names and at much lower prices. Many promote their toys on Douyin, and while Lin has struggled to take legal action, he acknowledges that some of the imitations are well made.

Wang, the Shanghai graduate student, once paid 189 yuan for a copy of a slider, less than half the price of the original. “In terms of feel, it’s practically indistinguishable from the original, although a few of the tracks aren’t as refined,” he says.

With hundreds of brands vying for collectors’ attention, Lin believes the bigger challenge now is coming up with original designs. “We’re not afraid of great products appearing,” he says. “We’re afraid of too many identical ones.”

Lin acknowledges that at 01EDC, too, the focus has long been on making reliable, well-crafted toys rather than experimenting with more imaginative designs.

“Next year,” he says, “we’re going to focus on something that really catches people’s eye.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A collector tries out a fidget spinner at an EDC toy exhibition in Beijing, Oct. 31, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
World.title: A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019318/A Chinese University’s New Weekly Allowance: 100 Million AI Tokens
World.content:
A Shanghai university is now giving each student and staff member up to 100 million AI tokens a week, saying that it hopes to make tokens a standard teaching resource equal to books, lab equipment, and databases.

University members may use the tokens to access a range of AI models and tools after signing in to the university website with their campus ID, as announced by Shanghai University of Finance and Economics’ (SUFE) official WeChat account on Nov. 21.

Tokens are the smallest pieces of information that AI models can process. Students can use them to debug code, clean data, conduct research, and even build their own AI agents.

China’s daily token consumption hit roughly 500 trillion in June, nearly four times that of December 2025. State-owned telecommunications carriers now sell token plans to consumers, with China Telecom’s cheapest plan costing 9.9 yuan ($1.50) a month for 10 million tokens — a 10th of SUFE’s weekly, per-person limit.

SUFE is the latest Chinese university to provide computing power and free token quotas to students and staff as a public resource, a trend that began earlier this fall.

Starting this September in Beijing, Tsinghua University began offering each student and staff member 1,000 yuan in “computing vouchers,” while Peking University offers a year of free access to Qoder, a cross-LLM AI coding assistant, and 3,000 credits a month. In the central Hunan province, Hunan University students receive 2 million tokens a day. Shanghai’s Tongji University also launched its own plan in October, giving students and faculty 100 million tokens a week.

“In the past, when you’d say a school had good infrastructure, you’d be referring to its gym and library,” Xue Lan, dean of the Institute for AI International Governance at Tsinghua University, told domestic media. “Going forward, computing platforms, LLM data centers, and high-powered internet may be the important infrastructure of schools in the future.”

However, education researchers also report concerns that access to free tokens may fuel “idle teaching,” where teachers create assignments using AI and students submit AI-generated answers, creating a loop in which the work is completed but no real learning takes place.

“Measuring the value of token use is not about how many tokens are actually consumed but what kind of learning they advance in students,” Zhang Duanhong, director of the Center for Educational Policy Research at Tongji University, told domestic media.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.title: A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019309/A Simple Question About Leftovers Divides China’s Internet
World.content:
“Xiao Ming and his mom and dad are eating out at a restaurant. After they finish eating, his mom wants to take home the leftovers, but his dad thinks it’s unbecoming. What would you do and say if you were Xiao Ming?” poses a Chinese exam question.

“If I were Xiao Ming, I would tell my mom not to pack the leftovers because we have plenty of money, and it would be embarrassing if people saw us doing so,” one student responds.

This answer to a primary school Chinese language exam question has sparked online debate over how schools should balance encouraging children to express their opinions with promoting moral values, with a related hashtag attracting over 46 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

The controversy began when the parent of a third-grader in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, shared a photo of the assignment alongside their child’s answer in a WeChat parent group, which was later leaked, according to domestic media. The child’s teacher marked the answer incorrect, deducting all four potential points. Above, a large red check mark adorns a revised answer written by the student that states: “1) I would pack the leftovers with my family. 2) I would tell my dad that all food is grown through the hard work of farmers, and we shouldn’t waste it just because we’re afraid of losing face.”

Many social media users pointed out the apparent conflict between nurturing critical thinking and penalizing it. “It’s unreasonable to punish students for such answers in a Chinese language exam,” one user wrote. “While it may appear to promote ‘the right values,’ deducting scores as a means of enforcement only teaches children to lie to get what they want.”

Others agreed with the teacher, saying that schools also have a responsibility to help children develop sound values and moral judgment. “(Children) should be encouraged to think outside the box, but their ideas must be grounded in the correct values,” wrote another user.

In recent years, China has sought to curb food waste, enacting the Anti-Food Waste Law in 2021 to cut waste across the food supply chain. In 2020, the Ministry of Education also urged schools to teach frugality and the importance of reducing leftovers. Authorities have also cracked down in recent years on banquets, discouraging excessive food ordering as a display of wealth and generosity.

Zhao Tongwei, a senior teacher and principal of Shanghai-based Shengqiao Central Primary School, told local media that the student’s response reflected a tension between attitudes absorbed from everyday life and the values schools seek to promote.

“Chinese language education is about more than teaching practical skills; it also has a humanistic and educational role. Upholding sound values is a principle that must not be compromised,” he said.

The aim, Zhao said, should be to help students think for themselves. Simply deducting marks could discourage children from expressing what they genuinely believe, he warned, and instead advocate reflection through writing exercises, one-on-one conversations, or whole-class discussions on the topic.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.title: Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019315/Singled Out: What’s Behind the Mismatch on China’s Marriage Market?
World.content:
Almost 30 years ago, Carrie Bradshaw opened the TV phenomenon “Sex and the City” with a question: “Why are there so many great unmarried women, and no great unmarried men?” Later, she backs up her assertion with data, declaring that “there are 1.3 million single men in New York, (and) 1.8 million single women.”

Carrie was speaking about turn-of-the-millennium New York, but women in major Chinese cities such as Beijing and Shanghai will have little problem understanding her plight. Marriage rates have declined across the board in recent years, but the drop has been felt most keenly by two very different groups: urban women and rural men.

To get an idea of the problem, take a map of China and color each prefecture-level city red if men there are more likely to be single than women, and blue if the reverse is true. The result is striking. Less developed inland provinces such as Yunnan, Guizhou, and Gansu turn deep red. The country’s richest urban clusters — the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, and the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region — turn deep blue. The line between them follows, almost exactly, the line between China’s poorer and wealthier regions.

In other words, China’s cities are full of highly educated single women. In less developed areas, singles are disproportionately men with little education.

China’s skewed sex ratio can explain why there are more single men than single women overall. Yet it cannot fully explain the geographic distribution of single men and women. For its part, media coverage tends to oversimplify the phenomenon as a problem of willingness, with young Chinese rejecting the concept of marriage altogether.

But is that true? Our research, based on two decades of data from national population censuses and the comprehensive China Family Panel Studies (CFPS) surveys, paints a more complete — and complex — picture of how demographic transformation in educational attainment, regional imbalances in skills and industries, and cultural norms have contributed to China’s unbalanced marriage market.

Let’s start with education. Over the past several decades, Chinese women have quietly but quickly caught up with men in educational attainment. Among Chinese born between 1960 and 1995, the education gap between men and women steadily narrowed. For the cohort born around 1985, women college graduates outnumber their male counterparts. And for Chinese born in the mid-1990s or later, the gap in women’s favor is large and continues to widen, especially at the postgraduate level.

This shift coincided with a decisive transformation in China’s economic structure. The services sector, which is disproportionately concentrated in major cities, has grown, drawing women, especially those with degrees, out of agriculture and manufacturing. In 2000, college-educated women were 17 percentage points less likely than college-educated men to work in the services sector; by 2015, they were 21 points more likely to hold such positions.

Service jobs — whether in finance, professional services, education, health care, or technology — cluster in big, wealthy cities, and so do the women who hold them. But while China’s educational and employment landscape has transformed dramatically, marriage norms haven’t. Census data show a strong and remarkably stable pattern of hypergamy, in which women marry men with higher socioeconomic status. This norm spans regions and educational backgrounds, meaning that urban women with higher degrees also tend to marry those who are more educationally and professionally advanced than they are.

This norm made sense in a world in which men were usually more educated than women. In a new reality where urban women are more likely to attend college and have a decent job, it becomes counterproductive for matchmaking.

Together, these three factors have contributed to a mechanical mismatch. But how can we quantify it? After all, no one can run a real-world experiment on national marriage rates.

To find the answer, we built a model of a counterfactual parallel world — one in which gender differences in education, occupation, and migration patterns in 2015 were the same as they were in the year 2000.

In that counterfactual world, the national singles rate, defined as the proportion of individuals who stay single from the earliest legal marriage age to the time they turn 45, falls by roughly 30% for women and 12% for men. In developed cities, the female singles rate drops by nearly 40%, and among highly educated women there, by more than half.

About one-third of this drop comes from the narrowing education gap; the other two-thirds comes from the reduction of service jobs in large cities available to women in this hypothetical world.

What does that mean for the future? While we do not have access to perfect projections, if the gender gap in educational attainment and service sector employment in developed cities merely widens at the same speed from 2015 to 2030 as it did between 2000 and 2015, our model suggests that by 2030, the singles rate among highly educated women in developed cities will rise to 15.2% — roughly one in seven. Meanwhile, among low-skilled men in less developed regions, it will rise from 8.7% to 12%, or about one in eight.

Of course, history is rarely linear. The Chinese government has made marriage rates and fertility rates a top priority, with local officials experimenting with all kinds of interventions and welfare policies to prevent marriage rates from entering a free fall. Some regions have even introduced cash rewards for newlyweds.

But our findings raise questions about the effectiveness of such policies, showing that financial incentives alone are not enough to reverse the trend. Using our model, we expect a subsidy as high as 10% of household income to lower the national female singles rate from 3.46% to 3.17% and the male singles rate from 8.17% to 7.89%.

This is because no amount of money can conjure up a partner who fits traditional expectations. Other interventions, such as encouraging more educated men to move to big cities or encouraging more educated women to move back to smaller cities, might work on paper, but they would raise serious gender fairness questions by effectively punishing educated women.

What is urgently needed is a rethink of hypergamic norms. Educated women should be celebrated as proof of the transformative power of education, migration, and hard work. They are no longer passive participants in a marriage market, but active planners of their own lives who can and should choose partners regardless of educational and financial status.

Men must also adjust their expectations to accommodate partners who may not meet hypergamic norms. And the gatekeepers of those norms — families and relationship gurus among them — must catch up with contemporary society, realizing that no single mode of relationship is the key to a fulfilling life.

It is likely that the red and blue on China’s marriage map will grow darker in the coming years. Yet nothing is set in stone. After all, even Carrie Bradshaw eventually found love.

Huang Zibin of Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Wang Yushi of Hainan University, and Yang Yu of Peking University made equal contributions to this research.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
World.content:
Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.

The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.

Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.

Excavation of the fourth site, Laohudun cemetery in Hubei, began this year. According to researchers, the area contains the highest concentration of Qin dynasty (221–206 BC) tombs in southern China.

At the site, archaeologists unearthed bamboo and wooden slips — writing materials used before the invention of paper — along with numerous inscribed lacquerware and wooden artifacts. The inscriptions cover a wide range of topics, including politics, military affairs, literature, medicine, folklore, and art, offering greater insight into society at the time.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Stone artifacts found at the Taohuahe site in Sichuan province. From the National Cultural Heritage Administration)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
World.title: Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
World.content:
For coffee growers in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Starbucks and Nestlé used to be the only buyers in town. Every harvest season, their purchasing stations would have lines of loaded trucks stretching for days.

Plantation owner Zou Qingquan recalls once waiting a whole week to sell her beans to Nestlé. Back then, she says, the company revised its purchase price twice a week based on changes in the international commodity market, “so your beans were making or losing money as they sat there in the truck.”

Over the past five years, however, these two global giants have been losing their grip on the Yunnan coffee market. Rapid growth among domestic brands such as Seesaw, Manner, Luckin, and the Mixue Group, along with a shift toward specialty coffee, has opened new sales channels for farmers and pushed up prices.

According to the agricultural industry analysis platform Beedata, Nestlé and Starbucks paid an average of 48.09 yuan ($7.20) and 48.18 yuan per kilogram, respectively, for commercial-grade Yunnan green beans in the first quarter of 2026. For Luckin, it was 50.37 yuan.

But while growers’ incomes have risen, some warn that an increasingly indiscriminate buying frenzy, which in some cases is leading to the sale of unripe beans, risks disrupting established trade relationships and negatively affecting the quality and image of Yunnan coffee.

Light roast

Ma Xiaojin, who manages two coffee-growing cooperatives in Yunnan’s Menglian Dai, Lahu and Va Autonomous County, used to regularly drive the 10 hours from his farm to the Starbucks Farmer Support Center, a training and purchasing facility in central Pu’er, a city arguably best known for its eponymous tea. There, he’d join the line of trucks and wait four or five days to have his beans graded, costing him at least 2,000 yuan in truck rental costs.

Starbucks has exacting quality standards and purchases beans only from growers certified under its Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) Practices program, which in January included 3,400 farms in Yunnan. The American company is also known for paying more for high-quality beans than its Swiss competitor, Nestlé.

“You can’t just show up and expect Starbucks to take your beans,” says Hao Yi, who used to work for Starbucks in coffee production. “They don’t just check each batch; they monitor your quality over several consecutive years. That’s why, in the early days, getting your beans into Starbucks was a source of pride. It also brought your subsequent harvests to the attention of specialty coffee roasters.”

In 2017, Starbucks began selling selected Yunnan beans as part of its high-end Reserve line. For growers, making the cut was no easy feat. If their products passed a preliminary check, they had to provide three large samples from each sack for testing and agree to follow-up screenings.

Specialty beans from Zou’s estate were selected in 2021, with Starbucks offering 48 yuan per kilogram. At the time, her farm was selling to the open market for more than 60 yuan per kilogram. “We earned less, but working with a big brand was good publicity for us, so it was still a net gain,” she says. The following year, many new buyers approached Zou to purchase the same beans.

Nestlé and Starbucks’ strong bargaining power stemmed not only from their steady and large purchasing orders but also from their role in establishing industry rules and standards in the region. In 1989, Nestlé introduced the province to catimor, an arabica coffee cultivar popular for its high yields and resistance to coffee leaf rust, while Starbucks has helped standardize commercial production here since the late 2000s.

Both companies also set up local agricultural support centers, dispatching agronomists to train farmers and promote good practices. Ma, whose beans were selected for the Starbucks Reserve line in 2025, remembers training sessions taking place every month or two in the early days.

“The older generation of coffee growers is very grateful to Nestlé,” says Zhang Yong, founder of Pushan Coffee, a local bean trading company. He notes that while visiting Yunnan’s coffee-growing regions last year, he found multiple farmers who were still willing to sell to the Swiss company even though its prices were lower than other brands.

However, not everyone has remained loyal to the two biggest players. On a recent trip to Pu’er, Hao talked with coffee growers and traders who said they had sold very little to Starbucks in 2025. One farmer whose beans had previously been selected for the Reserve line revealed he was now targeting other specialty coffee brands that pay more.

Ma’s two cooperatives produce 120 to 130 tons of beans a year. More than half of this output used to go to Starbucks, but over the past two years this has fallen to just over 10 tons of Reserve-grade coffee.

“It’s hard enough to buy beans in Pu’er, but it’s even more competitive in Baoshan,” Hao says. Baoshan, Yunnan’s other main coffee-growing area, is almost 10 hours by road from the Starbucks Farmer Support Center in Pu’er. With the demand for beans soaring, few are now willing to make the trip.

Working with Starbucks and Nestlé once brought huge pride and prestige, but Ma believes that the global titans’ stringent standards are increasingly seen as “too demanding,” particularly by younger farmers. It’s just easier to sell directly to smaller companies, he adds.

Taste test

Seesaw and Manner, both founded in the eastern metropolis of Shanghai, were among the first domestic coffee brands to establish a presence in Yunnan.

After launching a 10-year plan in 2014, Seesaw sent buyers to teach growers in Pu’er and Baoshan refined harvesting and processing techniques, and introduce them to specialty coffee.

Hua Runmei, a third-generation coffee grower from Pu’er, took over the family farm in 2015 after graduating from university. That year, international coffee futures — the global benchmark for pricing — were depressed, and Yunnan beans were typically sold cheap.

She agreed to transition toward growing specialty coffee in collaboration with Seesaw, which assigned a technician to guide her and assist with processing. “They tell us what they’re looking for, coffee with a clean taste and certain flavor notes, and we need to figure out how to achieve that,” Hua explains.

Her farm delivered its first 3 tons of specialty coffee beans to Seesaw in 2016. The following year, the company placed an order for 40 more.

Manner, which operates about 2,000 outlets nationwide, entered the Yunnan market in 2018, opening purchasing stations in Menglian and Baoshan. “It’s not just about a commitment to buying local. Yunnan beans are genuinely high-quality,” Wang Xu, an executive assistant to Manner CEO Jin Binbin, told the domestic media outlet Kankan News in March 2025.

The shift toward specialty coffee brought greater financial returns for growers. Hua recalls that many brands offered favorable prices and advance payments. “I think the brands that came to Yunnan in the early days were genuinely driven by a passion for locally grown coffee,” she says.

Brands generally set prices for premium beans based on production costs, allowing farms a profit margin of about 20%. They would pay up to 40% above the international futures price, sometimes more depending on the beans’ flavor profile. This not only secured beans that met their specific requirements but also encouraged growers to continue investing in cultivation and processing.

However, as domestic brands expanded, specialty coffee prices began to align with those for bulk-bought commodity coffee. “Starting around 2019 or 2020, companies changed the way they purchased beans,” Hua says. “Everyone started to want coffee that was both good and cheap.”

What emerged was a new category of bean between commodity-grade and specialty: premium commercial beans. These beans don’t have distinct flavor notes, but they do have cleaner flavor profiles and lower defect rates than standard commercial-grade beans, and typically sell for 1 to 3 yuan per kilogram more than the international futures price.

Specialty coffee brands bought relatively limited quantities of these beans. The real force reshaping supply and demand in Yunnan was companies with larger needs, such as Mixue Group and Luckin.

Mixue, a food and beverage giant based in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, acquired the budget coffee chain Lucky Cup in 2020 and expanded it as a franchise, requiring vast quantities of beans. After visiting dozens of farms, the company decided to offer freshly brewed Yunnan coffee in all of its 20,000 outlets nationwide and signed agreements with several growers for their green beans.

Chen Junxian, whose trading company Senyu Coffee was among Mixue’s first suppliers in Yunnan, recalls that local farmers and processing plants were initially lukewarm toward the Zhengzhou company, best known at the time for its ice cream and tea products.

“People didn’t really know the brand,” he explains. “They thought it was purely a milk tea company and didn’t believe it actually wanted to buy coffee beans. Now the processing plants are far more friendly.” Chen says that orders from Mixue to his business alone have nearly doubled since 2020. “We’re delivering a lot.”

The largest buyer of Yunnan beans in 2026 has been Luckin, headquartered in Xiamen, in the eastern Fujian province. Unlike other brands, which sent teams to purchasers in the region, Luckin relied for years on trading companies to handle procurement. It wasn’t until 2024 that it built its own coffee processing plant in Baoshan.

During Luckin’s Q1 2026 earnings conference call in April, co-founder and CEO Guo Jinyi announced the company had purchased more than 30,000 tons of Yunnan coffee during the 2025–26 harvest season. According to government-run news outlet Yunnan.cn, Luckin’s target is 80,000 tons a year by 2030.

For growers, the expanding market has led to enormous orders, more flexible requirements compared with Starbucks and Nestlé, and higher prices. For domestic brands, Yunnan beans mean lower transportation costs and provide an opportunity to tell the story of China-grown coffee.

Fresh take

The challenge now is keeping up with the huge demand. Industry insiders point out that even if coffee plants were grown in every suitable place in China, there would still be a supply shortage.

Chen, who started his business in 2018, says most Yunnan growers were struggling to make a profit before the market boom. Now their beans are a hot commodity, they no longer seek his help to find buyers — he needs to beg them to sell to him.

“Many aren’t comfortable with digital communication; you have to meet them in person,” says Chen, explaining that his team had to visit countless plantations, processing plants, and even farmers’ homes to secure enough beans to fill orders. This involved traipsing across sparsely populated countryside and driving 13 hours between various counties across Pu’er and Baoshan.

The thriving local economy has also attracted many Yunnan natives to return home to open coffee farms, while Pu’er tea growers have even cut down trees to make space for more coffee plants.

Some farms are also taking a chance on rare and prestigious varieties, such as Geisha, which can command a price of up to 1,500 yuan per kilogram. However, Zhang is concerned for those rookie growers who expect to sell the beans from their newly planted trees for less than 500 yuan per kilogram.

“They are investing heavily, perhaps recklessly,” he says. Geisha plants take at least three years to bear fruit and typically reach peak production around six to eight years old. No one knows what the market will look like by then, Zhang adds.

Trouble brewing?

As the buying frenzy continues, concerns about quality also grow.

Last year, Ma had to reject a whole batch of beans delivered by one of the farms he manages. “They were so bad that I couldn’t stand looking at them,” he recalls.

Coffee cherries ripen at different times, so pickers typically make three or four passes over the three- to four-month harvest season, selecting only fully ripened cherries to ensure quality and consistency. Now, in the haste to satisfy demand, some growers are cutting corners, making only two passes and picking unripe green cherries together with ripe red ones.

“Some people are willing to buy beans like these. I just don’t understand it,” Ma says. “If people keep harvesting so carelessly, in another two or three years, Yunnan coffee will be worthless.”

Chen sees the same problem. Once the outer fruit has been removed, it’s extremely difficult to distinguish between ripe and unripe beans during sorting, increasing the risk of defects. When his company tried to enforce quality standards at the source, growers simply told him that if he didn’t buy their cherries, someone else would. “There’s nothing we can do; we have to buy them,” Chen says.

When prices were 20 to 30 yuan per kilogram, his company would take green beans classified as Grade 1 — the highest level, applying to plump, unbroken beans measuring at least 6.5 millimeters — and sort through them again to try to reduce the defect rate.

But when ripe and unripe cherries are harvested together, quality control becomes impossible. “At prices above 60 yuan per kilogram, even a 4% loss is a huge amount of money. We can’t afford to do it anymore. We have no choice but to bow to market pressure,” Chen adds.

Even with a 5% defect rate, the market average, Chen’s company had sold its entire inventory by the end of April 2025.

Nestlé originally chose Yunnan because it provided a stable, low-cost source of beans for its instant coffee factory in the southern Guangdong province. Later, domestic coffee brands came to capitalize on both the market appeal of the homegrown coffee story and the logistical advantages.

However, as prices continue to rise, Pushan’s Zhang has observed that the market is starting to look overseas for alternative suppliers.

From January to May this year, China’s coffee bean imports from Vietnam increased 76.9% year on year by volume and 87.1% by value. Unlike Yunnan, which primarily grows arabica beans, Vietnam is a major producer of robusta, a cheaper variety with higher caffeine.

With this in mind, Zhang highlights a recent shift he’s noticed in how Chinese brands market their coffee. “Previously, many would advertise that they used 100% arabica, but as costs have risen, they’re no longer making that claim. They may well be blending in robusta,” he says.

Ultimately, the effects of the influx of domestic brands and rising prices will be felt in the consumers’ coffee cups.

(Due to privacy concerns, Hao Yi is a pseudonym.)

Reported by Li Dan.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Mirror. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
World.content:
China has successfully tested two large unmanned cargo aircraft: one with a 5-ton payload capacity and the other capable of flying 3,000 kilometers, laying the groundwork for future commercial and emergency transportation systems.

On Tuesday, the country announced that the Changying-8, a domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, had completed a test delivery. Three days prior, another domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, the W5000, also completed its maiden flight.

The milestones come as China’s drone market is expected to exceed 140 billion yuan ($19.6 billion) by the end of 2026, with the industrial drone segment alone projected to reach 84 billion yuan, up 12.5% from last year.

China began testing large cargo drones as early as 2017 and incorporated the concept of the “low-altitude economy” into government policy in 2021. The Civil Aviation Administration of China has also laid out a roadmap to establish an air transportation system for unmanned aircraft by 2035.

During its delivery test, the Changying-8, developed by China North Industries Group Corporation, released a cargo pallet at an altitude of 300 meters before returning to its base.

The aircraft, whose maiden flight took place in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, on March 31, has a maximum range of over 3,000 kilometers, measures 17 meters in length, has a 25-meter wingspan, and an 18-cubic-meter cargo compartment volume, domestic media reported.

In the event of extreme disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and mudslides destroying roads and bridges, the aircraft can be used to transport up to 3.5 metric tons of goods, equal to over 700 disaster-relief tents, the head of the Changying-8’s development team told state news agency Xinhua.

According to its engineers, future applications could include transportation of regional cargo, emergency supplies, and cold-chain deliveries, domestic media reported.

On Saturday, the W5000, an unmanned cargo aircraft developed by Chinese aviation company Air White Whale, also completed its maiden flight in northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

The aircraft flew for about 30 minutes at an altitude of 1,000 meters, completing a series of test maneuvers before landing. The test focused on the aircraft’s flight stability and the coordinated operation of its propulsion, flight control, electronics, and ground-based monitoring and control systems.

With a maximum payload capacity of 5 metric tons, the W5000 is billed as one of the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft by payload capacity. Made of carbon fiber and weighing less than 6 metric tons, the aircraft measures over 22 meters in both length and wingspan and can fly at a cruising speed of 526 kilometers per hour, with a maximum range of 2,600 kilometers, domestic media reported.

Hu Zhendong, founder, chairman, and CEO of Air White Whale, said the W5000 could reduce logistics costs per ton-kilometer by more than 60% compared with comparable crewed cargo aircraft.

The W5000 is expected to begin commercial operation by the end of next year, according to domestic media.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: The W5000, billed as the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft, on display at Airshow China 2024 in Zhuhai, Guangdong province, Nov. 12, 2024. VCG)

World.title: [Market Rider] PSE’s 2027 rebalancing: Will it unlock broader market activity?
World.content:
The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi.

In the search for new catalysts that could lead to unlocking broader market activity and growth, the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) is implementing its biggest index management overhaul since 2011 starting with the February 2027 rebalancing, using the whole-year trading data of 2026.

The revised framework applies to the PSEi, PSE MidCap, PSE Dividend Yield, and sector indices. (READ: What is the PSEi, and why does it matter?)

Unveiled last July, the new rebalancing framework radically departs from the pure market cap methodology by introducing three core changes in the rules for eligibility and liquidity for inclusion in the bourse’s index as it shifts toward free-float trading velocity.

As evaluated, many of our large conglomerates have a high total valuation, but a huge portion of their shares are locked up with founding families or strategic insiders. Under the old rules, a large company could enter or stay in the PSEi simply because of its sheer size and overall peso trading volume, even if its actual public float rarely changed hands.

Three pivotal rule changes

The first of the three pivotal changes made in the rule is that the PSE instituted a 98% cumulative market capitalization screen. Before even undergoing liquidity evaluations, companies must fall within the top 98% of cumulative total market capitalization among eligible securities. This also effectively filters out the exchange’s smallest listed names from the outset.

Second, the exchange replaced its legacy single liquidity metric with a rigorous dual liquidity test combining the Median Trading Activity Ratio (MTAR) and Monthly Average Daily Value Turnover (MADV). MTAR measures how fast a stock’s publicly available shares are being bought and sold relative to its size, rather than just looking at the raw amounts of pesos traded, while MADV is a liquidity metric that measures the average monetary value of a stock traded per day over a given month.

For the PSEi, MidCap, and Dividend Yield indices, prospective entrants must achieve an MTAR of at least 15%, whereas existing constituents need 10% to retain their spots, a buffer designed to prevent excessive index turnover while sector indices require 7%. Simultaneously, both new and current members of the primary indices must rank in the top 25% of all listed stocks by MADV for at least nine of the 12 months in 2026. For sector indices, the bar is looser. A stock only needs to rank in the top half by daily traded value in at least eight of the 12 months.

Third, the PSE introduced a P250-billion mega-cap float carve-out. While the standard minimum public float remains 20%, corporate giants valued at P250 billion or more can now qualify with a 15% float, provided they satisfy all liquidity tests.

Despite these sweeping updates, several foundational eligibility rules remain intact for the 30-member PSEi. Companies must still maintain a PSE Main Board listing tenure of at least 12 months, or six months for early inclusion if they rank among the top 25 firms by market value.

Once candidates clear the market cap screen, public float minimum, and dual liquidity filters, the top 30 eligible companies ranked by full market capitalization secure their places in the index. Furthermore, the exchange retains its semi-annual rebalancing cadence every February and August.

Ultimately, these revisions carry profound implications for market participants. Under the 2011 framework, tightly held conglomerates could qualify through size and sporadic block trades, creating liquidity bottlenecks for institutional funds trying to execute large orders without distorting prices.

Rule recap

The message is clear: Size alone is no longer enough for a sure spot of a company’s stock in the PSEi. A company can be worth hundreds of billions of pesos, but if its public shares sit idle without regular trading turnover, it risks being dropped from the benchmark index. Shares need to trade under the new rules.

For domestic institutional investors, including Unit Investment Trust Funds (UITFs), mutual funds, pension systems, and exchange-traded funds (ETFs), enforcing MTAR reduces execution friction and tracking error. Because trading large institutional blocks in large-cap stocks with tightly held floats or thin turnover can push prices sharply against a fund, requiring active trading relative to free float ensures deeper tradable liquidity during rebalances. This allows funds to buy newly added and sell deleted index stocks cleanly at or near benchmark prices and weights, preventing their returns from diverging from the benchmark index. (READ: EXPLAINER: How mutual funds and UITFs make investing beginner-friendly)

Additionally, the P250-billion carve-out creates an immediate pathway into the PSEi for tightly held utility giants. Conversely, the strict nine-month MADV requirement mathematically delays late-2026 mega-IPOs like Mynt (GCash) from immediate entry, ensuring that new additions prove sustained trading depth before attracting passive institutional capital.

By transitioning from static size metrics toward dynamic free-float trading velocity, the PSE is aligning domestic index construction with international institutional standards and mitigate structural illiquidity — standards that is followed by major global stock indexes like the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) index and the Financial Times Stock Exchange Russell (FTSE Russell) index. – Rappler.com

A veteran stock market analyst, Den Somera has long years of professional experience in investment banking and stockbroking and founder-convenor of The Monday Circle. You may reach the writer at kapitaltek@gmail.com
