The story sparked widespread discussion on social media. Razmadze faced a wave of insults and accusations that echoed the narrative promoted by the fake videos. At the same time, many users expressed their support. Other bloggers and government critics voiced solidarity with Razmadze, warning the authorities that such campaigns could have dangerous consequences. YouTube bloggers and sports commentators also expressed their support.

Comedian Onise Okriashvili wrote on Facebook that this appeared to be the first case in Georgia in which someone had tried to discredit a person using hyper-realistic AI-generated videos rather than satirical ones.

Background: fined over remarks about Russian propagandists

A month before the campaign began, Razmadze was fined 3,000 lari. In September, the Interior Ministry opened administrative proceedings against him. The case concerned a Facebook comment containing obscene language directed at Kremlin propagandists Margarita Simonyan and Vladimir Solovyov. They had previously described Georgian King Erekle II as a ruler who “knelt down”. Razmadze’s video addressed those remarks.

A newly established Interior Ministry unit responsible for combating “hate speech” initiated the case. The Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association described it at the time as a precedent for censorship.

Razmadze says he expected a campaign against him after the authorities opened the case.

What happens next?

Razmadze is discussing further legal action with his lawyers. The Interior Ministry has yet to say whether it has launched an investigation following his complaint.

Georgia’s first AI smear campaign against an activist

World.title: Georgia awarded contracts worth nearly $499m without competitive tenders – TI
World.content:
Non-competitive public procurement in Georgia

Between January and October 2026, almost half (45%) of tenders announced in Georgia attracted only one bidder. The lack of competition meant that these contracts cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) more.

This is according to a new study by Transparency International Georgia.

According to the study, in the first ten months of 2026, government agencies awarded contracts worth a total of 4.09 billion lari (approximately $1.57 billion) through 16,222 electronic tenders.

A total of 7,364 tenders – 45% of all those announced – attracted only one bidder, either a company or an individual entrepreneur. The contracts were worth a combined 1.31 billion lari (approximately $499 million), accounting for almost a third of all public procurement spending.

According to the organisation, the winning bids in single-bidder tenders were, on average, just 4.3% below the initial estimated value set by the authorities. By comparison, prices in competitive tenders fell by an average of 15.4%.

TI estimates that if prices in non-competitive tenders had fallen by the same proportion, public contracts would have cost the state around 150 million lari (approximately $57.5 million) less.

The study also found that in 2,883 tenders, worth a total of 572 million lari (approximately $219.6 million), the winning bid exactly matched the estimated value set by the government in advance. In these cases, the state made no savings.

The largest public procurer using non-competitive procedures is the Special Penitentiary Service

According to TI, in 2026 the Special Penitentiary Service was the largest public procurer using non-competitive tenders. Through this mechanism, the agency awarded contracts worth a total of 203.7 million lari (approximately $78.6 million).

Almost the entire amount – 201.4 million lari – went towards two contracts for providing meals to prisoners.

In May 2026, the Special Penitentiary Service awarded contracts worth 152.4 million lari to Giorgi 2020 and 49 million lari to Delfood.

Both companies were the sole bidders in their respective tenders. Moreover, their bids exactly matched the estimated values set in advance.

The contracts were awarded amid a scandal over the quality of food served in Georgian prisons. Earlier, in March, the Special Penitentiary Service terminated its contract with Ili Group, which had been responsible for providing meals to prisoners.

According to TI, Giorgi 2020 had never previously won a public procurement tender.

On 3 April 2026 – the day the tender was announced – the company’s owners transferred 33% of its shares to Irakli Letodiani free of charge.

According to the TV Pirveli television channel, Letodiani is a former employee of the State Security Service.

Which sectors have the least competition?

According to the study, several sectors have particularly high proportions of tenders with only one bidder:

Transport services – 85%;

Software and information systems – 81%;

Repair and maintenance – 78%;

Medical equipment and medicines – 59%.

The proportion of construction tenders attracting only one bidder was relatively low, at 29%. However, construction ranked first in terms of the total value of contracts awarded.

Non-competitive construction contracts were worth a total of 517.9 million lari (approximately $199.8 million).

Tbilisi and Batumi account for the largest sums in non-competitive procurement

According to TI, 43% of tenders organised by municipalities – including those run by mayors and bodies established by them – attracted no competition. The figure for central government agencies and other state institutions was 48%.

Municipalities awarded contracts worth a total of 625 million lari (approximately $241.1 million) without any competition.

In monetary terms, Tbilisi ranked first, with 277 million lari, accounting for 38% of the capital’s procurement spending. Batumi came second, with 63 million lari, or 30% of its procurement spending.

In terms of the proportion of non-competitive tenders, the highest figures were recorded in Ambrolauri (61%), Terjola (59%) and Khulo (55%).

The risk of tailoring tender requirements to specific companies

TI notes that one possible reason for the high proportion of tenders with only one bidder is that authorities tailor procurement requirements to suit specific suppliers. The organisation cites several examples of this practice.

In June 2026, TI reported on five road repair tenders announced by Batumi’s Department of Infrastructure and Improvement.

Under the terms of the tender, bidders had to either own an asphalt plant within a 30km radius of the work site or provide a contract with such a facility. This requirement applied to a tender worth 29.2 million lari (approximately $11.3 million), in which Gza was the sole bidder.

Another example is a security services tender announced by Georgian Railway in 2023. To qualify for the contract, worth 7.8 million lari (approximately $3 million), bidders had to demonstrate at least 20 years of uninterrupted experience.

According to Transparency International (TI), only two companies in the entire country met this requirement. The sole bidder was Intersecurity Georgia LLC, owned by Ioseb Alavidze, a former head of the Tbilisi police. The company’s bid exactly matched the estimated contract value.

The organisation also cites a tender for the provision of social canteen services announced by Rustavi City Hall in 2022.

In that case, the company offering the lowest price was excluded from the tender because its revised price schedule listed figures to four decimal places instead of two. The contract was ultimately awarded to a company whose bid was 155,000 lari (approximately $59,800) higher.

The problem extends beyond large-scale tenders

TI says that a lack of competition in public procurement is not a new problem. The organisation refers to a 2024 study which found that half of the large tenders – those worth more than five million lari – announced between January and July 2024 attracted no competition.

Figures for 2026 show that the problem is not limited to large-scale procurement: only one bidder took part in half of all tenders worth up to 100,000 lari.

The organisation also criticises reports prepared by the State Procurement Agency. TI notes that although the agency’s reports point to an increase in competition, none of its annual reports published since 2019 has mentioned that almost half of all public tenders attract only one bidder.

Photo: Ministry of Youth and Sport of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 27. The cities of Tartar and Masalli have been designated as Azerbaijan’s “Youth Capital” and “Sports Capital,” respectively, for 2028.

The Ministry of Youth and Sports announced the decision.

World.title: Azerbaijani athlete Gashim Magomedov to compete in Grand Prix Final in Astana
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. Azerbaijani taekwondo athlete Gashim Magomedov will compete in the World Taekwondo Grand Prix Final, which will be held in Astana, the capital of Kazakhstan.

Magomedov will compete in the under-58 kg weight category.

World.title: Tokayev calls TikTok dangerous platform that destroys human brain
World.content:
Photo: Press Office of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 26. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has described TikTok as a dangerous platform that destroys the human brain, particularly among young people.

He made the remarks during a meeting with young artificial intelligence talents held as part of the international conference “AI Journey 2026: A Journey into the World of Artificial Intelligence,” organized by Sberbank in Moscow.

“Nowadays, everyone uses smartphones, but for some reason, many people think they are only meant for making calls, sending messages, or watching movies. And then there is TikTok. TikTok is a dangerous thing that destroys the human brain, especially that of young people,” Tokayev said.

According to the president, Kazakhstan aims to develop a people-oriented digital economy.

He stressed that the effective use of smartphones and access to the internet provide opportunities to earn money even for people living in rural areas and small towns.

“However, if you use a smartphone properly and skillfully, you can earn money even while living in a village or a small settlement. All you need is internet access,” he noted.

Tokayev also highlighted the importance of providing relevant training to citizens, enabling them to generate legitimate income through digital technologies.

“This is what I call a ‘people’s digital economy,’” the Kazakh president added.

World.title: Meet the eight Aussie women travelling the globe to watch Harry Styles
World.content:
For a group of young Australian women, a concert is more than just a live performance — it is the reason they are best friends.

Natalie Fleming is a 22-year-old Melburnian who met her seven best friends while "barricade camping" for music artists including Olivia Rodrigo, Gracie Abrams and Billie Eilish.

The girls say Harry Styles's music brings them together. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming )

The phrase "barricade camping" covers scenarios when concert-goer camps out for hours or even days before a gig to get a spot right against the barrier, directly in front of the stage.

"It's more than music, it's the community you create and get to see," Ms Fleming said.

Despite living in Melbourne, Perth, Brisbane and Townsville, the women would often bump into each other at these concerts and soon became best friends.

But there is one artist the group put their entire lives on hold for a year for, seeing more than 110 shows between them: Harry Styles.

Harry Styles plays his first of four shows in Melbourne tonight.

Harry Styles is set to kick off the Melbourne leg of his tour. (Supplied: Niamh Hall )

A world tour for all

From Wembley Stadium to Amsterdam and Madison Square Gardens, and now with Sydney and Melbourne, Ms Fleming will have seen Styles's latest tour Together, Together 14 times.

For this group of Aussie girls, going to concerts is being a part of a community. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming )

"Harry's our favourite artist, we just love his music," she said.

"We knew that we wanted to go to Europe and especially Wembley, because he loves Wembley — he just shines there."

The girls spent about a month living in London for Harry's London residency.

Natalie Fleming says her favourite Harry Styles songs are Fine Line and Satellite. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming)

"I think because I'm best friends with these girls, it's normalised to go to all these shows and to dedicate a year basically to going to concerts," she said.

"His music is just so impactful — it's always been a constant in my life growing up with [Styles's former band] One Direction."

It's the group's passion for music that has brought them together. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming)

Ms Fleming said the group has just returned from New York, where Harry Styles had a residency, and finished off with "Harryween" — a Halloween-themed concert.

"A lot of people say, 'oh, doesn't he just perform the same show every night?' but the experience is never the same," she said.

"I could be at the back of the pit, where I'm dancing with a bunch of girls who are my best friends, or swapping stories and meeting people, which I love.

"Or I could be on the barricade, where you might get an interaction with [Styles].

" It's just a place where I feel completely myself and happy, and where I can forget about the outside world for an hour and a half and just dance and sing and be surrounded with my best friends. "

The girls playing tourist while in New York for a gig. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming )

'No different' to AFL fans

Ms Fleming said they were often called "crazy fangirls".

"But I don't hear any of [that language] when people spend thousands of dollars on a ticket to see American football or go to an AFL game and scream out at the players," she said.

"We do the same thing but, I feel, in a more respectful manner."

The women have a tight bond forged through music. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming )

Ms Fleming said when women care about things to a similar extent that men do about sports, they are treated differently.

"I think that there is a difference in the way that girls get treated in relation to an artist to boys," she said.

Spent enough to buy 'small apartment'

Niamh Hall said the feeling she gets while at a Harry Styles concert is "indescribable". (Supplied: Niamh Hall )

Niamh Hall, 19, from Perth, will have been to 22 Harry Styles concerts by the time the Together, Together tour is over.

"Harry's music means everything to me," she said.

"There's just something about Harry and his music and personality that brings you in and it's so comforting.

" And then I also met my best friends through his music and his tour — it's just so special. "

Niamh Hall says following Harry Styles has enabled her to travel the world. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming )

Ms Hall said she encouraged people who "don't get it" to experience it for themselves.

"I've brought my mum to a show before and she said seeing the crowd and how special [Harry's] relationship with his fans is changed her perspective on it," she said.

Niamh Hall says the community of Harry Styles fans brings people together. (Supplied: Niamh Hall )

But attending 22 concerts across the globe is not cheap.

"I worked out [that with the money I spent on] my tickets alone, I could have bought a small car," Ms Hall said.

" All of us together, we definitely could have bought a small apartment in Melbourne. "

"But I would not want to be spending my money on anything else in this point in my life because I'm travelling the world with my best friends, as well as seeing [Styles]."

The group were in New York last month for "Harryween". (Supplied: Natalie Fleming)

How the girls afford it

Perth 19-year-old Caitlin Carlton will have gone to 12 shows by the time the tour is up.

She said while it was expensive it was completely worth it.

"[The concerts] are everything I look forward to," Ms Carlton said.

Caitlin Carlton says it feels like the girls have been friends forever. (Supplied: Natalie Fleming)

"It's just fun, we get to dance together and sing together and cry together and share that same love for something."

Ms Carlton, who finished high school last year said she has been working non-stop ever since graduating.

"I have two jobs in hospitality and I've been working double [shifts] every day," she said.

"It's quite difficult and it's quite draining, but it's so worth it.

"There's nothing I'd rather spend my money on."

World.title: Outback city's first new hotel in decades being manufactured 4,600km away
World.content:
An assembly line in Malaysia is a world away from Australia's biggest outback city, but a Swedish-owned modular building company is slowly piecing together the components for a new four-star hotel in regional Western Australia.

Amid construction cost blowouts and ongoing shortages of skilled tradespeople, the development of Kalgoorlie-Boulder's first new hotel in decades is shining a light on modular building techniques.

While proponents say it could speed up delivery projects across regional Australia, significant challenges within the construction sector remain.

The concrete foundations for the $40 million Kalgoorlie Airport Hotel were poured this month.

Rita Brooks and her son Jason Brooks on site for the pouring of the concrete foundations. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Decades in the making

The new hotel is the brainchild of Perth businesswoman Rita Brooks, whose family has owned The View on Hannans Motel in Kalgoorlie-Boulder since it was built in the 90s.

Ms Brooks bought the vacant land for the new hotel in 1996. Spent years searching for a builder, eventually engaging Stockholm-based firm SIBS after spotting an  promoting its modular designs during a visit to the Malaysian capital, Kuala Lumpur.

She subsequently toured the company's factory in Penang, where 90 modules for the hotel are currently under construction.

Construction is underway on the Kalgoorlie Airport Hotel at a factory in Penang, Malaysia. (Supplied: Rita Brooks)

The modules are to be shipped in late December from Malaysia to Fremantle and trucked nearly 600 kilometres to Kalgoorlie-Boulder, where installation will require a 300-tonne crane.

"This is the first design they've done for Australia, so it's a learning curve for them (SIBS) as far as reaching Australian compliance, which has taken about 18 months," Ms Brooks said.

"Every item has had to meet Australian standards and that in itself was a challenge, so that's probably why a lot of people haven't gone and done this path."

SIBS has since struck a deal with Singaporean-headquartered Centurion Corporation to supply modules for a seven-storey, 302-room hotel development in Port Hedland in WA's Pilbara.

Jason Brooks on a tour of the SIBS factory in Malaysia. (Supplied: Rita Brooks)

Critical skills shortages

Master Builders Western Australia has estimated the state will be short more than 10,000 key construction workers by 2030 without action to rebuild the industry's workforce.

It says the cost of building a new house in WA has more than doubled since the pandemic, increasing by 105.4 per cent, while building material inflation has recently accelerated to a three-year high.

WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti (left) and Matt Moran (middle) touring an under-construction home. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Master Builders WA chief executive Matt Moran said the increasing popularity of modular construction was due to skills shortages.

"With ongoing labour pressures, work is moving into factories to keep up with demand … this form of construction offers a high level of control over quality, safety and speed," he said.

Matt Moran speaks at a press conference on a construction site in Sinagra earlier this year. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

But Mr Moran stressed, "there is never a one-size-fits-all solution".

"With modular, there are generally short site time frames where manufacturing for standard-type layouts can take weeks, with installation typically completed in days," he said.

"In regional and remote areas where transport and site preparation can be expensive … it can be complex, which does require careful planning and coordination.

"These challenges facing regional and remote WA show that modular construction can be in some cases a viable solution."

The proposed development has been reduced from four storeys to three due to escalating costs. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

The modular method has received significant state-level support, with the Cook government announcing a $49 million package in May to help 15 manufacturers move into modular construction.

But the sector's difficulties were underlined by the collapse of Welshpool-based Offsite (Maneon Pty Ltd), which manufactured prefabricated timber building components until it entered administration in October, with creditors seeking to recoup $41 million.

Massive cost blowouts

The Kalgoorlie Airport Hotel project has faced its own cost challenges since the state government's Regional Development Assessment Panel approval in 2024.

The original budget was $20 million but has doubled to $40 million, while the number of rooms has been reduced from 200 to 165.

Ms Brooks said the overruns meant she had seriously considered walking away from the project.

But it is scheduled to open next year and will be the mining city's first new hotel development since the Kalgoorlie Rydges Hotel was built in the early 2000s.

The proposed Kalgoorlie Airport Hotel development has been reduced in scale from 200 rooms to 165. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

It also arrives amid a crippling shortage of available hotel rooms amid the city's latest mining boom.

"For regional Western Australia, this type of building system is unique but will be embraced, I believe, going forward because it answers a lot of questions," Ms Brooks said.

"We want a quality build, and we want it within a year; we don't want to wait three years.

"This is what could be achieved, I believe, with this system."

Rita Brooks and her site manager watch the concrete foundations being poured. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

But Ms Brooks also expressed frustration at being unable to secure state and federal government support for her project, specifically for the installation of infrastructure like power and water.

"The private investor is taking 100 per cent of the risk, but 100 per cent of the benefit will be that we have a new housing system for regional Australia which can work," she said.

"If this system can be used, and if it can get government support, they will be the winners."

World.title: Minister says 3-day deadline for NT child protection consultation 'in error'
World.content:
The Northern Territory's child protection minister says a consultation paper that gave stakeholders just days to respond to proposed law changes was sent "in error", with the deadline for consultation now extended to three weeks.

But sector advocates say they need "months" to respond to complex proposed changes to child protection laws and they are "frustrated" at being repeatedly given limited consultation time.

Alarm at NT child protection plan The Northern Territory is considering further child protection changes that would limit judicial oversight of care arrangements and give child protection workers the ability to issue domestic violence orders, the ABC can reveal.

The consultation paper obtained by the ABC has revealed plans by the NT government to introduce a second round of reforms to child protection laws, just months after passing sweeping changes in July.

The paper includes 86 questions about 20 areas of reform including the length of protection orders, care plans, family visitation arrangements and domestic violence orders.

The ABC understands just a handful of organisations received the consultation paper.

They were given just three business days to provide submissions on the 43-page document after receiving an email from the Department of Children and Families on Tuesday night.

In the initial email sent to stakeholders, the department said there was "no wriggle room available for submissions" and flagged the department would be seeking cabinet endorsement for the changes "before the end of the year".

On Thursday, following backlash about the lack of sector consultation, Children and Families Minister Robyn Cahill told NT parliament the paper sent by her department had been circulated by mistake.

The NT government is planning to introduce a second round of reforms to child protection laws. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Cahill said the paper was originally due to be sent out in early November, but a decision was made to delay consultation due to an ongoing recruitment process for a permanent department chief executive.

"A decision was made that it would be best to wait given that decision was imminent," she said.

"So, when they sent it out, they forgot to change the date for consultation and that is being corrected as we speak."

A spokesperson for Ms Cahill said the deadline had been extended until December 18 but declined a request for an interview yesterday, citing a bomb threat targeting NT government ministers and bureaucrats.

The minister was later seen speaking with constituents at a public engagement event in the Smith Street Mall alongside other government members, including Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro.

Sector says 'months' of consultation needed

The proposed changes, if introduced, would include limiting judicial oversight of care arrangements and giving child protection workers the ability to issue domestic violence orders.

Despite the now-extended timeline, legal organisations and children's advocates have said the consultation period still is not long enough to provide thorough feedback.

"The proposed changes are incredibly technical," Top End Women's Legal Service chief executive Caitlin Weatherby-Fell said.

" This consultation paper will need months of consultation … dedicated time for services to be able to provide meaningful input. "

The NT government was criticised over previous child protection reforms, including by sector representatives and Aboriginal organisations. (ABC News: Olivana Lathouris)

Ms Weatherby-Fell said frontline services that were already struggling to keep up with caseloads were becoming "increasingly frustrated" by having limited time to provide feedback on important changes.

It follows the government being strongly criticised over the first set of child protection reforms, with sector representatives and Aboriginal organisations arguing they were not given an adequate opportunity to voice their concerns.

"As frontline services, we can't just drop our pens and erase ourselves from our clients," Ms Weatherby-Fell said.

"We continue to see increases on demand, year on year, for domestic violence-related help, for care and protection-related help, particularly after changes to the Care and Protection [of Children] Act earlier in the year."

National children's commissioner not consulted

Australia's national commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people, Sue-Anne Hunter, said she was not invited to consult on the second round of reforms.

"I was emailed by a community organisation and that's the first time I saw it," she said.

"[I was] really surprised there are more amendments considering no one really agreed on the first amendments."

Sue-Anne Hunter says she was "really surprised" to see more amendments were in the pipeline. (ABC News)

Ms Hunter said she was concerned about the prospect of some changes potentially being introduced without adequate scrutiny from the sector or Aboriginal voices.

"We're talking about children's lives," she said.

"We need to get this right because you just keep coming back to the table and making the same mistakes again and again."

World.title: 'Pigeon heaven' comes at a hefty price in WA
World.content:
Increasing numbers of pigeons are defecating and nesting in public buildings across regional Western Australia, racking up damage bills and causing human health concerns.

In Geraldton, 420 kilometres north of Perth, the iconic St Francis Xavier Cathedral, nesting pigeons create an ongoing maintenance and damage bill of up to $15,000 a year.

"The gutters get blocked, the downpipes get blocked and it starts damaging the fabric of the cathedral," said Geraldton diocese director of heritage Robert Cross.

Father Cross said pigeons were causing similar issues in other buildings owned by the Catholic Church in Geraldton.

"They like heights, they like to look down on the rest of us," he said.

A pigeon sits on one of Geraldton cathedral's church bells. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Father Cross said any plan of attack needed to include the state's main grain handler, the CBH Group.

"It's really an issue that needs a coordinated approach by those people and places in Geraldton that are either creating a problem, or providing what we just say is pigeon heaven here on Earth," he said.

"Once upon a time you just go out and have a few shots at them and scare them off, but these days we've got all these safety regulations that make it so much more difficult to do something about the problem."

Pigeons feed at a Geraldton CBH site near the port. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Feed availability

City of Greater Geraldton mayor Jerry Clune agreed Geraldton's pigeon problem was growing due to 'so many feedstocks' being readily available.

"This time of the year of course there's so much grain, not (just) in huge stacks but on the roadside as well so, they're everywhere," he said.

"It becomes a health problem as well, the city are doing their best to control it but if it's not a community effort then those actions will be all in vain."

Pigeons eat the spilled grain coming from trucks during harvest time. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Clune said the city had previously participated in a joint control program with CBH and the Mid West Ports Authority where pigeons were baited with contraceptive laced grain.

"I think CBH and the port have sort of given up on that, and I think the city will probably move in a similar direction, because there's so many other sources of grain that that is not the solution," he said.

"There's all sorts of ways (to control pigeons), you can anaesthetise them, you can get licensed shooters, you can trap them with a gas type thing.

"It is a community problem, and people who do have properties, then the onus relies with them to take control of what to do with those pigeons.

Jerry Clune says the city's pigeon problem is getting worse. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"Unfortunately around Geraldton we've got a lot of federation style buildings and they've got a lot of ledges and all that and it's perfect for pigeons.

"They just love those sort of buildings and consequently they tell all their mates to come and share the digs with them."

Exterminator prompts police reports

Business owners in Albany, 400km south of Perth, have complained of a spike in pigeon numbers this year with flocks of the bird visible in the CBD and near the port's grain terminal.

Earlier this week, reports of a man with a gun on a building in Albany was actually a pigeon exterminator.

Police issued a public notice after calls were made to emergency services after spotting a man with a firearm on top of a York Street liquor store.

Pigeons like to nest near solar panels where it's protected from the elements. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Albany police officer-in-charge Senior Sergeant Carlos Correia said the contractor had not advised authorities of his plans.

"[The contractor] didn't let anybody know and they've been told there is procedures to let people know so we don't scare our community when they see people on a roof with a firearm.

"More often than not they do it at night-time when they can't be seen."

Sergeant Correia thanked the public for being vigilant.

Acid droppings corroding metalwork

Pigeons are causing similar concerns in WA's Avon Valley, 95km north-east of Perth.

Northam Chamber of Commerce chief executive Theresa Lee said she had heard reports of pigeon 'debris' from roof spaces landing on desks in offices, and the chamber was attempting to lead a collaborative control program across Northam.

"We're looking at asset damage, the pigeons (are) affecting corrosion on metal roofing and structural elements due to the acidic nature of their droppings," she said.

" The droppings themselves are highly toxic when they dry, the powder form becomes airborne and can cause up to 28 health conditions in humans if inhaled or ingested. "

Pigeons often nest on people's roofs creating noise and poo problems. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Ms Lee said the chamber was surveying all businesses to find out where pigeons are nesting across the community in a bid to create a more effective control program.

BirdLife Australia senior adviser Sean Dooley said pigeons were technically rock doves, and were not an ecological threat as they lived near humans.

"They're pretty much street kids really," he said.

"They need buildings and grain or bread or something to feed on, but they are remarkable birds, they've got this reputation as rats with wings and all that sort of stuff but they're incredibly intelligent birds and really adaptable.

"They're one of our oldest domesticated animals and they were initially bred for food but because they have this innate ability to find their way back to their nesting sites, they've been used for communication for centuries."

The ABC has repeatedly requested interviews with the CBH Group.

A 2018 planning document from CBH says pigeons are a "predominant problem in major centres such as ports and major depots" and details CBH's control of pigeons using a narcotic compound in a bait, and shooting.

Pigeons sit on top of the Geraldton cathedral. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

World.title: Live: Victorian Coalition's election eve kinder cut slammed by union
World.content:
Ben Carroll has criticised opposition leader Jess Wilson for seemingly breaking a promise on privatising Melbourne Water while simultaneously calling on her to break another promise.

Earlier this year, the Coalition said it had "no plans" to privatise Melbourne Water.

"We have not considered this in any way, shape or form," she said in August.

But yesterday, Wilson announced her plan for a long term private lease on Melbourne's sewerage facilities which is expected to add $13 billion to the state's coffers by 2030/31.

Carroll criticised the move but called on Wilson to change her pledge on treaty.

World.title: Wind-monitoring mast removed as pilots raise safety concerns
World.content:
A Danish renewables company has taken down one of two wind-monitoring masts at a proposed wind farm site in Queensland, which local agricultural pilots said was "nearly impossible to see".

Grain grower Kieran Cook, who lives near the site south of Tara in the Western Downs, said he had experienced several "frightening near misses" with the 120-metre masts while flying his aircraft for crop spraying and fertilising.

Mr Cook said a collision with a tower could be fatal.

"If you hold a bit of fishing line up, whirl around in a room and try to see it against different backgrounds, that's what the pilot's got to look at," Mr Cook said.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) confirmed it had received multiple reports of safety concerns about the Tara wind-monitoring towers.

The ATSB said it was in the final stages of consulting with the regulator and would publish a report in the coming weeks.

A wind monitoring tower in South Australia, photo taken in 2022. (Supplied: Tom Cheesman )

Wind tower safety questioned

Renewables company Vestas installed the two wind-monitoring towers in December 2023.

Wind-monitoring masts are temporary structures that measure weather and atmospheric conditions at proposed wind farm sites.

While it is standard industry practice, landholders said they were not consulted about the towers' locations.

There are strict rules about tall structures near airports, but it is looser around the small airstrips that farmers and firefighters use on rural properties.

Turbines at a separate wind farm also on the Western Downs in Queensland. (ABC Rural: Brandon Long)

Mr Cook said when they first went up, the towers were not lit or marked properly.

"They were actually in conflict with a couple of our firebombing strips and ag strips," he said.

In a previous statement, a Vestas spokesperson said the company had addressed visibility issues of the masts more than 12 months ago.

It repainted the masts, marked the foundation, added marker balls on the guy ropes and installed 24-hour flashing lighting.

"Vestas is confident that the monitoring masts are lit and marked to industry best practice and comply with the relevant approvals," the spokesperson had said.

Kieran Cook reports several near misses with the tower while flying. (Supplied: Kieran Cook)

But Mr Cook said the changes were "too small to make a difference".

"A Telstra tower you can see a few miles away, you scan the horizon, and you pick it up straight away," he said.

"But you can't see the wind-monitoring tower."

Last Friday, Vestas workers removed one of the two masts.

A spokesperson said its wind specialist advised enough data had been gathered and that one wind-monitoring tower would be sufficient going forward.

Regulatory 'grey area'

The federal member for Maranoa, David Littleproud, said Vestas removing the tower was an "admission of guilt" that it was unsafe.

"Someone should have to pay a penalty for it because otherwise we would have heard about this through the coroner," he said.

David Littleproud has slammed the company, Vestas. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Littleproud said there was a legislative "grey area" around regulating agricultural aviation.

The local planning authority, the Western Downs Regional Council, approved the Vestas application for the towers in 2023.

The Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) was notified because the towers were more than 100 metres tall, but a spokesperson said the body had no authority over enforcing compliance.

CASA updated its guidelines in October and noted that wind-monitoring masts were a "recognised hazard" that needed mitigating.

"They are narrow, are frequently guyed, are often unlit and unmarked … and in several jurisdictions are exempt from planning approval because of their height or their temporary nature," the report read.

A Vestas windfarm turbine in Macarthur in Western Victoria. (Supplied: Vestas Wind Systems A/S)

Mr Littleproud said there were constitutional issues around whether it was the state or federal government that could take action against non-compliant companies.

He said there had been a failure at all levels to protect agricultural aviators.

"The onus of responsibility should go to the wind companies to actually do the on-ground consultation, identify all the aircraft-landing areas and have them registered with CASA," he said.

"Otherwise, we will lose lives."

World.title: 'Significant concern' as summer bushfire risk grows
World.content:
Authorities are warning conditions will be ripe for bushfires across large parts of Australia this summer, particularly as hotter temperatures dry out landscapes that have seen prolific vegetation growth in recent months.

The seasonal outlook, developed by the Australian and New Zealand Council for fire and emergency services (AFAC), shows an increased risk of fires across all states and territories except Queensland and the ACT.

While 2026 is on track to become Australia's wettest El Niño year on record, forecasts suggest drier conditions could start to take hold across northern and south-eastern states over the coming months.

The Bureau of Meteorology's summer outlook also points to above-average temperatures across most of the continent.

Fire risk is increased in large swathes of northern and south-eastern Australia due to low soil moisture and forecast dry conditions. (Supplied: AFAC)

AFAC chief executive Rob Webb said some regions faced a higher threat due to prolonged drying, but even areas that saw higher spring rainfall were at risk.

"The recent rainfall has been a blessing in some ways in that the chances of early starts in some places are reduced," he said.

"But wherever you are, you see the impact of two, three, or four 40-degree days, and we see in our own gardens the impact of that.

"Imagine those conditions over several weeks — it's not hard to imagine how quickly fire conditions can develop."

Spring has been wet, particularly through the interior of the country. (Supplied: BOM)

Climate change and El Niño have driven global temperatures to record highs this year, while unusually warm temperatures helped drive a particularly bad wildfire season across Europe, the United States and Canada during the Northern Hemisphere summer.

Widespread risk for some

The warning comes months after the state was devastated by bushfires during the 2025–26 season, during which about 440,000 hectares of land were burnt.

Heavy growth means increased risk of fires is forecast for Victoria's northern and western grasslands. (Supplied: AFAC)

The AFAC outlook said there was "significant concern" around extreme grass and crop growth in northern and western parts of Victoria due to high rainfall in October.

Spring rainfall will likely limit forest fire activity in December, but the risk will increase in woodland areas towards the state's south-west and far east early next year.

"It is likely that a hotter pattern will lead to a rapid switch in forest flammability with significant bushfires a real possibility in January and February," the outlook said.

Only northern NSW and Queensland are forecast to see above-median rainfall, while large parts of SA, WA and the NT look to be dry. (Supplied: BOM)

There could be more intense fire behaviour in eastern Tasmania due to low rainfall and drier soils.

While the top end fire season is winding down, large parts of Central Australia are expected to see an elevated fire risk from January.

A warm, dry year has significantly increased fuel loads across eastern Tasmania, and increased fire risk this summer. (Supplied: AFAC)

There are warnings that dryness combined with above-average temperatures could drive fast-moving fires that are difficult to control across parts of southern New South Wales and the state's Hunter region.

NSW is expecting an increased risk of bushfire in parts of the Hunter, south-east and south-west this summer. (Supplied: AFAC)

The outlook highlights that regions with elevated fire risk in Western Australia and South Australia are more scattered, compared to other states.

Despite Queensland and the ACT facing a normal fire risk this season, authorities have warned that fires can still occur in those regions.

"Wherever you are in Australia at the moment, we're coming into the warm season, and wherever you are, it's about knowing where your fire risks are, understanding whether it's normal or above normal or below normal," Mr Webb said.

"Knowing whether your area is affected by bushfire and just take the precautions no matter what, do it ahead of time when the skies are blue."

Hot nights could worsen conditions

Firefighters have raised concerns about the long-range forecast showing both daytime and overnight temperatures will likely be higher than usual across most of the continent over summer.

Typically, evaporation is higher during hotter daytime temperatures, before landscapes have a chance to take in some water when it cools overnight. This means fires need to use more energy to evaporate water in soils and vegetation and do not burn as intensely.

Before: Most of Australia is projected to have four times the chance of being unusually hot. . . After: Night-time temperatures are also forecast to have a high chance of being in the top 20 per cent for the time of year. . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Most of Australia is projected to have four times the chance of being unusually hot. / Night-time temperatures are also forecast to have a high chance of being in the top 20 per cent for the time of year.

But Mr Webb warned hotter temperatures not only ramped up evaporation but also meant there would be less relief at night.

New age of climate-driven fires The anatomy of the Natimuk fire offers a glimpse into a new and faster kind of bushfire, fuelled by dangerous conditions in our changing climate.

"Vegetation not only will be under more stress but will be under stress more quickly," he said.

"The rate at which things dry, how long things will burn into the night and be dangerous into the night, will change.

"I remember teaching fire weather 25 years ago, and the anatomy of bad fire days were the ones that stayed warm and windy overnight."

World.title: Major Thanksgiving storms inundate US with heavy rain, wind and flooding
World.content:
Thanksgiving storms have forced the postponement of Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York and brought flooding, power outages and heavy snow to other parts of the United States.

The strengthening storm along the eastern seaboard raised worries about how the annual parade's massive balloons would fare in the wind-swept canyons between Manhattan's skyscrapers.

Macy's said in a statement that it was postponing the event from Thanksgiving Day (Thursday, local time) until Saturday in an abundance of caution after consulting with city officials.

Workers rushed to deflate the parade's balloons following the rescheduled New York event. (AP: Yuki Iwamura)

Nearly 200,000 homes and businesses had no power in Virginia and another 177,000 in Maryland, according to poweroutage.us.

The storm was expected to hamper air travel at eastern US airports on Thanksgiving Day into Friday morning, with reduced visibility, greater turbulence, strong winds and aircraft icing, the National Weather Service said.

A person holds onto their upturned umbrella outside Radio City Music Hall as winds rattle New York. (Reuters: Adam Gray)

Heavy rain and high wind hit both coasts

The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic to southern New England.

All of New Jersey was under a state of emergency, as were parts of New York.

Across the east coast, wind gusts of up to 112 km/h toppled trees and power lines.

The storm was flooding coastal villages and cities from North Carolina through New Jersey as the high tide rolled in on Thursday morning.

Avalon, New Jersey, saw some of the worst flooding in its history, said Scott J Wahl, the business administrator for the Borough of Avalon.

"Not quite Hurricane Sandy," Mr Wahl said, for his village on the far south of New Jersey's Atlantic coast.

Two men kayak down a street in Norfolk, Virginia. (AP: Stephen M Katz/The Virginian-Pilot)

Lance Miller, 54, said floods in his neighbourhood of Ocean City, a small coastal town in New Jersey, were about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest grocery store would probably "destroy your car".

"I wouldn't do that, I'm a car guy," said Mr Miller.

"You're gonna have a good foot of water that you'd have to drive through."

Mr Miller, who had his Thanksgiving Day meal preparations set, said he would be staying indoors and having dinner with his wife and daughter.

But he said that some of his friends in the area were "not so lucky" and had flooding inside their homes.

"So they're dealing with clean-up, you know," he said.

Weird side dishes of Thanksgiving A lurid combination of jelly, pineapple and shredded cheese is just one of the weird side dishes served up at Thanksgiving.

More than 600,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday afternoon, with the majority of those outages in East Coast states, according to poweroutage.us.

Highways were also shut down.

The nearly 29-kilometre Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel over the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia was closed for several hours on Thursday morning because of high winds.

NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes again and covered the two-lane highway.

Crews did not know when it might reopen.

In Norfolk, Virginia, tornado warnings blared on phones around the metro area as families prepared to celebrate Thanksgiving.

Winds topping 80 km/h were reported all around the metropolitan area of more than 1.8 million people.

Loading...

Central states see heavy snow while California faces coastal floods

Winter storm warnings and watches were posted for parts of Missouri and Illinois, with up to 33 centimetres of snow expected around St Louis by Thursday afternoon.

Snow fell as far south as North Alabama, where giant flakes dropped from the sky on Thursday morning.

King tides have caused coastal flooding in low-lying communities along portions of the east coast and California on the west. (Reuters: Mike Blake)

King tides continued surging on the West Coast, with coastal flood warnings issued from Southern California to the San Francisco area to the Oregon and Washington coasts.

A video showed a massive wave tearing down a portion of the pier in the city of Pacifica, California, on Wednesday and slamming it into the ocean.

AP/Reuters

World.title: Labor refuses to say how much bills will fall under new gas reservation scheme
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGas Labor refuses to say how much bills will fall under new gas reservation scheme Brittany Busch November 27, 2026 — 10:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australians will have to wait to find out how much cheaper their gas bills could be under the domestic gas reservation scheme, after Resources Minister Madeleine King declined to set a target price. The country’s biggest gas companies will have to keep up to 20 per cent of supply for the domestic market after the laws passed the House of Representatives on Friday morning, after the Coalition waived the measure through the Senate late on Thursday night. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor made no apologies for siding with consumers. Dominic Lorrimer King said Labor would not set a price when asked what the government considered affordable. “We don’t want that figure to then become the floor, which is what happens with a cap,” she told ABC Radio National.



The government is avoiding setting a target after vowing ahead of the 2022 election that energy bills would be $275 cheaper under Labor, only for prices to continue to rise. Related Article Updated

Energy Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws “Australians rightly expect that our resources should serve the national interest, and that Australian users should have access to the gas they need at an affordable price,” King told the chamber as the laws cleared their final parliamentary hurdle. “This reform means more Australian gas for Australian users and downward pressure on prices. It means greater certainty for manufacturers to invest, remain competitive and employ Australians.” Opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan proposed last-minute changes to boost transparency over the advice the regulator provided to the minister – doomed to fail because the opposition does not have the numbers in the lower house – and said the Coalition remained concerned the scheme could discourage investment.



“If you tank the gas sector in Australia, you will get short-term political gain, but you will get long-term political pain for this nation,” Tehan told the chamber. “We want to make sure that we’re going to get future investment in this nation.” The Coalition’s energy spokesman, Dan Tehan, speaking in the House of Representatives on Friday morning. Dominic Lorrimer He said the Coalition was worried the scheme would work for a couple of years, but eventually kill the Australian gas sector. “Even the prime minister has said we need gas for revenue, and we need gas to remain a trusted trading partner with key allies in the Indo-Pacific region.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor made no apologies “for siding with Australian households and Australian manufacturers rather than producer profits”. Related Article Energy Can Australia dodge the next Iran oil shock? “We must remember what the objective of this legislation is. It is about making sure that Australians get the benefit of the resource that is ours, that is owned by Australians,” he said, adding that the latest Australian Bureau of Statistics investment figures showed explorations development at a 10-year high. Retaining a modest oversupply of gas in Australia is designed to put downward pressure on prices and better insulate the country against global price shocks. Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie said the Coalition had been able to secure enough concessions to support the scheme, including a review into how the reservation would affect investment and a carve-out for Western Australia.



“We took a gas reservation policy to the last election, so at a principled level, we absolutely believe that Australian gas should be there to be used and support Australian households and businesses,” she told Radio National. “When you talk to industry, they are concerned. I think also realising that Labor doesn’t have a great track record when it comes to energy and gas policy – I mean we’ve seen energy prices go up 40 per cent.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

Looking for something truly different to a typical sand and surf getaway this summer? Head south and discover the beauty of Australia’s southernmost capital city, Hobart. Not to mention the wonderful diversity of Melbourne, our second largest city, perched on Port Phillip Bay, north of Bass Strait, which separates mainland Australia from Tasmania. Given there are multiple daily direct flights of around an hour and 20 minutes between the cities, it could not be easier to experience both Hobart and Melbourne in one holiday. Both destinations punch well above their weight when it comes to cultural attractions and dining opportunities. Plus, Melbourne is a sports lover’s paradise over summer, hosting the Australian Open tennis grand slam, the Boxing Day Test in cricket and A-League Men and Women’s football. Art and culture lovers can anticipate a broad spectrum of galleries and precincts, including the world famous must-see National Gallery of Victoria (NGV) in Melbourne, and Hobart’s incredibly quirky and fun Museum of Old and New Art (MONA). Spend even a few nights in each city, and you’ll quickly fall in love with the lively shopping scene full of singular boutiques, plus the buzzing little streets and laneways filled with wine bars, specialty coffee shops and alfresco dining focused around fresh regional produce, including local seafood.



These charming cities both score highly on walkability and vibe. And both feature landmark historic and contemporary architecture, layered with a creative, European-influenced character that feels very different from the country’s northern capitals. 



Sleep on top of the world at Crowne Plaza Hobart. IHG Hotels & Resorts Wander the laneways, enjoy the coffee, and the arts and crafts shops, ride the regular passenger ferries around Derwent River, or further afield – then head back to Crowne Plaza for a drink on the rooftop bar The Deck, followed by dinner at Core – an on-site farm-to-table restaurant on Level 4. For an elevated stay, enjoy Club Lounge access with its panoramic views for eligible guests. Just book a dedicated Club Room or Suite or use eligible IHG One Rewards milestone reward benefits. Who doesn’t love Collins Street? There’s nothing quite like that brand new hotel smell when you’re travelling. Find it at Hotel Indigo Melbourne Little Collins, which only opened in late 2025, and puts you in the heart of Bourke Street mall and leading into “the Paris end of Melbourne” as the area of Collins Street east of Swanston street is known. Wander this lovely tree-lined street’s many luxury shops, theatres and stately churches. And do treat yourself to one of the nearby top restaurants like Vue de Monde, or Reine & La Rue at 380 Collins St, housed in the 1891 Gothic Revival Cathedral Room of the former Melbourne Stock Exchange.



With beautifully designed rooms created to feel like an oasis in the city, boutique Hotel Indigo Melbourne Little Collins offers something for everyone – from standard rooms through to one-bedroom suites, some with private balconies. A sleeping beauty. Hotel Indigo Melbourne Little Collins. IHG Hotels & Resorts Enjoy delicious on-site dining at the Fern Bar & Dining, plus a bar. Select something from the extensive Grill menu and a signature cocktail – then stride out to browse Bourke Street Mall and Melbourne Walk. It’s also close to Flinders Street Station and the NGV. Collins Coffee House or the Tea Room 1892 are perfect for a delicious High Tea. How very Melbourne. Fern Dining at Hotel Indigo Melbourne Little Collins. IHG Hotels & Resorts Messing about on the Yarra



The 242-kilometre Yarra is one of Melbourne’s most loved landmarks. With walking, jogging and cycle pathways – and the chance to row or take a boat ride along the Yarra – this famous river is a winner with families of all ages. A great option for those wanting to be close to the Yarra is the well-priced Holiday Inn Express Melbourne Southbank, which offers a complimentary breakfast. Fuel up before heading out to nearby landmarks like the NGV, the Arts Centre Melbourne, Melbourne Skydeck and Flinders Street Railway Station. Breakfast at the Holiday Inn Express Little Collins. This family-friendly, thoughtfully designed hotel (with rooms that comfortably sleep up to four people) is truly your home away from home with endless creature comforts. World.title: Chalmers’ electorate facing some of the highest unemployment rates nationally
World.content:
NationalQueenslandJobs Chalmers’ electorate facing some of the highest unemployment rates nationally Shane Wright November 27, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Workers in Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ home electorate are facing some of the highest unemployment rates in the country as higher interest rates and inflation combine to weaken the jobs market and squeeze family budgets. Even as evidence grows that the AI data construction boom is approaching levels not seen since the mining boom of the early 2010s, figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show suburbs such as Springwood, Kingston and Browns Plains have soared beyond 8 per cent or are approaching it. The national unemployment rate reached 4.9 per cent in October, with the country shedding almost 80,000 jobs over the past two months. Despite inflation hitting 4.9 per cent, financial markets believe the Reserve Bank will start cutting interest rates from August to support the rapidly softening jobs market.



This week, Chalmers said his mid-year budget update would reveal Treasury expects unemployment is likely to climb above 5 per cent in 2027. The combination of high unemployment and inflation has sharply lifted pressure on Chalmers to unveil spending cuts in next month’s budget update. The federal opposition is demanding the treasurer be sacked. Rankin stretches from the Brisbane suburbs of Algester and Calamvale into northern parts of Logan, such as Slacks Creek (pictured). Markus Ravik The regional unemployment figures from the bureau highlight that parts of the country are already dealing with job losses before the full impact of the Reserve Bank’s most recent rate increases filter through the economy. The highest unemployment rate is in Chalmers’ seat of Rankin, hitting 8.7 per cent in the suburbs of Springwood and Kingston. A year ago, the jobless rate in these areas was 7 per cent.



In nearby Browns Plains, the jobless rate has lifted from 6.3 per cent last October to 7.7 per cent this year. Related Article Analysis

Australian economy Chalmers cannot spin a silver lining out of this grim story Unemployment is also rising quickly in other parts of Queensland, including Ipswich, Caboolture, the state’s far west and Maryborough. The western suburbs of both Sydney and Melbourne are exposed most to the sharp lift in interest rates and inflation. High petrol prices, which have climbed by more than a third since the start of the war against Iran, have delivered particular financial pain. Women are paying the highest price for the unemployment increase. Across Melbourne’s western suburbs, the female jobless rate has climbed from 5.8 per cent to 7.8 per cent. Among men, it has risen from 6 per cent to 6.6 per cent.



The increase in unemployment is occurring despite one of the nation’s largest construction booms. Bureau of Statistics figures released on Thursday showed private spending on new buildings and equipment jumped by 18.6 per cent over the past year. It reached $59.7 billion in the September quarter, the highest level since 2014. In the September quarter alone, capital spending jumped by 12.2 per cent due largely to a 23.1 per cent jump in spending on new equipment and machinery such as computer servers for data centres. It was the single largest quarterly increase since the early stages of last decade’s mining boom. And businesses are not showing signs of plans to slow down. Expected spending was lifted by 11.8 per cent to a record $223 billion through 2026-27.



NSW and Victoria are attracting the most AI investment, with spending in both lifting by more than a third over the past 12 months. Chalmers described the figures as “absolutely stunning”, saying they confirmed that capital spending by the private sector was “booming”. But under pressure from the Coalition over the state of the jobs market, the treasurer admitted the situation was poor. “When it comes to the tick-up in unemployment, we have acknowledged that for those Australians who are impacted, then that is very bad development,” he told parliament.



AMP economist My Bui said the investment boom in AI-related technology had grown on average by 46 per cent a year since 2001. Related Article Inflation Stagflation fears grip Canberra as inflation, unemployment surge She said private business investment remained strong despite the lift in interest rates, although that situation could change. “The outlook for next year will be tougher though, as higher cash rates and bond yields will make it harder for firms to finance their capex plans and the productivity gains from AI are yet to arrive.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Australia news LIVE: Damning report lays out ‘extraordinary’ failures of DFAT’s sanctions office; Houthis strike Saudi oil refineries
World.content:
Liberal senator Dave Sharma says he is not sure what Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen is actually doing for everyday Australians and the climate after COP31 talks led by the minister collapsed in Turkey last week.

“We’ve got a situation in Australia where we’ve got higher electricity prices. You know, they’re up about 25 per cent over the last year, according to the latest inflation figures. Despite Chris Bowen and Anthony Albanese promising they will be lower,” he told the Today show.

Senator Dave Sharma. Alex Ellinghausen

“But we also don’t have them meeting their emissions targets. And we have him spending most of last year overseas presiding over this failure of a diplomatic negotiation. So you have to ask yourself, what is Chris Bowen actually doing right here?”

Appearing alongside Sharma on the morning panel was deputy leader of the Greens Steph Hodgins-May, who said Labor’s climate targets were “woeful” to begin with.

“We’re going to see that Labor is going to fall incredibly short of the already pretty woeful targets that the Labor government set. And I mean, it’s not really any surprise when you see that the fossil fuel corporations essentially run the Labor Party,” she said.

World.title: ‘Scary’: Why a World Cup-winning coach wants Mark and Semi in the same Fiji back line
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘Scary’: Why a World Cup-winning coach wants Mark and Semi in the same Fiji back line Iain Payten November 27, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

World Cup-winning coach Jake White has laid out his strong desire to recruit Mark Nawaqanitawase for Fiji, and says he’d be happy to add the Australian dual international to his squad on the eve of the World Cup next year, without having played a game in the white jersey. After starring for the Roosters in their NRL premiership win, Nawaqanitawase returned to rugby in Japan and caused a stir in October when he revealed he was considering switching allegiances and playing Test rugby for either Fiji or Italy. Loading The 26-year-old played 11 Tests for the Wallabies and sevens for Australia at the Paris Olympics, but also has Fijian and Italian heritage. Under World Rugby rules, Nawaqanitawase can play for either of those nations after serving a three-year stand-down, which will expire on July 31. Wallabies coach Les Kiss has spoken with Nawaqanitawase and is hopeful he will return to the gold jersey for the World Cup in Australia next year, but he’s not alone.



White, who coached the 2007 Springboks to a World Cup win and recently took over as coach of Fiji, said he was very keen to snare Nawaqanitawase, saying a back line featuring the ex-Rooster, and Fijian stars Semi Radradra, Kalaveti Ravouvou and Jiuta Wainiqolo, would be “scary”. “Everyone would want to use him and I would never say no to a guy like him,” White said in London ahead of Fiji’s final match against Italy in the Nations Championship at Twickenham on Saturday morning (AEDT). “Obviously I knew who he was. I knew he played for the Wallabies and I knew I watched him with interest when I was watching rugby long, before I got involved with Fiji. Semi Radradra did a jersey swap with Mark Nawaqanitawase at the 2023 Rugby World Cup. World Rugby via Getty Images “Then I saw his code swap and how successful he was at rugby league. When I joined Fiji, then a lot of talk came about, “Hey, do you know that he’s Fijian? And there’s a lot of talk in Australia he could be eligible, etcetera?



“Obviously you’d grab a guy like that, anybody that sees a guy play like that (would). He’s a real winner. “He could add value to the Fijian group we have. If you look at Semi Radradra and Kalaveti Ravouvou and Jiuta (Wainiqolo) and those guys, putting him in amongst those outside backs would be scary.” “I suppose, just like Les, my answer to you is, s**t, we’d love to take him. And I’m sure when he makes his decision, whoever gets him will be really happy. And whoever doesn’t get him will be disappointed.” Mark Nawaqanitawase scores in the NRL grand final against Newcastle. Getty Images Italy appear to not be in the mix, having said they were unaware of his eligibility until recently.



The potential hurdle for Nawaqanitawase playing for Fiji at next year’s World Cup is that his eligibility switch only becomes possible in August, three years after he lost in the bronze medal game for Australia at the Olympics. The Wallabies will have already started playing in the Rugby Championship in July. But Fiji’s only scheduled game ahead of the Rugby World Cup, so far, is against South Africa on September 18 in Gosford. Negotiations are underway about staging a Pacific Nations Cup, involving Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and Australia A, in July in Suva. But it is unclear if that tournament will still be going after Nawaqanitawase becomes eligible on July 31, and before September 13, when all teams have to submit their final World Cup squads. Jake White was recently appointed head coach of Fiji. Getty Images But White said he would not be open to bringing Nawaqanitawase into the squad in August, based on Japanese club form.



“Once we’re in camp in August-September, he’s a talented player, he’s not going to take six weeks to adapt,” White said. “And he’s playing rugby anyway. It’s not like he’s coming from nowhere. He’s playing rugby in Japan in a good club. So yeah, I would let him come in August.” Whether that extends to being picked in Fiji’s 33-man World Cup squad is unclear, however, and it could prove a key distinction for Nawaqanitawase, given he would also likely get a call for Wallabies duty in July. Related Article Wallabies Big in Japan: Nawaqanitawase impressing new teammates in first week White said he had not spoken with Nawaqanitawase or his representatives, and he believed if the flyer made the switch to Fiji, it wouldn’t be just to play in the 2027 Rugby World Cup. “I’d love to have him earlier rather than later, but if it means he joins in August and stays with Fiji for four more years and plays the next World Cup (in 2031), well, that’s also a bonus, isn’t it?” he said.



The former Boks and Brumbies coach is also looking to help Fiji by standing up to clubs that White claims are pressuring his players to prioritise club over country. “I’ve used my influence in World Rugby to put pressure on people that have been abusing the Fijian players,” White said. “So much so that I’ve written a letter in this tour as well to say to World Rugby, listen, I can’t have players getting text messages from coaches and directors of rugby saying, ‘Can you ask your coach if I can release you this weekend because we’re playing 11th and 12th?’ There’s no other player (from other countries) that have been asked by his club to go back... and they’re at the same club.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: When Olivia said she wanted to be an actor, her teacher laughed. Now, she’s a movie star
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Olivia Hargroder is accustomed to being underestimated. When she was born in 1999, with Down syndrome and a hole in her heart, doctors gave her a 20 per cent chance of surviving the operation she underwent at nine weeks. Specialists predicted she’d struggle to walk, talk or maintain a regular job. When Hargroder declared her wish to study acting at NIDA, her school careers counsellor laughed. The famed institution, the teacher told her, was for “the elite”. In the ensuing years, Hargroder proved them all wrong. The 27-year-old, who was one of the subjects of the ABC series Better Date Than Never, has worked at a local supermarket for almost nine years. She sings, dances and loves cracking jokes during conversations. Not only did she graduate from NIDA’s Young Actors Studio; she scored the lead role in Boss Cat, a feature-length Australian movie. Made by Bus Stop Films – a not-for-profit global leader in inclusive filmmaking – it stars Hargroder as Sonja, a young woman whose mother has just died. When her estranged grandmother tries to force her into a group home, Sonja channels her explosive temper into something more positive: a high-energy dance style known as krumping. “If you dream and believe, you can achieve anything,” says Hargroder, speaking via Zoom alongside her mother, Kerry Read, whom she tearfully describes as “non-stop supportive of me”. Worst habit? Dancing wherever I go. I work at Coles and I got into trouble for dancing to Coles Radio. [It’s worth noting that her boss has praised her work ethic and the “good vibes” she creates in the store.] You cannot stop me from dancing; from connecting with that feeling, that song, and telling a story. That’s something that connected me to Sonja, because she has the same dream I do: becoming a professional dancer. She dances to process difficult emotions and so do I, but not so aggressively. When Sonja gets angry, she dances at people whereas I dance with them.



Greatest fear? Being typecast as a person with Down syndrome. I worry that people won’t see that I’m an actor and that was a part [in Boss Cat]. If there’s a character that doesn’t have Down syndrome, I don’t want people to think someone with Down syndrome can’t play that role. It should be open to everyone. The line that stayed with you? “I have really good aim.” It’s one of my lines from Boss Cat, and I had a lot of fun playing around with it. (“It’s also because people underestimate you,” Read adds, “and you actually do have very good aim!”) ‘I got into trouble for dancing to Coles Radio; you cannot stop me from dancing.’ Biggest regret? Sometimes, when things don’t work out, another opportunity comes along – so why bother having regrets? I do get sad but then I pull myself up and go, “You know what? I’m going to move on.” I auditioned for the movie Reminders of Him. I was really excited about that, and then they switched the filming dates for Boss Cat and I couldn’t be available. I was a bit upset but then I filmed Boss Cat and had the time of my life.



Tell us about your turning point. The two operations on my knees [in 2015 and 2016]. I had hypermobility in both of my knees; every time I would start to walk, I would fall over and break a bone. The one sport I could do was swimming because I couldn’t fall over in the water. I went to a regular high school and I couldn’t light a bunsen burner or do cookery classes; I couldn’t stand at a bench and chop something. I couldn’t even dance safely – it affected all areas of my life. When I had the operation on my first knee, I couldn’t believe how many things I could do: I could run, I could jump, I could dance, I could literally do anything. The surgeon told me I had to wait a year for the second operation. He gave me a list of rehab exercises to achieve and I absolutely smashed it. It was very tough but I got through it. The surgeon thought I’d have to wait a year for the second operation but he was very impressed and did the second knee [sooner than planned]. I would love to thank my surgeon because if it wasn’t for him, I wouldn’t have these amazing knees that can do absolutely everything. Hargroder dancing up a storm in Boss Cat. Lisa Tomasetti The artwork or song you wish was yours? Shake it Off by Taylor Swift. You might get a negative comment in your life and then that song will remind you to just be yourself. I went to Taylor Swift’s concert and it was absolutely incredible. I would love to go on tour with Taylor Swift as a dancer one day. That’s been a dream of mine for such a long time.

Stocks rose as investors in Europe took their cue from a comeback in technology shares on Wall Street after days of sharp swings. Europe’s Stoxx 600 rallied 1.7 per cent. A gauge of Asian stocks climbed 0.9 per cent, only its second daily advance in 11 sessions. The gains followed late-session dip buying in the US that pulled the Nasdaq 100 back from the brink of a bear market. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.7 per cent on Thursday, with Wall Street closed for trade due to the Thanksgiving holiday. AI stocks boosted global indexes overnight. Reuters The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures pointing to a gain of 12 points or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was steady at US66.32¢. Technology shares led gains in many markets. Memory giants SK Hynix and Kioxia Holdings outperformed in Asia. Taiwan and South Korea’s technology-focused benchmarks rose more than 2 per cent. While Europe’s rally was led by auto and mining stocks, the region’s technology sector climbed more than 2 per cent.



The return of buyers to the artificial intelligence trade offers an encouraging sign after a bruising November. Markets have whipsawed since the US midterms, with a leadership crisis at Nvidia deepening a selloff that pushed major gauges into corrections. “AI capex remains intact, financing is still readily available and pricing power is exceptional,” said Marija Veitmane at State Street Global Markets. “Sentiment cracked, fundamentals didn’t. With tech valuations looking increasingly attractive, the selloff may be starting to create its own reversal.” Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump strikes again even as America feels the pain Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The improvement in risk appetite was also evident in copper, with the metal advancing 1.7 per cent from an 11-month low. Brent crude topped $US96 a barrel for the first time in more than a week as an attack on Saudi refinery threatened to undermine a recovery in the region’s crude exports. It has risen almost 6 per cent over the previous two sessions. Tehran-backed Houthi rebels attacked the 400,000 barrel a day Jazan refinery on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said in a post on X. European bonds fell on waning demand for havens. Meanwhile, Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become European Central Bank president when Christine Lagarde leaves in February.



For Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum, caution remains warranted for stocks, especially because there was no clear catalyst for the tech rebound. The likelihood of a US interest rate hike next month threatens to push the cost of capital even higher, adding to headwinds for the AI trade. “It’s a real mystery why dip buyers emerged,” he said. “Friday will be the real test if the recovery has staying power.” It’s not yet time for investors to make directional bets, said Nadege Dufosse, head of multi-asset at Candriam. She is looking to credit markets for signals on whether stress in stocks is becoming more serious. “The credit market has held so far, so that’s a good sign,” she said. “As long as the economy and earnings hold and the Fed stops raising rates next year, I think equities can make some gains.” Another notable mover was Imperial Brands, which jumped 13.3 per cent after US tobacco group Altria said it was considering a possible all-cash offer for the UK-based company.



Altria also said that it was in talks with another party over part of the British company’s business, as Japan Tobacco also was reported to be weighing a bid. Related Article Opinion

RBA There’s a number the RBA has been hiding. Here’s why Millie Muroi Economics Writer Among underperformers, Commerzbank lost 2.6 per cent after Italy’s UniCredit said it planned a management shake-up at the German bank. BAWAG dropped 5.7 per cent after Ireland’s High Court refused to sanction the company’s proposed €1.62 billion ($2.7 billion) acquisition of Permanent TSB.
