World.title: I’ve applied for 100 board roles with no interviews. How do I break in?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion I’ve applied for 100 board roles with no interviews. How do I break in? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor November 27, 2026 — 5:01am

November 27, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I am in my 60s and looking forward to retirement. I have worked my career in IT and just completed my masterʼs degree in a related field. I am looking for options in retirement to give something back. Recently, I attended a lecture through my alumni network about putting my name forward for board positions. I have tried this for voluntary positions and positions that come with a small stipend. But I’ve now made over 100 applications and I cannot even crack an interview. What would you suggest for someone in my position? If previous board experience is the deciding credential, where is someone supposed to get their first seat? John Shakespeare One hundred applications and no interviews is a story I’m now painfully familiar with. It’s fascinating, and frankly dispiriting, to know that it’s happening with board positions as well as in standard employment. I spoke with Dr Hongbo Guo, who’s a lecturer in management at the University of Canberra, and he said one possible reason for the paucity of interviews, perhaps ironically for such an accomplished practitioner, is a lack of experience.



“A survey circulated by the Australian Institute of Company Directors (AICD) last year found that about two-thirds of directors reported having seven or more years of board experience. That made me wonder how boards assess people coming from outside the boardroom,” Guo said. “If previous board experience is the deciding credential, where is someone supposed to get their first seat?” To put it another way, you may be stuck in a vicious circle, one acknowledged by the AICD, which suggests that “the most difficult paid board role to get is usually the first one you seek”. There’s some good advice in the article from which I’ve taken this quote, including an option you may not have considered: looking at directorships outside corporate IT, specifically in the not-for-profit sector. Although it’s not a blanket rule by any means, not-for-profits and charities can have less competition for board roles and are often considered a starting point for those seeking to contribute as a director.



An NFP board position might allow you to determine whether it’s indeed a form of volunteering you enjoy, while also helping you develop (or build on) skills and knowledge in areas like governance and strategy, which translate across all board roles. Editor's pick Opinion

Jobs These seven jobs don’t exist. By 2050, they’ll have millions of workers Tim Duggan Work columnist Another option comes from Guo, who wonders whether your alumni network might be the best place to seek advice on why you’ve been unsuccessful so far. “I’d go back to the alumni network and ask for an introduction to someone who has actually shortlisted directors. Show them an application and ask something like ‘What would you have needed to see to put me on the shortlist?’” If, after all of this, you keep confronting only barriers in your search for a board position of any kind, it might be worth considering what other voluntary roles you might find rewarding.



“I keep thinking about the reader’s decision to go back and study IT while getting ready to retire after spending a whole career in the field,” Guo said. “What’s interesting to me is that they are looking for somewhere they can use what they already know and still have something to learn. In other words, there are parts of the work they’re still curious about and would happily keep doing. I’d start here.” Guo said he was curious to know what part of the work you’ll miss most in retirement. Will it be helping a junior colleague work through a problem? Explaining a messy system? Stopping an organisation from spending money on the wrong thing? He said that this self-analysis might help you find voluntary work outside a boardroom that is both challenging and gratifying. “Work psychologists call the desire to pass on what we know as a way of helping others develop ‘generativity’,” Guo explained. It’s been described by researchers as an inclination to use your experience to “benefit future generations”, which sounds very much like the “giving back” you talked about in your email. And if you find such volunteering opportunities aren’t available in the IT sector itself, perhaps education is an alternative.



“As the reader had just finished a degree, I would suggest getting in touch with someone who taught them during their master’s and offering one specific contribution. For example, mentor a student project team or run guest sessions on an IT decision they’ve had to make,” Guo says. “Decades of experience can be useful to someone in academia even if all they need from you is an hour.” Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.content:
PoliticsFederalGas Labor refuses to say how much bills will fall under new gas reservation scheme Brittany Busch November 27, 2026 — 10:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Australians will have to wait to find out how much cheaper their gas bills could be under the domestic gas reservation scheme, after Resources Minister Madeleine King declined to set a target price. The country’s biggest gas companies will have to keep up to 20 per cent of supply for the domestic market after the laws passed the House of Representatives on Friday morning, after the Coalition waived the measure through the Senate late on Thursday night. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor made no apologies for siding with consumers. Dominic Lorrimer King said Labor would not set a price when asked what the government considered affordable. “We don’t want that figure to then become the floor, which is what happens with a cap,” she told ABC Radio National.



The government is avoiding setting a target after vowing ahead of the 2022 election that energy bills would be $275 cheaper under Labor, only for prices to continue to rise. Related Article Updated

Energy Gas exporters to be forced to prevent Australian shortfalls under new laws “Australians rightly expect that our resources should serve the national interest, and that Australian users should have access to the gas they need at an affordable price,” King told the chamber as the laws cleared their final parliamentary hurdle. “This reform means more Australian gas for Australian users and downward pressure on prices. It means greater certainty for manufacturers to invest, remain competitive and employ Australians.” Opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan proposed last-minute changes to boost transparency over the advice the regulator provided to the minister – doomed to fail because the opposition does not have the numbers in the lower house – and said the Coalition remained concerned the scheme could discourage investment.



“If you tank the gas sector in Australia, you will get short-term political gain, but you will get long-term political pain for this nation,” Tehan told the chamber. “We want to make sure that we’re going to get future investment in this nation.” The Coalition’s energy spokesman, Dan Tehan, speaking in the House of Representatives on Friday morning. Dominic Lorrimer He said the Coalition was worried the scheme would work for a couple of years, but eventually kill the Australian gas sector. “Even the prime minister has said we need gas for revenue, and we need gas to remain a trusted trading partner with key allies in the Indo-Pacific region.”



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Labor made no apologies “for siding with Australian households and Australian manufacturers rather than producer profits”. Related Article Energy Can Australia dodge the next Iran oil shock? “We must remember what the objective of this legislation is. It is about making sure that Australians get the benefit of the resource that is ours, that is owned by Australians,” he said, adding that the latest Australian Bureau of Statistics investment figures showed explorations development at a 10-year high. Retaining a modest oversupply of gas in Australia is designed to put downward pressure on prices and better insulate the country against global price shocks. Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie said the Coalition had been able to secure enough concessions to support the scheme, including a review into how the reservation would affect investment and a carve-out for Western Australia.



“We took a gas reservation policy to the last election, so at a principled level, we absolutely believe that Australian gas should be there to be used and support Australian households and businesses,” she told Radio National. “When you talk to industry, they are concerned. I think also realising that Labor doesn’t have a great track record when it comes to energy and gas policy – I mean we’ve seen energy prices go up 40 per cent.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Looking for something truly different to a typical sand and surf getaway this summer? Head south and discover the beauty of Australia’s southernmost capital city, Hobart. Not to mention the wonderful diversity of Melbourne, our second largest city, perched on Port Phillip Bay, north of Bass Strait, which separates mainland Australia from Tasmania. Given there are multiple daily direct flights of around an hour and 20 minutes between the cities, it could not be easier to experience both Hobart and Melbourne in one holiday. Both destinations punch well above their weight when it comes to cultural attractions and dining opportunities. Plus, Melbourne is a sports lover’s paradise over summer, hosting the Australian Open tennis grand slam, the Boxing Day Test in cricket and A-League Men and Women’s football. Art and culture lovers can anticipate a broad spectrum of galleries and precincts, including the world famous must-see National Gallery of Victoria (NGV) in Melbourne, and Hobart’s incredibly quirky and fun Museum of Old and New Art (MONA). Spend even a few nights in each city, and you’ll quickly fall in love with the lively shopping scene full of singular boutiques, plus the buzzing little streets and laneways filled with wine bars, specialty coffee shops and alfresco dining focused around fresh regional produce, including local seafood.



These charming cities both score highly on walkability and vibe. And both feature landmark historic and contemporary architecture, layered with a creative, European-influenced character that feels very different from the country’s northern capitals.

World.title: Chalmers’ electorate facing some of the highest unemployment rates nationally
World.content:
NationalQueenslandJobs Chalmers’ electorate facing some of the highest unemployment rates nationally Shane Wright November 27, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Workers in Treasurer Jim Chalmers’ home electorate are facing some of the highest unemployment rates in the country as higher interest rates and inflation combine to weaken the jobs market and squeeze family budgets. Even as evidence grows that the AI data construction boom is approaching levels not seen since the mining boom of the early 2010s, figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics show suburbs such as Springwood, Kingston and Browns Plains have soared beyond 8 per cent or are approaching it. The national unemployment rate reached 4.9 per cent in October, with the country shedding almost 80,000 jobs over the past two months. Despite inflation hitting 4.9 per cent, financial markets believe the Reserve Bank will start cutting interest rates from August to support the rapidly softening jobs market.



This week, Chalmers said his mid-year budget update would reveal Treasury expects unemployment is likely to climb above 5 per cent in 2027. The combination of high unemployment and inflation has sharply lifted pressure on Chalmers to unveil spending cuts in next month’s budget update. The federal opposition is demanding the treasurer be sacked. Rankin stretches from the Brisbane suburbs of Algester and Calamvale into northern parts of Logan, such as Slacks Creek (pictured). Markus Ravik The regional unemployment figures from the bureau highlight that parts of the country are already dealing with job losses before the full impact of the Reserve Bank’s most recent rate increases filter through the economy. The highest unemployment rate is in Chalmers’ seat of Rankin, hitting 8.7 per cent in the suburbs of Springwood and Kingston. A year ago, the jobless rate in these areas was 7 per cent.



In nearby Browns Plains, the jobless rate has lifted from 6.3 per cent last October to 7.7 per cent this year. Related Article Analysis

Australian economy Chalmers cannot spin a silver lining out of this grim story Unemployment is also rising quickly in other parts of Queensland, including Ipswich, Caboolture, the state’s far west and Maryborough. The western suburbs of both Sydney and Melbourne are exposed most to the sharp lift in interest rates and inflation. High petrol prices, which have climbed by more than a third since the start of the war against Iran, have delivered particular financial pain. Women are paying the highest price for the unemployment increase. Across Melbourne’s western suburbs, the female jobless rate has climbed from 5.8 per cent to 7.8 per cent. Among men, it has risen from 6 per cent to 6.6 per cent.



The increase in unemployment is occurring despite one of the nation’s largest construction booms. Bureau of Statistics figures released on Thursday showed private spending on new buildings and equipment jumped by 18.6 per cent over the past year. It reached $59.7 billion in the September quarter, the highest level since 2014. In the September quarter alone, capital spending jumped by 12.2 per cent due largely to a 23.1 per cent jump in spending on new equipment and machinery such as computer servers for data centres. It was the single largest quarterly increase since the early stages of last decade’s mining boom. And businesses are not showing signs of plans to slow down. Expected spending was lifted by 11.8 per cent to a record $223 billion through 2026-27.



NSW and Victoria are attracting the most AI investment, with spending in both lifting by more than a third over the past 12 months. Chalmers described the figures as “absolutely stunning”, saying they confirmed that capital spending by the private sector was “booming”. But under pressure from the Coalition over the state of the jobs market, the treasurer admitted the situation was poor. “When it comes to the tick-up in unemployment, we have acknowledged that for those Australians who are impacted, then that is very bad development,” he told parliament.



AMP economist My Bui said the investment boom in AI-related technology had grown on average by 46 per cent a year since 2001. Related Article Inflation Stagflation fears grip Canberra as inflation, unemployment surge She said private business investment remained strong despite the lift in interest rates, although that situation could change. “The outlook for next year will be tougher though, as higher cash rates and bond yields will make it harder for firms to finance their capex plans and the productivity gains from AI are yet to arrive.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Liberal senator Dave Sharma says he is not sure what Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen is actually doing for everyday Australians and the climate after COP31 talks led by the minister collapsed in Turkey last week.

“We’ve got a situation in Australia where we’ve got higher electricity prices. You know, they’re up about 25 per cent over the last year, according to the latest inflation figures. Despite Chris Bowen and Anthony Albanese promising they will be lower,” he told the Today show.

Senator Dave Sharma. Alex Ellinghausen

“But we also don’t have them meeting their emissions targets. And we have him spending most of last year overseas presiding over this failure of a diplomatic negotiation. So you have to ask yourself, what is Chris Bowen actually doing right here?”

World.title: ‘Scary’: Why a World Cup-winning coach wants Mark and Semi in the same Fiji back line
World.content:
SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘Scary’: Why a World Cup-winning coach wants Mark and Semi in the same Fiji back line Iain Payten November 27, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. World Cup-winning coach Jake White has laid out his strong desire to recruit Mark Nawaqanitawase for Fiji, and says he’d be happy to add the Australian dual international to his squad on the eve of the World Cup next year, without having played a game in the white jersey. After starring for the Roosters in their NRL premiership win, Nawaqanitawase returned to rugby in Japan and caused a stir in October when he revealed he was considering switching allegiances and playing Test rugby for either Fiji or Italy. Loading The 26-year-old played 11 Tests for the Wallabies and sevens for Australia at the Paris Olympics, but also has Fijian and Italian heritage. Under World Rugby rules, Nawaqanitawase can play for either of those nations after serving a three-year stand-down, which will expire on July 31. Wallabies coach Les Kiss has spoken with Nawaqanitawase and is hopeful he will return to the gold jersey for the World Cup in Australia next year, but he’s not alone.



White, who coached the 2007 Springboks to a World Cup win and recently took over as coach of Fiji, said he was very keen to snare Nawaqanitawase, saying a back line featuring the ex-Rooster, and Fijian stars Semi Radradra, Kalaveti Ravouvou and Jiuta Wainiqolo, would be “scary”. “Everyone would want to use him and I would never say no to a guy like him,” White said in London ahead of Fiji’s final match against Italy in the Nations Championship at Twickenham on Saturday morning (AEDT). “Obviously, I knew who he was. I knew he played for the Wallabies and I watched him with interest when I was watching rugby long, before I got involved with Fiji. Semi Radradra did a jersey swap with Mark Nawaqanitawase at the 2023 Rugby World Cup. World Rugby via Getty Images “Then I saw his code swap and how successful he was at rugby league. When I joined Fiji, then a lot of talk came about, “Hey, do you know that he’s Fijian? And there’s a lot of talk in Australia he could be eligible, etcetera?



“Obviously, you’d grab a guy like that, anybody who sees a guy play like that (would). He’s a real winner. “He could add value to the Fijian group we have. If you look at Semi Radradra and Kalaveti Ravouvou and Jiuta (Wainiqolo) and those guys, putting him in amongst those outside backs would be scary. “I suppose, just like Les, my answer to you is, s**t, we’d love to take him. And I’m sure when he makes his decision, whoever gets him will be really happy. And whoever doesn’t get him will be disappointed.” Mark Nawaqanitawase scores in the NRL grand final against Newcastle. Getty Images Italy appears not to be in the mix, having said they were unaware of his eligibility until recently.



The potential hurdle for Nawaqanitawase playing for Fiji at next year’s World Cup is that his eligibility switch only becomes possible in August, three years after he lost in the bronze medal game for Australia at the Olympics. The Wallabies will have already started playing in the Rugby Championship in July. But Fiji’s only scheduled game ahead of the World Cup, so far, is against South Africa on September 18 in Gosford. Negotiations are underway about staging a Pacific Nations Cup, involving Fiji, Tonga, Samoa and Australia A, in July in Suva. But it is unclear if that tournament will still be going after Nawaqanitawase becomes eligible on July 31, and before September 13, when all teams have to submit their final World Cup squads. Jake White was recently appointed head coach of Fiji. Getty Images But White said he would not be open to bringing Nawaqanitawase into the squad in August, based on Japanese club form.



“Once we’re in camp in August-September, he’s a talented player, he’s not going to take six weeks to adapt,” White said. “And he’s playing rugby anyway. It’s not like he’s coming from nowhere. He’s playing rugby in Japan in a good club. So yeah, I would let him come in August.” Whether that extends to being picked in Fiji’s 33-man World Cup squad is unclear, however, and it could prove a key distinction for Nawaqanitawase, given he would also likely get a call for Wallabies duty in July. Related Article Wallabies Big in Japan: Nawaqanitawase impressing new teammates in first week White said he had not spoken with Nawaqanitawase or his representatives, and he believed if the flyer made the switch to Fiji, it wouldn’t be just to play in the 2027 Rugby World Cup. “I’d love to have him earlier rather than later, but if it means he joins in August and stays with Fiji for four more years and plays the next World Cup (in 2031), well, that’s also a bonus, isn’t it?” he said.



The former Boks and Brumbies coach is also looking to help Fiji by standing up to clubs that White claims are pressuring his players to prioritise club over country. “I’ve used my influence in World Rugby to put pressure on people that have been abusing the Fijian players,” White said. “So much so that I’ve written a letter in this tour as well to say to World Rugby, listen, I can’t have players getting text messages from coaches and directors of rugby saying, ‘Can you ask your coach if I can release you this weekend because we’re playing 11th and 12th?’ There’s no other player (from other countries) that have been asked by his club to go back... and they’re at the same club.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Friday.

World.title: When Olivia said she wanted to be an actor, her teacher laughed. Now, she’s a movie star
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Olivia Hargroder is accustomed to being underestimated. When she was born in 1999, with Down syndrome and a hole in her heart, doctors gave her a 20 per cent chance of surviving the operation she underwent at nine weeks. Specialists predicted she’d struggle to walk, talk or maintain a regular job. When Hargroder declared her wish to study acting at NIDA, her school careers counsellor laughed. The famed institution, the teacher told her, was for “the elite”. In the ensuing years, Hargroder proved them all wrong. The 27-year-old, who was one of the subjects of the ABC series Better Date Than Never, has worked at a local supermarket for almost nine years. She sings, dances and loves cracking jokes during conversations. Not only did she graduate from NIDA’s Young Actors Studio; she scored the lead role in Boss Cat, a feature-length Australian movie. Made by Bus Stop Films – a not-for-profit global leader in inclusive filmmaking – it stars Hargroder as Sonja, a young woman whose mother has just died. When her estranged grandmother tries to force her into a group home, Sonja channels her explosive temper into something more positive: a high-energy dance style known as krumping. “If you dream and believe, you can achieve anything,” says Hargroder, speaking via Zoom alongside her mother, Kerry Read, whom she tearfully describes as “non-stop supportive of me”. Worst habit? Dancing wherever I go. I work at Coles and I got into trouble for dancing to Coles Radio. [It’s worth noting that her boss has praised her work ethic and the “good vibes” she creates in the store.] You cannot stop me from dancing; from connecting with that feeling, that song, and telling a story. That’s something that connected me to Sonja, because she has the same dream I do: becoming a professional dancer. She dances to process difficult emotions and so do I, but not so aggressively. When Sonja gets angry, she dances at people whereas I dance with them.



Greatest fear? Being typecast as a person with Down syndrome. I worry that people won’t see that I’m an actor and that was a part [in Boss Cat]. If there’s a character that doesn’t have Down syndrome, I don’t want people to think someone with Down syndrome can’t play that role. It should be open to everyone. The line that stayed with you? “I have really good aim.” It’s one of my lines from Boss Cat, and I had a lot of fun playing around with it. (“It’s also because people underestimate you,” Read adds, “and you actually do have very good aim!”) ‘I got into trouble for dancing to Coles Radio; you cannot stop me from dancing.’ Biggest regret? Sometimes, when things don’t work out, another opportunity comes along – so why bother having regrets? I do get sad but then I pull myself up and go, “You know what? I’m going to move on.” I auditioned for the movie Reminders of Him. I was really excited about that, and then they switched the filming dates for Boss Cat and I couldn’t be available. I was a bit upset but then I filmed Boss Cat and had the time of my life.



Tell us about your turning point. The two operations on my knees [in 2015 and 2016]. I had hypermobility in both of my knees; every time I would start to walk, I would fall over and break a bone. The one sport I could do was swimming because I couldn’t fall over in the water. I went to a regular high school and I couldn’t light a bunsen burner or do cookery classes; I couldn’t stand at a bench and chop something. I couldn’t even dance safely – it affected all areas of my life. When I had the operation on my first knee, I couldn’t believe how many things I could do: I could run, I could jump, I could dance, I could literally do anything. The surgeon told me I had to wait a year for the second operation. He gave me a list of rehab exercises to achieve and I absolutely smashed it. It was very tough but I got through it. The surgeon thought I’d have to wait a year for the second operation but he was very impressed and did the second knee [sooner than planned]. I would love to thank my surgeon because if it wasn’t for him, I wouldn’t have these amazing knees that can do absolutely everything. Hargroder dancing up a storm in Boss Cat. Lisa Tomasetti The artwork or song you wish was yours? Shake it Off by Taylor Swift. You might get a negative comment in your life and then that song will remind you to just be yourself. I went to Taylor Swift’s concert and it was absolutely incredible. I would love to go on tour with Taylor Swift as a dancer one day. That’s been a dream of mine for such a long time.

World.title: ASX set for gains, global stocks rise; Oil prices climb
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set for gains, global stocks rise; Oil prices climb Andre Janse van Vuuren and Rivaldo Jantjies November 27, 2026 — 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Stocks rose as investors in Europe took their cue from a comeback in technology shares on Wall Street after days of sharp swings. Europe’s Stoxx 600 rallied 1.7 per cent. A gauge of Asian stocks climbed 0.9 per cent, only its second daily advance in 11 sessions. The gains followed late-session dip buying in the US that pulled the Nasdaq 100 back from the brink of a bear market. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.7 per cent on Thursday, with Wall Street closed for trade due to the Thanksgiving holiday. AI stocks boosted global indexes overnight. Reuters The Australian sharemarket is set to advance, with futures pointing to a gain of 12 points or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.8 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was steady at US66.32¢. Technology shares led gains in many markets. Memory giants SK Hynix and Kioxia Holdings outperformed in Asia. Taiwan and South Korea’s technology-focused benchmarks rose more than 2 per cent. While Europe’s rally was led by auto and mining stocks, the region’s technology sector climbed more than 2 per cent.



The return of buyers to the artificial intelligence trade offers an encouraging sign after a bruising November. Markets have whipsawed since the US midterms, with a leadership crisis at Nvidia deepening a selloff that pushed major gauges into corrections. “AI capex remains intact, financing is still readily available and pricing power is exceptional,” said Marija Veitmane at State Street Global Markets. “Sentiment cracked, fundamentals didn’t. With tech valuations looking increasingly attractive, the selloff may be starting to create its own reversal.” Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Trump strikes again even as America feels the pain Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist The improvement in risk appetite was also evident in copper, with the metal advancing 1.7 per cent from an 11-month low. Brent crude topped $US96 a barrel for the first time in more than a week as an attack on Saudi refinery threatened to undermine a recovery in the region’s crude exports. It has risen almost 6 per cent over the previous two sessions. Tehran-backed Houthi rebels attacked the 400,000 barrel a day Jazan refinery on the Red Sea coast of Saudi Arabia, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said in a post on X. European bonds fell on waning demand for havens. Meanwhile, Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become European Central Bank president when Christine Lagarde leaves in February.



For Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum, caution remains warranted for stocks, especially because there was no clear catalyst for the tech rebound. The likelihood of a US interest rate hike next month threatens to push the cost of capital even higher, adding to headwinds for the AI trade. “It’s a real mystery why dip buyers emerged,” he said. “Friday will be the real test if the recovery has staying power.” It’s not yet time for investors to make directional bets, said Nadege Dufosse, head of multi-asset at Candriam. She is looking to credit markets for signals on whether stress in stocks is becoming more serious. “The credit market has held so far, so that’s a good sign,” she said. “As long as the economy and earnings hold and the Fed stops raising rates next year, I think equities can make some gains.” Another notable mover was Imperial Brands, which jumped 13.3 per cent after US tobacco group Altria said it was considering a possible all-cash offer for the UK-based company.



Altria also said that it was in talks with another party over part of the British company’s business, as Japan Tobacco also was reported to be weighing a bid. Related Article Opinion

RBA There’s a number the RBA has been hiding. Here’s why Millie Muroi Economics Writer Among underperformers, Commerzbank lost 2.6 per cent after Italy’s UniCredit said it planned a management shake-up at the German bank. BAWAG dropped 5.7 per cent after Ireland’s High Court refused to sanction the company’s proposed €1.62 billion ($2.7 billion) acquisition of Permanent TSB. World.title: I’ve applied for 100 board roles with no interviews. How do I break in?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion I’ve applied for 100 board roles with no interviews. How do I break in? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor November 27, 2026 — 5:01am

November 27, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I am in my 60s and looking forward to retirement. I have worked my career in IT and just completed my masterʼs degree in a related field. I am looking for options in retirement to give something back. Recently, I attended a lecture through my alumni network about putting my name forward for board positions. I have tried this for voluntary positions and positions that come with a small stipend. But I’ve now made over 100 applications and I cannot even crack an interview. What would you suggest for someone in my position? If previous board experience is the deciding credential, where is someone supposed to get their first seat? John Shakespeare One hundred applications and no interviews is a story I’m now painfully familiar with. It’s fascinating, and frankly dispiriting, to know that it’s happening with board positions as well as in standard employment. I spoke with Dr Hongbo Guo, who’s a lecturer in management at the University of Canberra, and he said one possible reason for the paucity of interviews, perhaps ironically for such an accomplished practitioner, is a lack of experience.



“A survey circulated by the Australian Institute of Company Directors (AICD) last year found that about two-thirds of directors reported having seven or more years of board experience. That made me wonder how boards assess people coming from outside the boardroom,” Guo said. “If previous board experience is the deciding credential, where is someone supposed to get their first seat?” To put it another way, you may be stuck in a vicious circle, one acknowledged by the AICD, which suggests that “the most difficult paid board role to get is usually the first one you seek”. There’s some good advice in the article from which I’ve taken this quote, including an option you may not have considered: looking at directorships outside corporate IT, specifically in the not-for-profit sector. Although it’s not a blanket rule by any means, not-for-profits and charities can have less competition for board roles and are often considered a starting point for those seeking to contribute as a director.



An NFP board position might allow you to determine whether it’s indeed a form of volunteering you enjoy, while also helping you develop (or build on) skills and knowledge in areas like governance and strategy, which translate across all board roles. Editor's pick Opinion

Jobs These seven jobs don’t exist. By 2050, they’ll have millions of workers Tim Duggan Work columnist Another option comes from Guo, who wonders whether your alumni network might be the best place to seek advice on why you’ve been unsuccessful so far. “I’d go back to the alumni network and ask for an introduction to someone who has actually shortlisted directors. Show them an application and ask something like ‘What would you have needed to see to put me on the shortlist?’” If, after all of this, you keep confronting only barriers in your search for a board position of any kind, it might be worth considering what other voluntary roles you might find rewarding.



“I keep thinking about the reader’s decision to go back and study IT while getting ready to retire after spending a whole career in the field,” Guo said. “What’s interesting to me is that they are looking for somewhere they can use what they already know and still have something to learn. In other words, there are parts of the work they’re still curious about and would happily keep doing. I’d start here.” Guo said he was curious to know what part of the work you’ll miss most in retirement. Will it be helping a junior colleague work through a problem? Explaining a messy system? Stopping an organisation from spending money on the wrong thing? He said that this self-analysis might help you find voluntary work outside a boardroom that is both challenging and gratifying. “Work psychologists call the desire to pass on what we know as a way of helping others develop ‘generativity’,” Guo explained. It’s been described by researchers as an inclination to use your experience to “benefit future generations”, which sounds very much like the “giving back” you talked about in your email. And if you find such volunteering opportunities aren’t available in the IT sector itself, perhaps education is an alternative.



“As the reader had just finished a degree, I would suggest getting in touch with someone who taught them during their master’s and offering one specific contribution. For example, mentor a student project team or run guest sessions on an IT decision they’ve had to make,” Guo says. “Decades of experience can be useful to someone in academia even if all they need from you is an hour.” Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: USP appoints Solomon Islands' Transform Aqorau as next vice-chancellor
World.content:
Solomon Islands' Professor Transform Aqorau has been appointed as the next The University of the South Pacific (USP) vice-chancellor and president.

The USP Council, the regional university's main decision-making body, endorsed Prof Aqorau at its 102nd meeting in Apia, Samoa, the university said in a statement on Thursday.

Prof Aqorau is currently the vice-chancellor of the Solomon Islands National University based in Honiara.

His career spans higher education, international law, fisheries governance and senior leadership roles in Pacific regional organisations.

"Professor Aqorau brings a deep understanding of our region, a proven ability to bring Pacific countries together in pursuit of shared aspirations, and a strong appreciation of the University's unique mission," USP's pro-chancellor and council chair Siosiua 'Utoikamanu said.

He said the USP Council was confident in his ability to build on the university's recent progress and lead USP into the next chapter of its history.

Prof Aqorau will become the 10th vice-chancellor of USP, replacing Professor Pal Ahluwalia, who ended his term in September last year.

He is set to become USP's permanent leader once contractual arrangements are finalised, the USP statement said.

'A proud moment' - Prime Minister Wale

Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale said Prof Aqorau's appointment showed the high regard in which he is held across the region, "and the confidence our Pacific family places in Solomon Islanders to lead at the highest levels".

"This is a proud moment for Solomon Islands," Wale said in a statement.

Wale said while Prof Aqorau's depparture from SINU would be a "real loss", it was also "a gain for Solomon Islands and the region".

The prime minister said his government looked forward to working closely with Prof Aqorau in his new role.

"We remain committed to supporting USP and to strengthening its partnership with Solomon Islands as a member country," he added.

World.title: Poisonous invasive cane toad 'size of a guinea pig' captured in Tauranga
World.content:
A poisonous toad spotted in Tauranga has been caught and will be killed.

On Tuesday November 24, volunteer firefighter Annie Henley filmed an exotic cane toad, the size of a guinea pig, while at a night-time training session by the Tauranga Model Powerboat Club in Tauriko.

The video was reported to Biosecurity NZ.

Biosecurity's acting surveillance and incursion manager, Kelly McKenzie, confirmed they successfully caught the single male adult cane toad near a small lake in Tauriko during a ground search on Thursday night.

The incursion investigator capturing the cane toad on Thursday night. MPI / SUPPLIED

"We have checked the area thoroughly, and there were no signs of any further cane toads. We therefore believe it was a single hitchhiker.

"Cane toads can occasionally arrive here as single hitchhikers, most commonly from Australia. Cane toads aren't established here, possibly due to our cooler climate. The risk to the public is low, provided people avoid handling the toad and wash thoroughly after any contact."
